title: Loca Tychonis — every place in Tycho Brahe's life, from Knutstorp to the Týn church

periods.label: Childhood in Scania and Zealand
periods.description: From his birth at Knutstorp on 14 December 1546 to his dispatch to the University of Copenhagen in April 1559, Tycho's childhood was shaped by his abduction, aged about one, by his childless paternal uncle Jørgen Brahe, who with his wife Inger Oxe raised the boy at his ancestral seat of Tostrup in eastern Scania and at the royal castles he successively commanded — Næsbyhoved on Funen, Vordingborg on Zealand, Nykøbing on Falster. Latin instruction began about his seventh year; whether it came from a private tutor in the uncle's house or at a grammar school (Vordingborg is only a modern presumption) is unresolved, and is the period's one genuinely soft spot.

periods.label: Student at Copenhagen
periods.description: Tycho's first university period: nearly three years at the University of Copenhagen, from his arrival on 19 April 1559, aged twelve, to his departure for Leipzig on 14 February 1562. Sent by his uncle and foster-father Jørgen Brahe to read rhetoric and philosophy towards a career in law and statecraft, he followed the Melanchthonian curriculum while quietly assembling his first astronomical library — Sacrobosco, the Basel 1551 Ptolemy, Apian, Regiomontanus, the ephemerides of Carelli and Stadius. The famous story that the predicted solar eclipse of 21 August 1560 awakened his vocation is Gassendi's tradition, rejected by Norlind; the book purchases are the documented fact. Danish dates are Julian throughout.

periods.label: Leipzig with Vedel
periods.description: The first foreign study tour: three years at Leipzig university, nominally at Germany's best law school under the governorship of Anders Sørensen Vedel, in fact the clandestine beginning of Tycho's observational astronomy. The Saturn–Jupiter conjunction of August 1563 exposed the errors of every planetary table; compasses gave way from 1 May 1564 to a transversal-divided cross-staff, his first serious instrument. The Leipzig circle — Scultetus, Homelius, Camerarius, Valentin Thau — supplied his first instrument-craft and court-astrology contacts. Framed by the outward journey via Wittenberg (February–March 1562) and the return to Denmark in May 1565.

periods.label: The Wanderjahre
periods.description: The Wanderjahre carry Tycho from the wartime homecoming of May 1565, through Jørgen Brahe's death, across the second and third study journeys: Wittenberg (April–September 1566, cut short by plague), Rostock (the duel of 29 December 1566 that cost him the bridge of his nose), the 1567 interlude at home, the second Rostock residence of 1568 with the Roskilde canonry promise, matriculation at Basel in autumn 1568, and the fourteen Augsburg months (April 1569 – May 1570) that produced the Quadrans Maximus at Göggingen, the first sextant and the great globe commission. The Textor album leaf (Wittenberg, 9 September 1570) and the Helsingborg observation of 30 December 1570 fix the previously obscure homeward route to his father's deathbed.

periods.label: Herrevad, the nova, the lectures, the grand tour
periods.description: Otte Brahe's death at Helsingborg in May 1571 made Tycho a Scanian landowner; he divided the early 1570s between Knutstorp, his uncle Steen Bille's proto-industrial Herrevad Abbey, and Copenhagen. At Herrevad on 11 November 1572 he saw the new star in Cassiopeia, published as De nova stella (1573) — his first book, though not his first publication. He formed his lifelong union with Kirsten Jørgensdatter, lectured at the University of Copenhagen from 23 September 1574, and in 1575 made the grand tour — Kassel, Frankfurt, Basel, Venice, Augsburg, Regensburg (Rudolf II's coronation, 1 November), Saalfeld, Wittenberg — privately resolving to emigrate to Basel before reporting to Frederick II at Sorø at Yuletide.

periods.label: The lord of Hven
periods.description: Between the pre-dawn royal summons of 11 February 1576 and the coronation autumn of 1596, Tycho held the island of Hven as a lifetime fief and built there Uraniborg, Stjerneborg, the laboratory, printing office and paper mill. The grant sequence ran Ibstrup (11 February), Frederiksborg (18 February), first landing on Hven (22 February), the formal enfeoffment (23 May) and the foundation stone (8 August 1576). The continuous residence is one anchor stay; around it cluster the documented off-island trips — Copenhagen herredage, lawsuits and marriage negotiations, homage at Lund, weddings at Ribe and Bygholm, comet work at Helsingborg — until Christian IV's coronation opened the withdrawal of favour.

periods.label: The departure and exile
periods.description: The collapse and departure: the last Hven observation on 15 March 1597, the removal of the whole establishment to the Farvergade house in Copenhagen, the 2 June sailing into exile, the summer at Rostock, and the year as Rantzau's guest at Wandsbek, where the Mechanica was printed and the Elegia ad Daniam written. Then the interrupted first push toward Prague — Harburg, Magdeburg, a month at Dresden turned back by plague — and the Wittenberg winter in the Jessenius house until 14 June 1599. The itinerary's densest run of dated autographs and its hardest route reconciliations fall in these two years.

periods.label: Bohemia
periods.description: Summoned by Rudolf II, Tycho left Wittenberg on 14 June 1599 and travelled via Pretzsch and Dresden to Prague, where a wholly private imperial audience made him court astronomer at 3,000 gulden a year. Choosing Benátky nad Jizerou over Brandeis and Lysá, he built his last observatory there from August 1599, received Kepler in February 1600, and fled plague to Girsitz over the winter. Recalled to Prague in June 1600, he lodged at the Golden Griffin, set his twenty-eight instruments up at the Belvedere, and moved into the Curtius house in February 1601. The Rožmberk banquet of 13 October 1601 began the fatal illness; he died on 24 October and was buried in the Týn Church on 4 November.

stays.calendar_note: All dates Old Style (Julian); Denmark kept the Julian calendar until 1700. Tycho himself sometimes wrote 13 December, counting the astronomical day from noon.
stays.narrative: Tycho Brahe was born at his family's ancestral seat of Knutstorp in Scania on 14 December 1546, between nine and ten in the morning by his father Otte Brahe's own memorandum; the Stephanius notes, copied from Tycho's lost self-horoscope, give 10:47 a.m. The firstborn of twins — his brother was stillborn, later the subject of his first publication (1572) — he was baptised Tyge after his paternal grandfather, Latinising the name at university. Norlind and Thoren place the birth in the medieval manor that preceded the moated brick castle Otte built from 1551. He remained with his parents Otte Brahe and Beate Bille only until about mid-1548, when, after the birth of his brother Steen (21 December 1547), his childless uncle Jørgen Brahe carried him off, 'without the knowledge of my parents', to raise as his own. Knutstorp remained his lifelong territorial designation.

stays.disputes: Birth date: Gassendi canvasses 13/14/15/19 December 1546; Norlind pp. 11–12 rejects Gassendi's 19 Dec (mis-derived Tuesday) and Jessenius' funeral-oration 15 Dec — 14 December o.s., fixed by Otte Brahe's memorandum, followed (unanimous modern). Hour: the memorandum has 'between 9 and 10'; the Stephanius horoscope notes and Gassendi have 10:47 a.m. — both recorded, not harmonised. Abduction timing: Thoren has mid-1548 (middle of the second year, after Steen was past infancy dangers); Christianson 2020, Friis and Jönsson link it to after Steen's birth at about age one; Norlind commits only to 'before his seventh year' — c. 1548 followed (Thoren/Christianson). Birth building: Norlind and Thoren argue the medieval manor, not the 1551 castle of the later tradition.

stays.narrative: The fostered boyhood was based at Jørgen Brahe's ancestral seat of Tostrup in eastern Scania, where the childless Jørgen and Inger Oxe raised him as their only charge, with visits to Knutstorp to see his birth parents. From about his seventh year (c. 1553) he was put to Latin and the rudiments of learning — Dreyer and Friis with a private tutor (Hovmester) in the uncle's house, five years of schooling above all in Latin, in which he was soon writing letters and verse. Against the Brahe military tradition, Jørgen intended him for learned studies and a chancery career, and paid for his education until age eighteen. Friis, Norlind and Jönsson all hedge the Tostrup placement as inference from Jørgen's fief-holding; Thoren states it plainly. The stay, interleaved with residence at Jørgen's successive royal fiefs, closed when the boy was sent to the University of Copenhagen in April 1559.

The schooling is a second soft spot: Dreyer and Friis have a private tutor in the uncle's house; Norlind doubts a formal cathedral Latin school altogether ('mycket ovisst'); the school is never identified in any source (see the Vordingborg stay for the 'formodentlig' school conjecture).

The boy's presence is an inference from the structure of the foster household, not a documented sighting, and no other swept source places him there; the stay is graded accordingly.

stays.narrative: Jørgen Brahe received command of the immense medieval royal stronghold of Vordingborg on the south coast of Zealand in 1552, and Tycho passed part of his boyhood in the sprawling castle — Christianson recalls the connection when the 1597 exile caravan passed through the town. Vordingborg sat on the main route between Copenhagen and the continent: Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg came with his court in 1556, Christian III's peripatetic court stayed periodically, and Brahe, Oxe and Rud kin visited regularly — the boy's first exposure to high court traffic. The school question stays open: his autobiography has him at Latin school 'in his seventh year', and the Nationalmuseet education essay presumes ('formodentlig') Vordingborg Latin school because Jørgen was then lensmand there, but Facts of Life (1970) is silent on schooling before 1559, Dreyer and Friis have a private tutor at Tostrup instead, and Norlind doubts a formal school altogether. No school is asserted.

Held as C-grade conjecture inside a B-grade residence.

stays.narrative: Queen Mother Sophie had invested Jørgen Brahe with the fief and command of Nykøbing in 1555, and in 1557, having relinquished his royal fief in the power struggle that preceded Peder Oxe's fall, Jørgen transferred his seat to the island fortress between Lolland and Falster. On Thoren's 'presumably followed' reading of the foster household, the ten-to-twelve-year-old Tycho lived there until he was sent to Copenhagen in April 1559. Christianson notes that Jørgen also commanded Nykøbing but attaches Tycho's boyhood residence only to Vordingborg; the stay is therefore single-source and inferential.

stays.narrative: Tycho arrived at the University of Copenhagen on 19 April 1559, aged twelve — the first of his family to begin university studies — under Jørgen Brahe's plan for a career in law and statecraft, lodging in the household of a professor (unnamed in Christianson 2020; Thoren suggests possibly Niels Hemmingsen). He worked through the Melanchthonian trivium while turning himself, from 1560, into an astronomer by purchase: Sacrobosco's De sphaera (used in Scavenius's lectures), the Basel 1551 Ptolemy folio bought the last day of November 1560 for two Joachimsthaler (signed and annotated, now Prague University Library, also bearing Johannes Pratensis's name), Apian's Cosmographia and Regiomontanus's De triangulis signed 'Tycho Brahe, Anno 1561' — the first appearance of the Latinised name — and the ephemerides of Carelli (bought with Jens Nilsson) and Stadius, compared for Ptolemaic against Copernican predictions. The tradition that the predicted partial solar eclipse of 21 August 1560 awakened his vocation begins with Gassendi; Norlind rejects it as aetiological myth. He left for Leipzig on 14 February 1562.

stays.disputes: The 1560 eclipse-vocation story: Gassendi (origin), Dreyer, Christianson 2020 and Morsing assert it; Håkansson hedges ('kanske'); Norlind pp. 13–15 rejects it as aetiological myth (Tycho never mentions the eclipse, not even in his autobiography) — rendered here as tradition, not fact; the eclipse itself and the book purchases stand. Arrival 19 April 1559 rests on Stephanius' notes; Norlind warns it may be the inscription date (matricle lost 1728), and Thoren notes noblemen's sons usually only attended lectures without matriculating — day-precision kept with this caveat. Lodging: Christianson 2020 has an unnamed professor's household, Thoren offers two candidates — Scavenius (professor of mathematics, an Oxe client) and Hemmingsen — stated as possible, not merged. End date: 14 February 1562 (Dreyer, Norlind, Friis, the Nationalmuseet essays, Jönsson) adopted over Thoren's month-precision February 1562; no real conflict (Thoren's 24 March 1562 is the Leipzig registration).

stays.narrative: A waypoint of the outward journey, not yet a study station. Having crossed the southern Baltic in February 1562, Tycho and Vedel travelled up the Elbe to Wittenberg and continued overland — Thoren has them riding two more days — to Leipzig, where both were registered on 24 March 1562. Tycho's Wittenberg study residence belongs to a later period.

stays.narrative: Tycho reached Leipzig on 24 March 1562, five and a half weeks out of Copenhagen, with the twenty-year-old Anders Sørensen Vedel as preceptor, and matriculated as 'Ticho Brade ex Scandia'. Sent to read law, he lodged in a professor's household and studied astronomy secretly at night: a fist-sized celestial globe hidden from Vedel, Stadius's ephemerides, then the Alphonsine and Prutenic tables. The Saturn–Jupiter conjunction of August 1563, which the tables missed badly, prompted his first observation log, headed 'Anno 1563, seventeen years of age, Leipzig'. Sightings taken first with large compasses gave way from 1 May 1564 to a cross-staff after Gemma Frisius, transversal-divided by Bartholomaeus Scultetus, for whose faulty divisions he computed a correction table. His circle included Homelius, Camerarius and the electoral mathematician Valentin Thau; he also cast nativities, Peucer's among them. He and Vedel left on 17 May 1565.

stays.disputes: First recorded observation: Dreyer (p. 19) has 17 August 1563; Christianson 2020 (pp. 25–26) has first entry 18 August — Christianson followed (modern), Dreyer's day noted; Thoren gives only August 1563. Cross-staff origin: Thoren (pp. 18–19; his n. 27 hedges whether the two references are to one instrument) has Tycho ordering an Arscenius cross-staff from Louvain; Dreyer, Norlind and Christianson 2020 have a radius built at Leipzig after Gemma Frisius's instructions with Scultetus's transversal scale — both accounts preserved, not conflated. Norlind (p. 20) rejects Dreyer's inference of a second Leipzig sojourn in November 1565 as a copyist's misreading of the observation journal ('En andra resa till Leipzig kan det naturligtvis ej vara tal om') — no such stay created. Christianson 2000 gives no dates for Leipzig; its 1562–1565 span is this edition's approximation, not that source's assertion.

stays.narrative: Landing at Copenhagen from Rostock in late May or early June 1565, Tycho learned that his foster father Jørgen Brahe — captor of the Swedish flagship in 1564 — was now vice-admiral of the fleet, deep in preparations for the next engagement. From the capital he proceeded home through Scania. Weeks later Jørgen fell into the water at the bridge between Copenhagen castle and the town while rescuing King Frederick II, and died on 21 June 1565 of the illness contracted; no source places Tycho at the deathbed or funeral, and Dreyer expressly declines to say where he resided in the following months. Norlind's pole-height list supplies independent, if inferential, support for the passage through the capital.

stays.narrative: First touch of Wittenberg, in transit on the homeward road from Leipzig in May 1565. Thoren has Tycho and Vedel pass through purposefully, to see his former instructor Bartholomew Schultz (Scultetus), who had moved there the previous autumn; Friis conjectures a call on Caspar Peucer; Gassendi records only a regretted transit (in transcursu), the regret that motivated the deliberate residence of 1566. Norlind grounds the passage independently in the pole-height list of the oldest observation journal, whose sequence Leipzig–Wittenberg–Rostock he reads as the route home, and notes that Stephanius's later phrase 'rediit Wittebergam' for 1566 presupposes this earlier visit.

stays.narrative: Tycho and Vedel reached Rostock on 25 May 1565, eight days after leaving Leipzig (17 May, Hegelund's date) — the Baltic port's first appearance in his itinerary, as a mere embarkation point a year before it became his residence. The Northern Seven Years' War was in full course and hostile fleets cruised the Baltic, but merchant sailings continued and the pair crossed to Copenhagen without meeting hostile cruisers. The 25 May date rests on the Stephanius notes and is reported unanimously.

stays.narrative: Travelling home through Scania in June 1565, Tycho stopped at Helsingborg — the natural landfall of the Sound crossing — and made a determination of the local latitude, the first of three such stops (Helsingborg, Malmö, Knutstorp) that constitute his earliest recorded geodetic-astronomical fieldwork on home ground, made with the instruments and habits acquired at Leipzig. The stop rests on the pole-height list in his oldest observation journal, which Norlind reads as the itinerary of the journey itself.

stays.narrative: About a year at home in Denmark between the Leipzig and Wittenberg residences, June 1565 to April 1566, bracketed by the Stephanius notes (Rostock 25 May 1565; 'returned to Wittenberg on April 15, 1566, from his fatherland'). Jørgen Brahe's death on 21 June 1565 changed Tycho's status: the plan to make him heir to Tostrup lapsed, and Inger Oxe, widowed, continued to regard him 'with a quite special love'. He recorded no observations that year, occupied himself with ordering his money matters and gathering funds for the peregrination he had resolved on, and found the nobility's contempt for his studies galling — of his relations only Steen Bille approved. By spring 1566 he had won leave, or simply asserted himself, to depart.

stays.narrative: The second latitude-determination stop of the June 1565 homeward journey through Scania, between Helsingborg and Knutstorp. Malmö is the penultimate name in the pole-height list of the oldest observation journal (Leipzig, Wittenberg, Rostock, Copenhagen, Helsingborg, Malmö, Knutstorp), read by Norlind as the route of the journey with observations made under way; the observations were preserved in the notebook record but not printed by Dreyer, as Thoren notes from Norlind. As with the other Scanian waypoints, the presence rests on this journal inference.

stays.narrative: The second study journey's first station: Tycho arrived at Wittenberg on 15 April 1566, this time with the M.A. Hans Aalborg as preceptor rather than a noble hovmester, finding Vedel already there completing his degree among the traditional Danish student colony. The leading connection was Caspar Peucer, Melanchthon's son-in-law, professor of medicine and Preceptor primarius, whose teaching Tycho attended for a time — though he never formally matriculated (a lack he remedied ceremonially only in February 1599) and lodged with no professor, perhaps with Schultz. After five months plague broke out in the congested town and caused a general student exodus: he left on 16 September 1566 and reached Rostock on the 24th, an eight-day journey.

stays.narrative: First Rostock residence: arrived 24 September 1566, matriculated in October under rector Simon Pauli, lodging in the household of the theologian Lucas Bacmeister. No one taught astronomy, but the Paracelsian Levinus Battus and the empiricist Heinrich Brucaeus opened his lifelong medical-alchemical interests. On the lunar eclipse of 28 October 1566 he posted anonymous Latin verses foretelling Sultan Süleyman's death — the sultan had died on 9 September, before the prediction. At a betrothal dance in Bacmeister's house on 10 December he quarrelled with his kinsman Manderup Parsberg; the quarrel flared again on 27 December and on 29 December, about seven in the evening in deep darkness, a duel cost Tycho the bridge of his nose, concealed thereafter by a prosthesis. He observed the solar eclipse of 9 April 1567 at Rostock — 'the first he observed as a real astronomer' — and went home in the summer of 1567, departure undated.

stays.disputes: Cause of the quarrel — the primary note is read two ways: Norlind (p. 22) renders Stephanius 'propter choream' (over the dance), while Christianson's edition of the same note (Facts of Life 1970, p. 24) has the dispute arising 'concerning the movements of the stars' at the Bacmeister betrothal; Gassendi's specific prowess-contest version rests on a misreading of Laurus and is rejected (Norlind). The underlying cause is not settled. Duel date: 10/27/29 December 1566 sequence adopted (Stephanius, Norlind, the Nationalmuseet essays); Gassendi notes some referred the incident to October 1565 — rejected. Venue: Christianson 2000 places the duel in Bacmeister's house; Thoren (Stolterfoht tradition) and Jönsson a churchyard by night — quarrel indoors, duel outside adopted. Prosthesis: Gassendi's wax-gold-silver and Dreyer's gold-and-silver composition are debunked — copper-zinc alloy (brass) with traces of gold per the 1901 and 2010 exhumations. Jessenius's funeral-oration version (an assassin's night attack) was formally protested: Christian IV's letter of 4 May 1602 insists the two duelled 'redlich fur der faust'.

stays.narrative: During the undocumented second half of 1567 Tycho 'doubtless went to the university to renew old acquaintanceships' in Copenhagen and may also have appeared at court, where Peder Oxe — his foster mother's brother — had returned from exile and was consolidating power as governor of Copenhagen and, by August 1567, lord high steward. Both the university visit and the court contact are Thoren's inferences from the changed political landscape, not documented occasions; the stay is recorded on his authority alone and graded accordingly.

stays.narrative: Home from Rostock for the second half of 1567, scarred and wearing the prosthesis, in a country strained by the Seven Years' War: the Scanian borderlands lay wasted and his father Otte — promoted in 1567 to the front-line governorship of Helsingborg Castle — was organising a fresh offensive. Tycho ordered his affairs, visited kinsmen and friends ('better than I deserved', he later wrote of his reception), and announced against the expectations of his class that he would continue his scientific studies; Otte was among those upset, while Steen Bille, Peder Oxe, Inger Oxe and Beate Bille showed understanding. Christianson infers that the Christmas-holiday discussions with Peder Oxe and Steen Bille moved them to broker the Roskilde canonry charter that followed in spring 1568. He stayed through his twenty-first birthday and the holidays, then embarked on the third journey. No source names the residence; Thoren has him 'surely' with the family in their new Helsingborg quarters.

stays.narrative: From Basel Tycho visited Erasmus Oswald Schreckenfuchs, professor of mathematics at nearby Freiburg im Breisgau, admiring his collection of instruments and noting celestial models that demonstrated planetary motions according to the theories of Ptolemy and Copernicus — an early exposure to mechanical representations of the rival world systems, and one of the deliberate calls on astronomical authorities that punctuated this tour. The acquaintance bore fruit: in 1575 he would order a zodiacal armillary from Schreckenfuchs.

stays.narrative: Travelling south from Rostock in 1568 on the tour that would end in Basel and Augsburg, Tycho stopped in Nuremberg and purchased a fine cross-staff and a set of astronomical rings made by Walter Arscenius, nephew of Gemma Frisius — his first significant instrument purchases from the great south-German artisan market. The stop is attested by Christianson 2020 alone among the sources consulted and is graded accordingly.

stays.narrative: Second Rostock residence: Tycho dashed back without a tutor, arriving on New Year's Day 1568, lodging two weeks with the Paracelsian Levinus Battus before taking his own rooms in the Jurists' College — 'a very suitable place for observing' — and resuming observation on 2 January. His letter of 14 January 1568 to Hans Aalborg, the earliest preserved of his whole correspondence, asked him to 'bury in deep silence the cause of my departure' from home. The university levied a stiff fine of twenty Joachimsthalers, probably over the Parsberg duel; Brucaeus and Peder Oxe's influence aided the appeal, which proceeded without him. By royal letters patent dated Copenhagen 14 May 1568 — the first royal favour shown him, credited to Peder Oxe — he was promised the next vacant canonry at Roskilde cathedral, probably received at Rostock; law study yielded to his own formation, and he left, departure undated, for the south.

The Aalborg letter's recipient: former tutor Hans Aalborg (Christianson 2020, Thoren) against Norlind's 'bookseller Johan Ålborg' — same correspondent, divergent identification, both kept. Receipt of the canonry letter at Rostock carries Friis's 'rimeligviis'.

stays.narrative: By September 1568 Tycho was in Basel — city of Erasmus and Paracelsus, the university Peder Oxe had known in youth and exile — where he matriculated with cousins and several other Danes under the rectorate of Simon Sulzer, probably in August or September (standing no. 52 in the year's list). After nine years of university work he had exhausted teachers and texts: here he first worked on his own, experimenting with quadrant construction assisted by the young Hugo Blotius, later imperial librarian in Vienna — probably including the gilt brass quadrant with Nonnian subdivisions and 'an emblem of life and death' later depicted in the Mechanica, though a larger design of 1–1.5 m radius proved unstable in wind. Basel lodged itself in his affections: in 1575 he would seriously consider settling there for good. He stayed through the winter, leaving for the Danube road at the end of 1568 or in early spring 1569.

stays.narrative: Passing through Ingolstadt on the Danube, Tycho called on Philip Apian — son of Peter Apian of Astronomicum Caesareum fame, whose Cosmography Tycho had used to teach himself astronomy — a keen observer of heavens and earth whose huge triangulated map of Bavaria, printed at his own officin, was one of the cartographic marvels of the age; Håkansson suggests the visit may seriously have awakened the cartographic interest Tycho later applied to the Øresund region. The visit's date is the most contested waypoint of the tour: Norlind shows Apian was expelled from Ingolstadt for suspected heresy only in October 1569, making a call in spring 1569, on the road from Basel to Augsburg, the likeliest reading — followed here with Thoren.

Norlind's archival redating followed; the homeward-1570 tradition preserved here and at the homeward journey record.

stays.narrative: Following the Danube from Basel early in 1569 (Norlind: end of 1568 or spring 1569), Tycho called at Lauingen in Swabia on Cyprianus Leovitius, the astrologer of the Saturn-Jupiter conjunctions and ephemeride-maker whose tables he had used as a student. Invited home, he drew dinner out deep into the night in astronomical conversation — and found that this astronomer-astrologer never observed the heavens, owning no instruments and timing eclipses only with friends' clocks. The exchange sharpened his conviction that only a sustained course of observation could yield correct planetary tables, and strengthened his resolve on his chosen path. The encounter is recorded by Tycho himself (TBOO III, 221) and reported by every biographical tradition.

stays.narrative: The longest stop of the tour: some fourteen months in the imperial city, his observations there running from 14 April 1569 to 16 May 1570, with departure soon after. Admiring the city's fortifications, fountains and civic culture, he settled among its humanist patriciate — the brothers Paul and Johann Baptist Hainzel, the rector-librarian Hieronymus Wolf, the schoolman Johannes Major — and here established instrument-making as his metier: his first self-designed instrument, the great half-arc, was usable by November 1569; he designed his first sextant, left as a parting gift to Paul Hainzel; and he commissioned the great celestial globe of 1.5 m, unfinished at his departure and left in Hainzel's care. With Paul Hainzel he built the gargantuan oak Quadrans Maximus at Göggingen. Wolf introduced him to Petrus Ramus, in Augsburg in April 1570, who urged an astronomy rebuilt on observation without hypotheses. He was increasingly drawn to alchemy — the 'spagyrical arts' — from this period, and left, reluctantly and somewhat impromptu, probably in May 1570.

stays.disputes: Landlord: Christianson 2020 p. 36 names the goldsmith and Paracelsian Lorenz Thenn; Norlind pp. 25–26 a Danish countryman, magister Laurentius 'Den Danus' — plausibly the same Laurentius differently identified; both kept, neither asserted over the other. Globe maker: Thoren (following the tradition also in Jönsson and Tycho Brahes Verden) has Christoph Schissler make the 1.5 m globe core; Christianson 2020 says 'an unknown maker' and Norlind 'an Augsburg craftsman'; Mosley finds the Schissler attribution inconclusive, reading Johannes Maior's letter of 1 August 1576 (TBOO VII, 36.5-26) against it — left open, Schissler flagged as unproven. The Schissler workshop visit itself is Mosley's conjecture, not an assertion. Quadrant garden: all modern sources place it on Paul Hainzel's Göggingen estate; within Gassendi the funeral oration says Johann Baptist's garden while the index says Paul's. Departure: soon after 16 May 1570 (Thoren, Christianson 2020, Norlind) against Friis's 'toward the end of the year' — superseded by the Textor album leaf placing Tycho at Wittenberg on 9 September 1570.

stays.narrative: On the autumn 1570 homeward journey, after Wittenberg, Tycho 'probably visited with his former professors in Rostock before crossing the Baltic to Denmark' — a plausible but undocumented call on Brucaeus and colleagues, made while the Stettin negotiations were ending the Northern Seven Years' War. The stop is Thoren's inference alone: no document places Tycho in Rostock in 1570, and the stay is recorded at the corresponding grade.

stays.narrative: In the park of Paul Hainzel's country estate at Göggingen, just south-west of Augsburg, a crew of some twenty men erected the colossal oak Quadrans Maximus of Tycho's design — nearly 5.5 metres in radius (c. 14 cubits), brass scale divided to minutes and fractions of minutes, built in about a month, apparently March 1570, at Hainzel's cost. Tycho recorded his first observation with it on 1 April 1570 and observed at roughly weekly intervals; on 16 May 1570 he and Hainzel observed the Sun together with it for the last time. Petrus Ramus went out to the suburban villa after dinner to see 'a great machine he has invented' and debated whether an astronomy without hypotheses was possible. The quadrant — Tycho's first work with a large instrument, whose results he said agreed wholly with those later obtained in Denmark — stood in the open under tarpaulins, remained in use as late as 1577 by Norlind's account; Dreyer instead has it destroyed by storm in December 1574.

Within Gassendi, the funeral oration and the index disagree on whether the garden was Johann Baptist's or Paul Hainzel's; the moderns are unanimous for Paul. Fate of the quadrant: destroyed by storm December 1574 (Dreyer) against Norlind's 'still in use as late as 1577, and eventually decayed'.

stays.narrative: The one fixed point on the previously unknown homeward route from Augsburg: an album amicorum leaf of the Frenchman Claudius Textor (matriculated Wittenberg 1564), now in the Germanisches Nationalmuseum, Nuremberg, carries Tycho's autograph verses — six lines on the stars inclining but not compelling the rational soul — signed 'Witteberge: Anno: 1570: sept: 9.' It is the oldest known Tycho album autograph, and Norlind's discovery of it proved Tycho was in Wittenberg on 9 September 1570, certainly on the journey home to Denmark, nearly four months after his last Augsburg observation. The unhurried pace tells against the tradition that his father's illness triggered the departure.

stays.narrative: The Wanderjahre's terminus: summoned home with his brothers as their father's health failed, Tycho was at Helsingborg Castle — Otte Brahe's seat as governor — by the end of 1570; Thoren has him home probably by the time the Stettin peace was concluded (13 December, the eve of his 24th birthday). The first documented trace is an observation of 30 December 1570 from the castle (Venus and Jupiter per Dreyer; the journals cited at X, 37), made with one of the cross-staffs that were the only instruments he still possessed — the same season the treaty ending the war was signed. Otte, who had called his sons home and compiled a legal listing of his estate, was bedridden by spring and died on 9 May 1571 after a severe three-day ague, aged 53, his family around the bed; Tycho poured out his grief in the letter to Vedel of 18 May 1571. Knutstorp passed jointly to Tycho and Steen; burial was at Kågeröd church.

stays.disputes: First home observation: the journals' 30 December 1570 entry (Dreyer, Friis, Norlind — archival, X, 37) against Christianson 2020's Moon observation 'at the solstice on the eve of his 24th birthday' (c. 13 December) and Thoren's 'by Christmas' — the 30 December anchor is followed for the documented date; arrival by mid-December remains possible per Thoren. Gassendi dated the homecoming to 1571 with a Copenhagen landfall and court salute — rejected on the strength of the 30 December 1570 Helsingborg observations (Norlind). Motive for the return: the father's grave illness (Friis, Jönsson, Håkansson 'probably') is doubted by Norlind, who notes the unhurried route and that Otte died only in May 1571. | Gassendi has Tycho returning from Augsburg only in 1571; Norlind (p. 28) refutes this with the Helsingborg observation of 30 December 1570 (TBOO X, 37) — Norlind followed. Deathbed attendance is presumption, not documented in these sources.
stays.calendar_note: Start anchored to the first documented observation (30 December 1570); arrival by mid-December possible per Thoren/Christianson 2020.

stays.narrative: From late 1571 Tycho lived mainly with his maternal uncle Steen Bille, who held the secularised Cistercian abbey of Herrevad and ran it as a proto-industrial seat: glassworks with Italian blowers, the first paper mill in Skåne (which Tycho helped build), the Eket ironworks, smiths and cabinetmakers. Bille fitted out a chemical laboratory for him outside the abbey wall, and chemistry absorbed him wholly — not a single astronomical observation survives between 30 December 1570 and November 1572. On the evening of 11 November 1572, walking from the laboratory to supper, he saw the brilliant new star in Cassiopeia near the zenith, confirmed it by servants and passing peasants, and measured its distances through the winter with the newly finished walnut sextant built by the abbey's craftsmen, proving it beyond parallax — the observations published in De nova stella (1573) that redirected his life.

stays.disputes: Laboratory site: Tycho himself places it outside the abbey wall (Prog.; II, 307 f.), folk tradition inside the precinct — Norlind reports both. Jönsson's 'alchemy almost exclusively 1569–1572 at Herrevad' collides with his own Augsburg chronology; the Herrevad alchemy period can only begin in 1571. Kirsten's residence at Herrevad is possibility only — Christianson has her probably at Helsingborg.

stays.narrative: The family seat anchored Tycho's Scanian years: he and his brother Steen co-inherited Knutstorp at Otte Brahe's death, both styling themselves 'of Knudstrup' for life, while their mother Beate Bille kept dower occupancy. Here she revealed his stillborn twin, prompting the Latin elegy printed in 1572 as his first publication; here he formed his union with Kirsten Jørgensdatter, their first daughter born in October 1573. The De nova stella preface is dated 'Knusdorp', 5 May 1573; an ague kept him home that summer. On 8 December 1573 he observed the lunar eclipse foretold in his book with the new gilt-brass quadrant, assisted by his sister Sophie — his own note records 'Hanc ego Eclipsin in curia mea Knusdorpiana observavi diligenter'. Settlement of the paternal estate ran to spring 1575, from which he drew about 650 dalers a year.

stays.disputes: Eclipse date: Thoren (p. 75) has 3 December 1573; Dreyer (pp. 70, 73), Christianson 2000 (scan p. 65) and Christianson 2020 (p. 61) have 8 December – 8 December followed. Kirsten's origin: Gassendi (on Blaeu's oral testimony alone) makes her 'from the village of Knudstorp'; Håkansson, Norlind and Christianson make her in all probability the daughter of Jørgen Hansen, priest at Kågeröd — Kågeröd followed. Thoren notes the 'address' shift to Knudstrup from spring 1573 may be styling rather than residence.

stays.narrative: Tycho owned town houses in Helsingborg, below the castle his father had commanded until 1571, and Kirsten Jørgensdatter probably lived in one of them — 'formodligen periodvis ensam' in Håkansson's phrase — while Tycho spent ever more time at Herrevad. Christianson suggests it was perhaps in Helsingborg that he gave her the keys to larder, cabinets and doors, the act which under Danish common law made an openly cohabiting commoner a binding morganatic wife after three winters. The daughters Kirstine (b. 1573) and Magdalene (b. 1574) were raised there; little Kirstine died of plague in the town on 24 September 1576 and was buried in the Maria church, where Tycho's Latin epitaph for her survives. Tycho's own stays in the house are implied by the household, not documented.

The stay begins where the documented 1570–71 winter residence ends (May 1571); Tycho's own presence in the town house is inferred from the household — retained at grade C as the family anchor, not as documented presence.

stays.narrative: In 1572, per Christianson, Tycho took his Latin ode to his stillborn twin to the printer Mads Vingaard in Copenhagen and had it printed as his first publication — the broadsheet Carmen that antedates De nova stella by a year. The visit ties him bodily to the capital's printing trade at the very start of his publishing career, a decade before his own press on Hven. The printing itself is bibliographically certain (Nielsen 424); Tycho's personal presence at the press rests on Christianson's formulation alone.

stays.disputes: The Nielsen bibliography documents the 1572 Vingaard printing but not Tycho's presence at the press (an imprint does not place its author at the press); presence rests on Christianson 2000 alone.

stays.narrative: Knutstorp's parish church stood in Kågeröd, where Pastor Jørgen Hansen's daughter Kirsten Jørgensdatter lived — 'of whom little is known except that Tycho was drawn to her'. The liaison that became his lifelong common-law marriage began here in the early 1570s; around February 1573 Kirsten became pregnant with his first child, and Pratensis teased him in a letter invoking Venus, 'perhaps thinking of Tycho and Kirsten from Kågeröd'. Christianson elsewhere suggests he first saw her 'perhaps in Kågeröd church'. His bodily presence in the village is implied by the courtship rather than recorded as a dated visit.

stays.narrative: For King Frederick II's marriage to Sophie of Mecklenburg, held 20 July 1572 in Copenhagen Castle, the whole Danish nobility was summoned in new court attire; the next day the young queen rode to her coronation at Our Lady's, Peder Oxe carrying her crown, amid banquets, tourneys and university festivities. Thoren states Tycho 'probably borrowed attendants for the occasion and went too'; Christianson has him enrolled as a noble courtier during the wedding week, which implies presence. A probable rather than sighted attendance, at the festivity that bound him formally to the court whose patronage would shortly transform his life.

stays.narrative: Early in 1573 Tycho came to Copenhagen with the manuscript of his Diarium and account of the new star, lodging as was his custom with Johannes Pratensis, professor of medicine. Pratensis had not yet heard of the star; the French envoy Charles de Dançay, dining them, thought Tycho was mocking Danish savants until a clear evening let him point the star out in the sky. Pratensis urged printing; Tycho demurred — partly the little work's want of polish, mainly the prejudice that authorship ill became a nobleman — and returned to Scania with his manuscript. The visit sat within a periodic Copenhagen pattern of these years, his circle led by Pratensis and the long-serving envoy Dançay, more than thirty years his senior. To the same pattern belongs Pratensis's surviving invitation to his Martinmas feast of 11 November 1573 — coincidentally the first anniversary of the nova discovery — though Tycho's attendance is nowhere documented.

stays.narrative: During a second visit in spring 1573, after German pamphlets full of nonsense about the star had reached him, Tycho was pressed to publish not only by Pratensis but by his kinsman Peter Oxe, high treasurer of Denmark, who even suggested hiding his name in an anagram. He yielded — his consent must have preceded 16 April 1573, when Pratensis reported the figures being cut — and De nova stella was elegantly printed by Lorentz Benedicht, appearing early in the summer with the star still visible; the publication details kept him occupied past the normal spring departure times and postponed his planned journey abroad by a year. To the same Copenhagen orbit of 1573 belong the commissions to the royal clockmaker Steffen Brenner for the gilt-brass quadrant and a clockwork celestial globe.

stays.narrative: A documented observing run at Herrevad in the spring of 1574, part of the Skåne-Øresund circuit recorded in Tycho's own observation books: chiefly distance-measures of planets from fixed stars with the sextant, 'satis exquisite, subtracta instrumenti parallaxi', a small quadrant also mentioned. The 1746 compiler of Danske Magazin, reading the manuscript observation books, names March and April; Dreyer, from the same books, extends the run into May, after which Tycho removed to Copenhagen for the rest of the year.

stays.narrative: Tycho observed at Copenhagen on 24 April 1574 and spent most of the rest of the year in the city, where his daughter Magdalene was born (day and month unrecorded) and where he kept a large town house, probably with Kirsten. Urged by Pratensis and Dançay and decided by King Frederik's own request, he opened his university lectures on 23 September 1574 with the oration on the mathematical sciences — delivered before Dançay and virtually the whole university community, defending a reformed astrology and reaching public accommodation with Niels Hemmingsen — then lectured four mornings a week on planetary theory, treating Copernicus's models in geostatic form: among the first university lectures on Copernican astronomy anywhere, and he the only nobleman of his era to teach at Copenhagen. The student Peter Jacobsen Flemløs entered his service. The lectures closed around the turn of 1574–75; before departing he wrote the Latin rag-poem asking Danish women for linen so Vedel's Saxo could be printed on Scanian paper, and left as a grand seigneur about March 1575.

End of the lectures: Thoren has them run only until just before Christmas 1574, the second half cancelled for the journey; Dreyer ('finished early in 1575') and Friis ('sluttede i Foraaret 1575') let them run into 1575 — close put at the turn of 1574–75, departure c. March 1575 (Thoren). Magdalene's birth: Friis and the 1746 compiler suggest summer or autumn 1574, Christianson 2020 towards the end of the year — day and month unrecorded.

stays.narrative: On 20 December 1574 Tycho and his brothers Steen and Axel presented themselves to King Frederick II at Sorø Abbey and took their leave of the court — the brothers to marry in 1575, Tycho to abandon the Copenhagen classroom and travel abroad, carrying a royal commission to scout artists, artisans and technicians for the Kronborg project. A single-source datum, exactly dated by Christianson.

stays.narrative: Continuing southwest from Frankfurt, Tycho stayed some time at Basel and found it so agreeable that he resolved to settle there or nearby with his family: pure clear air and cheap living, an academy full of distinguished men in the Erasmian tradition, and above all the city's position at the meeting-point of Germany, France and Italy, whence his findings could spread and correspondence flow. Gassendi's funeral-oration source confirms that, returning homeward, he had fixed on 'Basileam Rauracorum, aut vicinum aliquem locum' as the chosen seat of his life. He deferred the final decision but carried the secret plan home at year's end — the private agenda that shaped the whole sequel, since Frederick II's offer of Hven in February 1576 was designed to forestall exactly this emigration.

evidence.quote: on to Basel, where he stayed for some time before crossing the Alps into northern Italy
evidence.note: the secret choice of Basel as future home, p. 73

evidence.quote: In Basel, he found a place that appealed to his search for peace, wisdom, and universal harmony

stays.disputes: Friis's own 1875 preface dates the Basel visit to a journey 'i Aaret 1576', contradicting his 1871 narrative's 1575 journey — 1575 (all other sources, and Friis 1871) followed. Håkansson has only 'a short stop' where Dreyer and Christianson have a stay of some duration — duration left open.

stays.narrative: On the return from Venice Tycho crossed the Brenner Pass before the fall snows made it uncertain and 'slipped through to Innsbruck', travelling a few days north to Augsburg — a pure transit waypoint in Thoren's account. Norlind holds the much-travelled Brenner road (Innsbruck, Trento, Treviso — the road Montaigne took five years later) to be the probable route of the outward journey as well, and the homeward journey probably retraced it. Trento and Treviso remain probable-route conjecture without any documented stop.

evidence.quote: he slipped through to Innsbruck and, from there, a few days north to Augsburg
sannolikt för han den av resande från Sydtyskland mycket trafikerade vägen över Innsbruck, Brenner-passet, till Trento (Trient), Treviso och Venedig
evidence.note: the homeward journey from Venice probably retraced the Brenner route

stays.disputes: Norlind places the Brenner-Innsbruck road on the outward journey as probable and the return as likely the same way; Thoren names Innsbruck only on the return — the return placement, where both attest it, is followed.

stays.narrative: Jönsson holds it 'hogst troligt' (highly probable) that Tycho visited the botanical garden at Padua on the return from Venice in 1575: the fourfold garden he later laid out around Uraniborg came to resemble the Paduan plan. The claim is offered as a strong probability explaining the garden design, not as a documented visit, and Christianson expressly warns that Paduan side-trips must not be asserted since Tycho recorded no details. Rendered as an unproven probability.

evidence.quote: Anläggningen kom att likna den botaniska trädgården i italienska Padua, som det år högst troligt att Tycho besökt på sin återfärd från Venedig 1575.

evidence.note: counter-witness: the Veneto academy venues are conjecture and 'Tycho did not record the details'

stays.disputes: Jönsson: 'hogst troligt'; Christianson 2020: side-trips to Padua must not be asserted — kept as a grade-C probability, excluded from the canonical tour route.

stays.narrative: Crossing the Alps from Basel, Tycho reached Venice — the farthest south he ever travelled — and stayed from some days to a few weeks. His own testimony survives (Progymnasmata; TBOO III, 234): about sixteen years on he recalled hearing very many Venetians, including men of the highest nobility, disputing acutely on lofty philosophical matters — words Norlind reads as attendance at the patrician learned academies, held in palaces such as the Morosini. He admired the 'splendid and grand' city, 'the Emporium of all Europe', and its most prudent government; saw the new Renaissance architecture of the Veneto, above all Palladio's, which fed directly into the Uraniborg villa ideal; and as Frederick II's agent made contacts among Venetian artisans for the Elsinore works. More than twenty years later he sent the Republic and Doge Grimani each a Mechanica with the manuscript star catalogue.

evidence.quote: Id enim nec sine voluptate, ante annos circiter sedecim cognoui, cum illic quam plurimos etiam precipua nobilitate claros ... disputantes, conferentesque ipsemet audierim.
evidence.note: Tycho's own testimony (Prog. III, 234) and Norlind's academy reading

evidence.quote: Venice was 'splendid and grand, the Emporium of all Europe' and Tycho became acquainted with members of the 'very magnificent Senate'
saw the new villas of Palladio in the Veneto, attended aristocratic academies in the Venetian Republic
Efter några veckor i Venedig, där han som alltid umgicks i samhallets översta skikt och knöt kontakt med en rad lärde

Fra Basel drog han igjennem Schweiz til Norditalien, og opholdt sig nogle Dage i Venedig.

stays.disputes: The academy venues (Accademia Parutiana; Palladio's Accademia Olimpica in Vicenza; the Rinascenti in Padua) are Christianson's conjectures — 'Tycho did not record the details' — so side-trips to Vicenza or Padua must not be asserted. Duration: 'some days' (Dreyer, Friis, Gassendi) against 'some weeks' (Håkansson; Thoren 'no more than a few weeks').

stays.narrative: First station of the 1575 tour: Tycho arrived with Flemløs a few days before Easter (3 April 1575) at the court of Landgrave Wilhelm IV, who had observed from the Zwehrer Thor since 1561. For more than a week — Gassendi says eight or ten days — the two conversed by day and observed by night: the nova's parallax, the retardation of the sun at the horizon (the refraction problem Tycho resolved to pursue, recalling Bernhard Walther), the position of Spica, the landgrave's azimuth quadrants, great celestial clock and Baldewein globe. Gifts were exchanged — the landgrave's star catalogue for De nova stella. When the infant Sidonia, taken ill on Maundy Thursday, died the day after Easter, Tycho withdrew as the court went into mourning. They never met again; the landgrave's later embassy to Frederik II urged support for Tycho. Tycho's own fond memories of the stay are printed (TBOO VI, 10 and 34).

Han begav sig først til Cassel, hvor han omtrent ved Paasketid besøgte Landgrev Wilhelm den Fjerde.

stays.narrative: Leaving mourning Kassel in April 1575, Tycho went to Frankfurt am Main for the spring book fair. He stayed some days, turning over a great variety of books and buying not a few — above all whatever published tracts on the new star of 1572 he did not yet possess, the pamphlets he would later dissect in the Progymnasmata. Thoren reconstructs the breadth of the purchases: Proclus, pseudo-Ptolemaic astrologica, Synesius, Bonatti, recent Philippist authors, French and Italian treatises including du Chesne and five works of Oronce Fine, Gesner's bibliography, and works on mining and minerals serving the alchemical interests. The stop ties the tour to his lifelong book-buying practice — in 1579 he would send Vedel to this fair with a marked-up catalogue.

evidence.quote: He travelled to Frankfurt am Main for the semi-annual book fair, and on to Basel
From Cassel, Tycho went to Frankfurt-on-the-Main, where he purchased some books at the half-yearly mart, particularly some of the numerous pamphlets on the new star
Fra Cassel begav han sig til Frankfurt am Main, især for ved den forestaænde Bogmesse at gjøre Indkjøb af Boger.
Francofurtum ad Maenum petiit, ut celebribus Nundinis, quae tum instabant, interesset. Dies aliquot ibi commoratus, ac pervolutatis libris variis, & nonnullis etiam coemptis

Efter ett besök på bokmässan i Frankfurt fortsatte Tycho Brahe till Basel
Från Kassel för Tycho till Frankfurt a. M., där bokmassa pågick, och han här förmodligen där köpt litteratur till sitt bibliotek.
From Cassel, Tycho went south to Frankfurt, where each spring and fall the booksellers of Europe gathered to vend their wares

stays.narrative: In late summer 1575 Tycho and Flemløs came from Italy to Augsburg, renewing the old circle — the Hainzel brothers, Hieronymus Wolf — though the second stay proved anticlimactic: the great Göggingen quadrant had been destroyed by a windstorm in December 1574 and left unrepaired, and Schissler's long-awaited celestial globe, ordered in 1570, proved imperfectly spherical and cracked at the joints. He prepared the globe for transport — it was freighted with great difficulty to Denmark the following year, trued with parchment, clad in brass and perfected on Hven, carrying the stars of his catalogue by 1595. He recruited the portrait artist Tobias Gemperlin into his service, the future painter of the mural-quadrant portrait, and scouted artisans for Frederick II, lingering into late October before dropping downriver to the Regensburg coronation.

stays.disputes: The globe's fate: Thoren (p. 97) has Tycho refusing Schissler's imperfect globe; Dreyer, Friis, Norlind, Jönsson and Gassendi have it prepared for transport, freighted to Denmark in 1576 and perfected at Uraniborg — the majority (and the globe's later Hven career) followed, Thoren's 'refusal' read as rejection of the workmanship, not of the object. Quadrant destruction: 'storm of 1574' generally; Dreyer and Thoren specify December 1574.

stays.narrative: Tycho attended the Regensburg festivities for the coronation of Rudolf of Habsburg as King of the Romans, performed with great solemnity on 1 November 1575 — his first bodily crossing of the path of the prince who would become his last patron. He had hoped to find Landgrave Wilhelm, who alone among the German princes did not come; instead he met the imperial physician Thaddaeus Hagecius, and in a few days the two formed a lifelong bond: Hagecius gave him his Dialexis on the new star, Munosius's Spanish tract, and — a most precious gift — a manuscript of Copernicus's unprinted Commentariolus, which Tycho later circulated to German astronomers, reciprocating with du Chesne's new book from Frankfurt. Hugo Blotius and Gemperlin were in the company; a manuscript De directionum significationibus he examined with Hagecius here was still on his mind in 1585 (TBOO VI, 95). Soon after the coronation he started for home to prepare the intended spring emigration.

stays.narrative: Starting north after the coronation, Tycho stopped in Nuremberg, centre of the German clock and instrument trade. He met Joachim Camerarius the Younger, physician-son of the humanist — the friendship 'contracted in a short time' that Tycho's first letter to him of November 1576 (TBOO VII, 42) fixes to this visit — and visited the shop of the fountain-maker Georg Labenwolf, whom he recommended for the Kronborg works and who later built Uraniborg's hydraulics. The contacts made here brought Nuremberg artisans to Denmark in 1577; the sculptor Johan Gregor van der Schardt was probably first met here or at Regensburg.

stays.narrative: On the road home Tycho visited Erasmus Reinhold the Younger at Saalfeld in Thuringia — the physician-son of the calculator of the Prutenic Tables, himself author of a tract on the new star. Reinhold showed him his father's surviving manuscripts, notably the Tables enriched with planetary equations of centre (prosthaphaereses) painstakingly tabulated for every ten minutes of anomaly, and — per Christianson — the elder Reinhold's annotations in Copernicus's De revolutionibus; he also gave Tycho the Almanach Astrologicum he had compiled for the previous year, for the sake of its matter on the new star. A formative encounter with the working papers behind the tables Tycho had just been lecturing from.

people.role: physician, custodian of his father's manuscripts; host and donor of his Almanach

Under vilken av resorna han i Saalfeld i Thuringen besokte Erasmus Reinhold d.y. (Prog.; III, 213), ar ej noga kant.

stays.disputes: Norlind leaves open on which journey the Saalfeld visit fell; Dreyer, Christianson 2020, Gassendi and Thoren all place it on the 1575 return — that placement followed.

stays.narrative: The last recorded station of the tour. At Wittenberg Tycho sought out Wolfgang Schuler, who had observed the new star with a parallax of nineteen minutes, expressly to inspect the instruments behind the figure: the large wooden triquetrum (probably built by Johannes Praetorius), still locally regarded as a great achievement, which Tycho found by no means as excellent as reported — marvelling that respected astronomers could think such a mean instrument sufficient — and the wooden quadrant with which the elder Reinhold had fixed the Wittenberg pole altitude, whose value Tycho judged nearly a sixth of a degree too great. He also found the university in chaos from the Elector's crypto-Calvinist purge, Caspar Peucer imprisoned, before completing the journey home to Denmark by the year's end.

people.name: Johannes Praetorius

Norlind flags the visit as self-reported, its placement on the 1575 return contextual rather than stated.

stays.narrative: Home about the end of 1575, Tycho made Knutstorp his base for the winter, secretly resolved to sell his share of the estate, buy property at Basel and leave Denmark for good — lying awake, in Christianson's phrase, wondering how he could escape. The Sorø, Copenhagen and Herrevad consultations of the following weeks all radiated from this base. In the early dawn of 11 February 1576, before he had risen from bed, a royal page who had ridden through the night was brought to his bedside with Frederik II's command to attend him in Zealand at once. The summons and its sequel belong to the next period.

stays.narrative: Back from the continental tour toward the end of 1575, Tycho presented himself to Frederick II at Sorø Abbey, where the court had come for the Yuletide. He reported his recruiting mission — glassmakers, papermakers, painters, sculptors and hydraulic engineers from Hesse-Kassel, Augsburg, Nuremberg and Venice, recommending Gemperle, Schardt and Labenwolf for the Kronborg project — and told of the courts he had visited and the Regensburg coronation, supping with the king at Abbot Iver Bertelsen's table. The king, primed by the returning Danish embassy carrying Landgrave Wilhelm's strong recommendation, received him with exceptional graciousness and asked him to name his requirements in fiefs and honours — Hammershus, Visborg, Helsingborg and Landskrona were the class of option. Tycho, privately set on Basel, demurred and was told to think it over; he afterwards wrote frankly to Pratensis refusing the 'golden shackles' of castle-holding.

stays.narrative: Throughout the Hven years Tycho went frequently to Copenhagen, as the Meteorological Diary shows, though nothing is known of his domestic arrangements there and no observations were made in the city. He owned a house in Farvergade in the south-west of the town; on 13 March 1589 the young king's government ordered the burgomasters to lend him the adjoining stone tower on the rampart for astronomical use (revocable if needed for defence), and on 25 March 1589 he received two empty houses next his own on condition of housing the displaced dyer. Dreyer counts the very frequent trips to Copenhagen and Scania among the burdens of the island residence, especially in winter. This recurring record anchors the diary-attested habit; individually documented Copenhagen trips stand as their own stays.

stays.narrative: The two-decade anchor residence. Frederik II's forleningsbrev of 23 May 1576 granted Hven rent-free for life so long as he pursued his mathematical studies, with 400 daler toward a house; Dançay laid Uraniborg's foundation stone at sunrise on 8 August 1576, and the solar series begun on Tycho's thirtieth birthday, 14 December 1576, opened an unbroken observational run to 15 March 1597. He commuted from the mainland until autumn 1576; Kirsten and the children settled from late 1577, the household moving into Uraniborg in November 1580. Around it grew Stjerneborg (from 1584), the sixteen-furnace laboratory, the instrument workshop, the printing office (1584) and paper mill (1592), and a familia of up to a dozen assistants; De mundi (1588) and the Epistolae astronomicae (1596) issued from the island press, and the comet of 13 November 1577 was sighted from his fishponds. Royal visitors included Queen Sophie (1586), James VI of Scotland (20 March 1590) and the king-elect Christian (3 July 1592, the gilt globe exchanged for the king's portrait on a gold chain). Dated Uraniborg autographs pin bodily presence across 1586–1596. Every documented off-island trip is itemised as its own stay.

stays.disputes: Foundation-stone date: Tycho's Mechanica gives 8 August 1576, the Lund fragment reads 1 August; Norlind supports 8 August astronomically (moon in Aquarius) — 8 August adopted. Departure date: 29 March 1597 (Thoren from Tycho's own statement; Dreyer's conclusion against the ledger's impossible '29 Aprilis'; Jönsson 'probably') vs 11 April (Christianson, diary entry of the household entering the Copenhagen museum) vs 29 April (Nielsen) — 29 March adopted for the end of residence, final resolution left to the period-7 reconciliation. Gassendi's index dates Christian's royal visit 1591; all modern sources 3 July 1592 — 1592 followed. Norlind (after Yrwing 1955) reads the departure as a feint to force restoration of income, which Thoren registers and finds unconvincing. Bjorklund's Bilag 4 dates the prebend loss 1596; Christianson/Thoren document the Roskilde canonry's transfer to Friis on 10 June 1597. First Hven solar observation: 14 December 1576 (Dreyer, Thoren, Jönsson) vs 13 December (Christianson 2020 p. 85) — 14 December adopted.

stays.narrative: Dreyer attests very frequent trips from Hven across the Sound to Scania throughout the residence years — Tycho held Knutstorp jointly until its sale (before 10 August 1594), the eleven Helsingborg-county farms and the Kullagaard fief, and kept an elk on his Scanian estate — but names specific destinations only rarely (Lund 1584, the Kullen order). Recorded at region level as the source states it; the individually documented Scanian stays (Helsingborg, Lund, Knutstorp, Eriksholm, Landskrona) stand separately.

stays.narrative: In the plague autumn of 1576 Tycho lodged Kirsten and Magdalene with the widow Margrethe Gagge at Tagalycka manor — his own presence inferred only from the act of escorting them. Kirsten gave birth there to a son on 2 January 1577 who died after six days; Tycho never saw the infant, and so was demonstrably absent at that point, composing a dolorous epitaph for his grave. Margrethe Gagge died 7 October 1577, whereupon Kirsten and Magdalene moved to Hven.

stays.narrative: From Herrevad Tycho went on to Copenhagen and talked the king's offer over with his best friend Johannes Pratensis and the French envoy Charles de Dançay — the two learned friends who had long urged him toward astronomy and who would donate the Uraniborg cornerstone. He privately told Dancey, himself an emigre after decades as ambassador, of the plan to leave Denmark, and inquired into Pratensis's failing health; Pratensis divined his inclinations and wrote at the end of January assuring him his interests were respected in Denmark. Only after this consultation, and further discussion with Kirsten, his mother and his brother Steen, did he decide to accept.

stays.narrative: In the days after the Ibstrup audience Tycho rode to Herrevad Abbey to discuss the king's proposal with his uncle Steen Bille, who had himself acted as a broker of patronage in shaping it. The consultation weighed the abandoned alternative squarely: with Peder Oxe dead since October 1575, selling his half of Knutstorp to fund a Basel establishment would entangle his mother and brother, and refusing the king's generosity would reflect on all his relations. Herrevad was the first stop of a deliberate circuit — Herrevad, then Copenhagen — before Tycho resolved to accept Hven.

stays.narrative: Tycho lay awake at Knutstorp planning how to slip away to Basel without alerting his relatives when, about two hours before dawn on 11 February 1576, a royal courier who had ridden all night arrived commanding him to the king at Ibstrup. He returned to Knutstorp the next day, 12 February, to contemplate the offer of Hven, struck that the courier had come at the very moment of his escape plan. From here he wrote the long letter to Pratensis describing the audience, consulted his mother, brother Steen and Kirsten, then rode out to Herrevad and Copenhagen before accepting at Frederiksborg on the 18th.

stays.narrative: Obeying the pre-dawn summons, Tycho rode from Knutstorp the same day and reached the royal hunting lodge of Ibstrup (later Jaegersborg) north of Copenhagen before sunset. The chamberlain Niels Parsberg — brother of his Rostock duelling opponent — showed him into the royal chamber, where in a long private audience Frederick II, who knew of the Basel emigration plan and had lately viewed Hven from the rising Kronborg, offered him the island for his experiments in astronomy and distillation, promising buildings and income so that foreigners would come to Denmark to see and learn. Tycho noted the island's dangerous landings, promised serious consideration, and was told to bring his answer to Frederiksborg. His own account, written three days later, is the primary source.

stays.narrative: One week after the Ibstrup audience, having consulted Pratensis and Dançay and certainly his mother, brother and Steen Bille, Tycho rode on 18 February 1576 to Frederiksborg Castle and accepted his sovereign's offer, renewing his service to Frederick II on new terms: an immediate annual pension of 500 dalers — nearly doubling his income — against his promise to be loyal and ready to serve when summoned. This audience formalised the contract of service that framed the whole Hven enterprise; the formal grant of the island followed on 23 May 1576, quit and free, with 400 dalers toward a residence.

stays.narrative: Four days after the Frederiksborg audience Tycho crossed to the island in the Øresund to acquaint himself with his new workplace — his first known visit, as its incoming lord over Tuna's freeholding peasants — and the same evening took his first observation there, a close conjunction of Mars and the moon ('Observatio haec facta in Huenna'). The formal fee of the island followed by royal letter given at Frederiksborg on 23 May 1576, the same day the treasurer Walkendorff was ordered to pay 400 daler toward building a house on Hven — the first documentary trace of Uraniborg.

stays.narrative: Until September 1576 Tycho probably commuted to Hven from Helsingborg, where Kirsten and the children were living. That month an epidemic sweeping from Copenhagen into Skåne carried off his eldest daughter Kirstine, not quite three; Tycho buried her in the church at Helsingborg and commissioned the bronze plaque, still in the church wall, recording her as his filiola naturalis who lived two years, eleven months, eleven days and eleven hours. For safety he took little Magdalene and the pregnant Kirsten out of the town and lodged them with the noble widow Margrethe Gagge at Tagalycka manor.

stays.narrative: After the September 1576 epidemic broke up the Helsingborg arrangement, Tycho probably went south to Landskrona and commuted across to Hven from there, unless he already had island quarters that would take him but not the family; by the end of the year he clearly had such quarters, observing on Hven through the Christmas holidays. The Landskrona lodging is Thoren's stated probability, not a documented residence, and is graded accordingly.

stays.narrative: A Latin letter written from Knudstrup on 3 September 1576 to the royal physician Peder Sorensen (Severinus) offers to pay for a monument to the recently dead Johannes Pratensis if Sorensen will compose the inscription; the monument was erected in Frue Kirke, Copenhagen. Document-grade evidence that Tycho was at his half-inherited family seat weeks after Uraniborg's foundation stone was laid — the dateline pair with the 21 November letter from 'Our Island of Hven' fixes the shift of his base onto the island during the first building season's autumn.

stays.narrative: Tycho attended the christening of the infant Prince Christian (born at Frederiksborg 12 April 1577) at Copenhagen on Trinity Sunday, 2 June 1577, with the usual solemnities, and on the two following days watched the students' plays of Susanna and of David and Goliath in the castle courtyard. He was then directed to prepare the prince's horoscope, delivering the detailed Latin report, with a German translation for the queen, on 1 July 1577.

stays.narrative: On 1 July 1577 Tycho delivered at Kronborg the extensive horoscope for the crown prince Christian, born 12 April 1577 — written in Latin with a summarising German section for Queen Sophie. It predicted a problem-free childhood, survival of a grave illness at about twelve, a life of 56-57 years under God's reservation, and a character fond of hunting and war; Tycho stressed that a four-minute error of the castle clock at the birth could overturn the whole prognosis. The astrologer-royal-adviser role in full function, five kilometres across the Sound from his building site.

stays.narrative: On a visit to Kronborg around 1578 Tycho met the master mason Hans van Steenwinckel, experienced in architectural design with a knack for perspective drawing; he invited him to Hven, taught him geometry, astronomy and Vitruvian architectural theory, and made him the practical builder of Uraniborg's complex roofs and later designer of Stjerneborg and the Hven mill house. Kronborg was the court pole of Tycho's world — artisans like Schardt and Labenwolf worked at both castle and villa — and such visits doubtless recurred, though this is the only one Christianson individually attests.

stays.narrative: In 1580 the Greifswald professor and Latin poet Johan Seccerwitz, in Denmark with the Duke of Pomerania for the christening of a new-born princess, met Tycho in the house of the Bishop of Lund, and recorded his joy at the acquaintance in a versified account of his journey. Dreyer does not state whether the bishop's house means Lund itself or the bishop's residence during the festivities; the meeting-place is recorded as the source gives it.

stays.narrative: During the comet of October 1580 Tycho notes in his own observation record that he observed it at Helsingborg from 20 to 27 October, while on Hven it was observed by 'Petrus and Paulus' — Peder Jakobsen Flemløs and the visiting Wroclaw mathematician Paul Wittich, working with a quadrant while Tycho used a radius across the Sound. A week's documented absence from the island, and a rare instance of Tycho conducting coordinated parallel observations from the mainland during the Hven decades; the town lay in the len whose Kulla farms he then held.

stays.narrative: Anders Sorensen Vedel, Tycho's old tutor and friend, retired from court and moved to Ribe in west Jutland, where Tycho attended his wedding in August 1581 — one of the family and social obligations that kept drawing Tycho away from Hven. One week later he was back on the island, where Kirsten gave birth to their son Tyge on 28 August 1581, the return fixing the trip's span within the month.

stays.narrative: As Prince Christian was hailed as future king in each province in the summer of 1584, Tycho appeared at Lund on 20 July among the entire nobility of Skåne and swore the solemn oath of loyalty, followed by representatives of clergy, burghers and peasants, the long ceremony closing with a festive banquet. Dreyer links to this period the curious unexecuted draft act dated 'Huenae in Autopoli Vranopyrgensi', 1 July 1584, by which the king would have granted Hven to Tycho and his heirs male for ever — evidence of Tycho's wishes and of an expected royal visit, but never engrossed or signed.

stays.narrative: Tycho went off to Jutland for the wedding of his brother Knud Brahe to Margaret Lange, celebrated at Bygholm Castle on 23 August 1584 and hosted by the bride's brother Erik Lange of Bygholm, the gold-making alchemist. He had sent his new Equatorial Armillary back for adjustments on 20 August before departing. The connection made here mattered: Lange's visit to Uraniborg followed a month later with his 'boy' Nicolaus Reymers in tow, seeding both the Ursus plagiarism feud and, through Sophie Brahe's later betrothal to Lange, the Urania Titani poem.

stays.narrative: Four months after Frederick II's death, Tycho sailed to Copenhagen on Sunday 18 August 1588 and stayed several days, speaking with the regents and mobilising his allies to secure Uraniborg's future under the new government. The lobbying — begun with visits by Kaas, Rosenkrantz and Vedel to Hven in July — bore fruit at once: on 23 August 1588 the Regency Council issued a patent proclaiming its desire to perpetuate the work of the Hven observatory, the crown having already agreed on 12 July to pay 6,000 dalers toward his building debt.

stays.narrative: During Rothmann's month-long visit of August 1590, Tycho took him into Skåne together with the aristocratic botanist Lauge Urne to Eriksholm Castle, where his sister Sophie Brahe lived; Rothmann admired her garden surrounding the 'distilling house' in which she prepared Paracelsian elixirs, perfumes, cosmetics and hermetically sealed preserves, and spoke of her after his return to Kassel. The party then returned to Hven, where Rothmann and Tycho observed together with the Triangular Sextant and Greatest Equatorial Armillary.

stays.narrative: In the elk exchange with Landgrave Wilhelm IV, who had offered a Hessian horse for a young elk, Tycho brought his pet elk from Knutstorp to Landskrona Castle, where it wandered into the great hall during a feast, drank so much strong beer that it fell down the stairs, broke a leg and died — as Tycho reported to the Landgrave by letter of 8 September 1591. His own presence at Landskrona is implied by Christianson's 'Tycho brought his pet elk' rather than stated as a dated visit.

stays.narrative: Shortly after Midsummer 1591 Tycho travelled from Hven to Copenhagen to attend a meeting of the State Council — the herredag gathering of the governing aristocracy. The departing guest-student Georg Ludwig Frobenius, whose memoir preserves the episode, sealed his trunk under Tycho's suspicious eye and travelled with him to the capital, where he promptly found a Lubeck ship and slipped out of Tycho's service.

stays.narrative: In February 1592 Tycho had to attend the provincial court (Landsting) of Zealand at Ringsted, probably in one of the matters of the Rasmus Pedersen tenant litigation referred there by the royal commissioners in 1591. A Latin epigram he wrote on the way home, 'In itinere a Ringstadio domum', complains of unfair treatment by the judge — the poem itself the contemporary trace of the journey.

stays.narrative: Plague on Hven had forced postponement of the king-elect's intended visit (Tycho sent his pupil Cort Axelsen across on 30 April 1592 to warn him off at the shore). When the disease vanished, Tycho himself crossed to Zealand on 30 June 1592 to the manor of Hørsholm, where the fifteen-year-old prince was residing against the plague, to announce that the visit could proceed; the governor could find no excuse to prevent it. Christian came to Hven on 3 July with three councillors, exchanged gifts — the self-moving gilt brass globe against a gold chain with his portrait — and promised support for training young men in navigation and astronomy. The 3 July visit is on Hven and belongs to the anchor stay.

stays.narrative: In September 1594 Tycho was in Copenhagen when Mogens Bertelsen Dallin, newly appointed superintendent of Holy Spirit Hospital and acting as Gellius Sascerides's marriage spokesman, approached him about a match with his daughter Magdalene; Dallin then sailed with Tycho to Uraniborg on Saturday 14 September 1594 to open the formal negotiations. The visit marks the start of the betrothal affair that would consume the next two years.

stays.narrative: Stung by a sharp royal reprimand over the ruinous state of the Chapel of the Three Holy Kings — with the threat that the canonry fief would be regranted if repairs were not done by Christmas — Tycho went to Roskilde on 26 September 1594 with Hans van Steenwinckel (or another master builder), inspected the chapel, and worked out a plan to replace the vaults with a flat beamed ceiling. The one documented bodily visit in a prebend tenure otherwise conducted entirely by letter.

stays.narrative: Tycho was in Copenhagen for almost two weeks, 6–18 November 1594, negotiating the terms and date of Magdalene's wedding to Gellius Sascerides. After continued negotiation through Gellius's spokesman Mogens Dallin, 15 December 1594 was fixed for the betrothal-or-wedding (the parties themselves seemed confused between the two); Gellius called on Tycho the next day, thanked him, and promised to act toward him as a son should. Tycho returned to Hven on 18 November believing the negotiations concluded.

stays.narrative: When Gellius raised new demands, Tycho sailed back into Copenhagen on 30 November 1594, presumably to attend to the wedding details, and conferred with his sister Sophie Brahe. On the evening of Tuesday 3 December he sent Niels Krag and Mogens Dallin to Gellius, who gave no clear answer; enraged, Tycho had a full summary of events drawn up and signed by Dallin, Krag, Else Mule, Sophie and himself. Next morning he stopped at Niels Krag's home to collect two Latin wedding verses of his own composing, stayed to dinner, declared he would leave public accusation to the Good Lord, and after dinner returned with Sophie to Hven — the diary noting on 4 December 'Rediit T. B. cum sorore S. B.' — to break the sad news to Magdalene. His formal declaration cancelling the wedding contract followed on 12 December.
