stays.narrative: In January 1595 Tycho was back in Copenhagen, where he first heard of the exchange between his friends and Gellius at Venusin's house a month earlier — gossip he judged to stem from Gellius's bragging around the city — and resolved to set the record straight. Rather than trying his complaint in Consistory, the university authorities mediated a settlement: a new contract dated Copenhagen 16 January 1595, signed by Rector Nicolaus Theophilus, Bishop Peter Winstrup and professors Anders Krag, Niels Krag and Anders Christensen, by which Gellius promised not to disturb Tycho or his family. Before leaving town Tycho had Anders Krag write up his account of the December scene; he returned to Hven on 21 January to bring the news to Magdalene and her mother.

stays.narrative: In the beginning of September 1595 Tycho spent a week at his mansion in Copenhagen. With his friend Bishop Anders Foss of Bergen in town, he hosted a dinner for the bishop, Jon Venusin, Anders Krag and the crown magistrate Peter Frandsen, at which he produced and read a documented list of the false rumours Gellius had been spreading — even Venusin, Gellius's brother-in-law, conceding some could hardly be denied — and warned that he would act if the slander continued. stays.narrative: To clear his name where Gellius now resided, Tycho travelled to Lund in January 1596 accompanied by Peter Frandsen, spoke with officials of the cathedral chapter, and put five written questions to Gellius at hearings before the chapter on 10 and 20 January 1596; Gellius promised answers within six weeks. The meteorological journal's note that Tycho was 'gone to Helsingborg and Skåne for ten days in January' evidently covers this circuit via Helsingborg. Immediately after the second hearing he wrote to Jørgen and Holger Rosenkrantz to shield the proceedings from court interference; on 5 February a royal missive ordered the Lund chapter to sit as a marriage court in the case.

stays.narrative: On 21 February 1596 Tycho sailed to Copenhagen and was gone from Hven for a month, pursuing his case against Gellius before the university court of Consistory. On the morning after Ash Wednesday, 25 February 1596, the appellate hearings opened in the medieval Consistory building; Tycho, accompanied by Dallin, Venusin and Carl Bryske, governor of Copenhagen Castle, declared he wanted no judgment, only a notarised public record, submitted the 16 January 1595 contract, and read into evidence a list of ten false rumours, standing to declare their authors liars. On 26 February Gellius pleaded illness and sent his brother David with power of attorney. The contemporary acts printed in Danske Magazin (1746) record these sessions and further proceedings in the Convent House; on 14 April 1596 the consistorium ruled on Tycho's preface, by which time some communications went by sent notes rather than appearance.

stays.narrative: In June 1596 Tycho was gone from Hven for nearly two weeks to attend the annual Diet of the nobility, which met to prepare the August coronation that would end the Regency. The great gathering assembled his brothers and kin at the peak of their oligarchic power: Steen Brahe on the Regency Council, Axel Brahe and Oluf Rosensparre admitted to the State Council that year, Jørgen and Knud Brahe holding the Varberg and Aarhus fiefs, cousin Steen Maltesen Sehested commanding Kronborg. His case against Gellius, however, was not ready in time for the Diet.

The business of the Copenhagen trip is not stated — the comet sighting itself is the trace of his presence in the city.

stays.narrative: Tycho left Hven from 28 August to 9 September 1596 to attend the coronation of Christian IV on 29 August, going with several famuli and wearing his golden chains with the Order of the Elephant and portrait medallions of two kings. His brother, Regent Steen Brahe, bore the royal orb; all four brothers played their parts and competed in the festive jousts while Tycho networked among the guests, including the Brandenburg court astronomer Johann Muller, who made a side-trip to Hven the day after Tycho's return, and the Scots ambassador Robert Anstruther, who also came on to Uraniborg. Bishop Peter Winstrup's sermon asserted that 'kings are gods' against the elective symbolism of the councillors' hands on the crown. Within a month the Nordfjord fief, at a thousand dalers his largest single revenue, was recalled.

The fief's recall dated 21 September 1596 was the first blow of the new reign.

stays.narrative: Tycho was in Copenhagen from 6 to 13 March 1597, still pursuing his case against Gellius Sascerides as his whole position crumbled — pension and Nordfjord already lost or about to be. The diary frames further commuting: an earlier Copenhagen absence had ended on 24 February ('Rediit Tycho cum mercatore quodam Germano Hafniensi'), and on Friday 18 March — the day his 500-daler pension was discontinued — it records 'Tycho goes to Copenhagen', the crossing that opened the removal itself.

stays.narrative: On Monday 11 April 1597 Tycho, Kirsten and the familia moved into the 'novum Museum Hafniense' — his own three-lot complex at the corner of Farvergade and Vestervold — with instruments on the rampart bastion granted him in 1589, the printing press and chemical laboratory in the house. The persecution peaked here: the pension had been stopped 18 March, and the assistants had already catalogued his books on Hven on 21 March; pastor Wensøsil, convicted at Roskilde 22 April, emerged from a month's dungeon to his shelter; the Hven peasants' charges were heard before the king; and in late May the town constable, on Lord Steward Walkendorf's orders, forbade him the bastion and city walls as an observatory. On 1 June he dismissed Longomontanus with a testimonial; on Thursday 2 June 1597 he left Copenhagen with a household of about twenty and every portable possession — instruments, laboratory, presses, books and papers — and never again set foot on Danish soil.

stays.disputes: Departure: Tycho's own statement 2 June 1597 (Acta 124; Christianson, Thoren, Norlind, Jönsson) vs Dreyer's inference 'between the 1st and 10th June' — 2 June followed. Start: household into Farvergade 11 April (diary; Christianson) vs Dreyer's April arrival and Thoren's rolling February–March move — 11 April taken as the residence anchor, earlier presence noted. The bastion observation ban rests solely on Tycho's own German justification (Acta 138) and 'sounds very apocryphal' (Norlind p. 255), though Christianson, Dreyer and Friis report it as fact; Björklund reads the Farvergade mob riot as camarilla-staged. Gassendi's hostile-commission and break-in details are Gassendi-only (grade C colour). The book cataloguing ('Registeret vi alle junkers bøger') stands under 21 March 1597 in the diary — on Hven, before the 11 April move; Christianson's weekday 'Saturday' for the 2 June departure is a slip (Thursday, Julian).

stays.narrative: Tycho travelled to Roskilde on Sunday 17 April 1597 — the meteorological diary records 'Profectus est Tycho Roschyldiam' — into a stormy night and next-day blizzard, in the week of the church-ordinance prosecution of his Hven pastor Jens Jensen Wensøsil, tried before Bishop Peter Winstrup on Friday 22 April with the Kronborg commander Ditlev Holck sent to 'assist'. On Wednesday 20 April he met his brothers Steen and Axel Brahe, both state councillors, presumably concerting a defence. Wensøsil was convicted on both charges — omitting exorcism, and failing to punish Tycho, 'who for eighteen years has not taken Holy Eucharist but has lived an evil life with a mistress'. The real target was Tycho himself; he still held the prebend of the Holy Three Kings chapel there, lost on 10 June to the chancellor. The diary stops abruptly on 22 April 1597, never resumed.

stays.narrative: At Gedser, the port on the southern tip of Denmark, the exile party took ship for the Baltic crossing to Rostock in the first half of June 1597: 'a few days later, they saw their last of Denmark. Tycho Brahe sailed away from his native land.' Most of the more than twenty travellers — Tycho, Kirsten, the six children, chaplain Wensøsil and the servants — would never see Denmark again. The embarkation point is Christianson's reconstruction; other sources have the ship taken at Copenhagen itself (Gassendi, Jönsson) or the route run via Lübeck (Norlind).

stays.narrative: Tycho and his familia of about twenty settled into temporary quarters in Rostock around mid-June 1597, warmly received in his old student city — Chytraeus wrote a welcoming note on 16 June, and Lucas Bacmeister still kept the house of the 1566 duel. At St Mary's he took Holy Eucharist with his family for the first time in eighteen years. On 10 July he sent Christian IV the proud Danish-language letter defending his departure and offering to continue his work 'on fair conditions'; the crushing answer, dated 8 October, reached him only at Wandsbek. He sought Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg's intercession (late July), wrote Erik Sparre on 7 September about a Baltic island from King Sigismund, and lent the young Mecklenburg dukes 10,000 daler at 12 per cent, bond dated 24 August, secured on Amt Doberan — he had not left Denmark impoverished. Plague striking the town, he accepted Rantzau's Holstein invitation and left on 8 September 1597. Sent originals to Moritz of Hesse-Kassel (17 July) and Sparre (7 September) anchor presence.

stays.narrative: The exile caravan passed through Vordingborg in early June 1597 en route to the Falster ferry — a resonant waypoint, for Tycho had spent part of his boyhood in the sprawling royal castle there commanded by his foster father Jørgen Brahe. Christianson stages here Tycho's meditation on exiled kinsmen who returned in honour: Peter Oxe, his brother Knud Brahe, Erik Sparre, Erik Lange. A transit stop within the reconstructed southern route; no dated document places him in the town on a specific day.

stays.narrative: From Segeberg Tycho and the familia proceeded to Bramstedt, where Viceroy Heinrich Rantzau received them with open arms in the second half of September 1597. Host and guest, friends since Tycho's Rostock student days, talked over patronage strategy and a suitable residence until a Danish restoration could be won. Under the delicate protocol of status Rantzau would not become Tycho's patron nor Tycho his client; as friend and equal he offered, of the eighteen castles and manors he and his sons owned, Wandsburg near Hamburg, over the head of its lessee Georg Ludwig Frobenius, Tycho's old Hven acquaintance. Thoren has Tycho still (or again) at Bramstedt on 8 October 1597, talking over the alternatives when he sent a letter to Basel.

Nothing is recorded of any halt, host or transaction; the party's pace between the fixed dates (Rostock 8 September, Segeberg by 17 September) brackets the passage.

stays.narrative: Leaving Rostock on 8 September 1597, the Brahe caravan proceeded westward through Doberan on the coastal road toward Wismar and Holstein — a pointed waypoint, since the whole Amt of Doberan had just been pledged as surety for Tycho's 10,000-daler loan to the young Mecklenburg dukes. Having refused to pay the sum out at Wismar, Tycho had offered to deliver it at Doberan in person, 'which probably happened' in Norlind's hedged wording; Friis, however, records only the promise, never the execution — and in 1601 it was Eske Bille and his servant, not Tycho, who travelled to Doberan and Rostock for the repayment. The passage is a named route stage in Christianson; no halt or business is independently documented.

stays.narrative: By 17 September 1597 the exile party had reached Segeberg fortress, seat of Viceroy Heinrich Rantzau's administration of royal Schleswig-Holstein — one of the castles Rantzau had offered — only to find the viceroy away at Bramstedt. From Segeberg Tycho wrote him the dated letter (TBOO VIII,5) that fixes his presence: the castle pleased him, but he had left Hven to relocate, not retire — he had books to finish and needed typographic equipment, engravers and printers, so he asked for a residence near a city like Hamburg or Lübeck and offered to come to Bramstedt to discuss plans. That criterion shortly selected Wandsburg. Thoren's 'first estate, too remote for his taste', from which the 17 September letter was sent, is this same station, not a separate unnamed castle.

stays.narrative: A year as Rantzau's guest — not client — at the moated castle of Wandsburg in Wandsbek on Hamburg's outskirts, living in quasi-princely style, honoured at church in a special loge. Christian IV's rebuff of 8 October 1597 reached him here; on 20 October he entered the account of his interrupted observations and composed the Elegia ad Daniam, and on 21 October resumed observing, at first with only a radius, from February 1598 with quadrants, sextant and armilla (pole height 53°36'; lunar eclipse 10 February with Rosenkrantz assisting, solar eclipse 25 February, lunar 6 August). His own press from Hven, worked by the Hamburg printer Philipp von Ohr, produced the Astronomiae instauratae mechanica (dedication to Rudolf II dated 31 December 1597, ready early 1598), while copyists lettered vellum exemplars of the 1,000-star catalogue; both went out to princes and scholars across Europe as the patronage suit which, brokered by Rantzau, Hagecius, Corraducius and the Elector of Cologne, produced the imperial invitation in the summer. He kept a laboratory, shared medical recipes with Rantzau, answered Kepler's Mysterium on 1 April 1598, and received a stream of Danish students, Müller, Fabricius and, from August 1598, Longomontanus. Day-dated letters and album leaves run from 2 January to 14 September 1598. Just after Michaelmas, 29 September 1598, the caravan rolled out toward the Elbe road.

stays.disputes: Arrival: late September 1597 (Christianson 2000 p. 220; 2020 'within the month' of 8 Sept) vs about mid-October (Dreyer p. 266, Thoren p. 381, Friis p. 246, Björklund p. 117, Bøggild-Johannsen) — mid-October adopted as the settlement date, supported by Thoren's 8 October Bramstedt letter; Frobenius found Tycho installed by 15 October (Christianson p. 285). Departure: 29 September 1598, just after Michaelmas (Christianson p. 233) vs 'beginning of October' (Norlind p. 297; Björklund Bilag 4) — Christianson's day-date followed. The Elegia ad Daniam: written at Wandsbek 20 October 1597 (Dreyer, Thoren, Christianson 2020, Björklund) vs Christianson 2000's vague 'later that same year'. Norlind doubts Christian IV personally composed the 8 October 1597 answer (a Saturday; the king had the letter only 'this week'). Christianson 2020 narrates the Brandenburg-electors meeting without a place inside his 1598 sequence — it belongs to Bramstedt, 22 December 1597.

stays.narrative: Viceroy Rantzau arranged for Tycho to meet Margrave Joachim Frederick of Brandenburg and Margravine Catherine of Brandenburg-Küstrin at Bramstedt on 22 December 1597, as the parents of Christian IV's bride returned home through Holstein from the royal wedding (Haderslev, 27 November). Tycho handed the margrave a letter and memorandum of his reasons for leaving Denmark, seeking intercession with his new royal son-in-law — either the permanent endowment of Uraniborg or leave to remove the four great instruments with compensation. The accommodating couple's letters to king and queen of January–February 1598 (25 January and days following) led to nothing. The meeting also renewed acquaintance with the Brandenburg court astrologer Johannes Müller, who had visited Hven in 1596 and would shortly join Tycho at Wandsbek.

stays.narrative: Tycho, his sons, Tengnagel and a small suite spent about a month in the Electoral Saxon residence city (late October to the first days of December 1598). He announced his approach to the imperial court through Vice-Chancellor Corraducius; the round trip of the inquiry took a month, Prague being gripped by plague and Rudolf withdrawn (to Pilsen, per Björklund's Bilag 4). Secretary Barvitius's reply — the emperor was pleased he was on the way but he should wait at a safe distance — turned him to wintering at Wittenberg. In Dresden he had an audience with Duke Frederick William of Saxe-Altenburg, administrator of Electoral Saxony, presenting illuminated copies of the Mechanica and star catalogue to the duke, the boy Elector Christian II and Chancellor Mosbach, and receiving a golden chain with three portrait medallions worth over 130 gulden. From Dresden on 28 November 1598 he dated the letter to the Doge of Venice — carried by Tengnagel across the Alps, proposing among other things the affiliate observatory at Alexandria — and wrote Magini after a seven-year silence. His son Tycho was sent back to Wandsbek to fetch the family.

stays.narrative: The caravan progressed up the Elbe to Magdeburg and halted about eight days in October 1598. Tycho met his long-time correspondent Rector Georg Rollenhagen — source of the first warnings of Ursus's plagiarism and of imperial-court intelligence via Caspar Lehmann, including the rumour that Rudolf meant to grant him Brandeis castle. Erik Lange, Sophie Brahe's absconded betrothed, turned up: Tycho barred him and his gold-making schemes from the Prague party, but before a summoned notary required his sworn public testimony on Ursus's 1584 conduct at Uraniborg — ammunition for the plagiarism war. Strategy changed here: the heavy instruments and baggage were stored at Magdeburg (they stayed until 1600), and Longomontanus escorted Kirsten and the daughters back to Wandsburg — prospects being too uncertain to drag the whole household on — while Tycho, his sons, Tengnagel and a few others pressed on toward Dresden.

stays.narrative: First call of the Prague journey: the caravan — three splendid carriages, Tycho's drawn by six horses, out of Wandsburg just after Michaelmas — crossed to the ducal seat of Harburg on the Elbe's south bank, where Tycho paid his respects to the aged Duke Otto II of Braunschweig-Lüneburg, whose daughter Duchess Elisabeth was married to Tycho's Swedish kinsman Count Erik Brahe. He presented an illuminated copy of the Mechanica bound in green silk, inscribed 5 October 1598; the fascinated duke asked for his nativity and reciprocated with a letter of recommendation to the imperial High Steward Wolfgang Rumpf — a document Tycho would produce at his Prague audience the next summer, alongside the commendations of Elector Ernest and Duke Ulrich.

stays.narrative: A dated album leaf — 'Suspiciendo despicio', Tycho's personal device (Sotheby's Paris, 15 December 2004, lot 36) — places him bodily at Wittenberg on 25 October 1598, between the Magdeburg week and the Dresden month. The Elbe road from Magdeburg to Dresden passed through Wittenberg, where, per Thoren, the Jessenius acquaintance was first made in passing; the leaf is therefore read as a transit attestation on the outward leg, not the start of the winter residence, which the biographies date from 4 December. A candidate host album, Johann Nesen's Stammbuch (Zittau, Christian-Weise-Bibliothek B 178, the Tycho leaf excised), records the entry under 26 October 1598 — a one-day discrepancy unresolved. An undated 1598 Wittenberg entry now trimmed into the Merseburg autograph collection belongs either to this passage or to the December residence.

stays.narrative: Tycho and his sons arrived in Wittenberg on 4 December 1598 and lodged with the anatomist Johannes Jessenius (Jan Jesenský) in Philipp Melanchthon's former house — later Caspar Peucer's, known to Tycho from his 1566 student days. He set up a chemical laboratory on the ground floor, observed the sun's meridian altitude on 9 December, and gathered a circle including the mathematician Melchior Jöstelius (who perfected prosthaphaeresis with him), the theologian Ägidius Hunnius and the poet Friedrich Taubmann. The total lunar eclipse of 31 January 1599 ran nearly half an hour against his lunar theory, halting the Progymnasmata Moon-section printing for recalculation — a manuscript ephemeris for 1599 was substituted as imperial gift. In February 1599, never before formally matriculated, he enrolled with his sons and famulus Johannes Eriksen; the rector feted him at the castle. Kirsten and the daughters, from Wandsburg 6 January, arrived mid-January. Coraduz's summons matured through the spring, but carriage horses, Magdalene's grave illness, thaw and floods delayed departure until 14 June 1599 — the farewell album leaf 'quo Witebergā discessi'. The densest dated-autograph run of his life spans the stay: 14 January (Hagecius Mechanica dedication), 28 February (his son's album), 6 March (Sinnich), 16 April (the Palingenius leaf, Sophia stock 6196), 8 and 29 May.

stays.disputes: Arrival: 4 December 1598 (Christianson p. 302, Norlind p. 298; Dreyer 'first week of December') vs an earlier back-calculation of this edition (c. 21 October, from a 236-day figure) and Nielsen's 'October 1598' interlude start — 4 December followed, the 25 October leaf read as an en-route touch. Departure: 'at Easter 1599' (Nielsen; Dreyer and Friis 'shortly after Easter'; Gassendi 'not before Easter, for the floods') vs the dated leaves of 16 April, 8 and 29 May and the 14 June 1599 farewell self-dating (Christianson, Norlind) — 14 June governs. Length: Jessenius's funeral oration says nine months; the documented span is about six and a half; the 236-day figure of that earlier reading (implying an October arrival) is unexplained. Cause of the halt: plague at Prague and the scattered court (all biographies, Gassendi, Jönsson) vs Šíma-Valeška's express rejection of the plague explanation — the plague account is far better attested but the objection is flagged. Calendar of 14 June: Thoren 'corrects Norlind' toward old style, yet Norlind's own text prints '14 juni 1599 g.st.' — a discrepancy of transcription, both in fact Julian. Family logistics: women from Wandsburg 6 January, arrived mid-January (Christianson) vs Dreyer's 'escorted by Longomontanus as far as Magdeburg, joined during the winter' vs Friis's separate route 'via Magdeburg to Dresden'. Dreyer additionally has the post-Easter departure leave the family 'half way, at Dresden' — against Christianson's 14 June departure 'with all his familia'; the day-dated leaf governs, the Dresden family-parking belongs, if real, to the 1599 journey.

stays.narrative: Inspection waypoint of the Bohemian settlement search. Offered the choice among the imperial castles of Lysá, Brandeis and Benátky 'zur Exercirung seines Studii', Tycho was driven around to view them all before choosing Benátky — Friis states expressly that he was conducted to all three. Nothing further is recorded of the Lysá visit itself; the viewing falls between the July 1599 audience and the removal to Benátky of 20–21 August.

stays.calendar_note: Bohemia used the Gregorian calendar. Dreyer has Tycho adopting new style from Prague onward (the 22 July 1599 eclipse date is n.s.); Thoren notes his 30 August 1599 letter to Rosenkrantz still dated old style.
stays.narrative: Arrival in Bohemia and the making of the imperial appointment. Reaching Prague in late June or the first days of July 1599 — Ursus fleeing the city at his approach — Tycho was greeted by the privy secretary Barvitius, received by High Steward Rumpf in long Latin conversation, and granted a wholly private audience by Rudolf II, who took his hand, accepted the three presentation volumes (the Mechanica, the vellum star catalogue, the sun-and-moon theory) and promised 3,000 gulden yearly with a hereditary fief to follow. He was lodged in the late vice-chancellor Curtius's house on Hradčany, where a painted pedestal in the Uraniborg manner was built; he signed the von Wicken album at Prague on 13 July; he observed the 22 July solar eclipse with his own instruments while his assistant watched from the Carolinum tower, and his Prague solar series ends 31 July. Finding the Curtius tower too small and dreading visitors, he asked for a country seat and was offered three castles.

stays.disputes: Arrival: 'late June' (Christianson 2000/2020), 'about the beginning of July' (Thoren, from Tycho's own letter; so too Jönsson), 'around St John's day/midsummer' (Norlind, Björklund), 'June' (Dreyer, Šíma-Valeška), 'spring' (Wolfschmidt) — late June/beginning of July followed; the 13 July album entry is the first day-precise anchor. Salary backdating: Friis has 'from 1 May 1599'; Thoren 'backdated to 1 May 1598' — left open. Salary amount: 3,000 gulden (Dreyer, Thoren, Friis, Christianson, Jönsson) vs Björklund's 4,000 — 3,000 followed. Lodging: Dreyer/Norlind/Gassendi/Björklund put him in the Curtius house at once; Christianson has 'suitable quarters' with the palace shown as an option; Thoren 'probably domiciled there' — Curtius-house lodging followed as best attested. Šíma-Valeška expressly deny plague in Prague at the arrival.

stays.narrative: First halt of the definitive move to Bohemia. Leaving Wittenberg on 14 June 1599 with the whole familia — a train of wagons, carriages and outriders — Tycho spent the first evening at Castle Pretzsch on the Elbe as guest of the Saxon hereditary marshal Johann (Hans) Löser, a courtesy the recently money-humbled astronomer thought worth recording for Rosenkrantz. The party continued upriver toward Dresden the next day.

stays.calendar_note: Saxony kept the Julian calendar: 14–16 June 1599 o.s. = 24–26 June n.s.; the Bohemian dates that follow are new style.

stays.narrative: The Dresden split of the household. Arriving on 16 June 1599, two days out of Wittenberg, Tycho left Kirsten, the daughters and their servants in the care of Johann Tauchmann, a high Saxon court official and brother-in-law of his Wittenberg collaborator Jöstelius, and went on toward Prague in his finest carriage with his sons and Claus Mule — a deliberate strategy of appearing before the emperor unencumbered, and of holding a line of retreat. On imperial instructions after the first audience the family was fetched, reaching Prague eight days after being sent for.

Datelines from Bohemia are new style — Tycho says so expressly in the 22 March 1600 letter ('epther denne Ny Stil'). Arrival is bracketed by the Brandeis letter of 20 August 1599 and the first instrument set up by 28 August; departure by the end of the observation series (end of June 1600, Studnicka) against Norlind's early July and Dreyer's c. August.
stays.narrative: The last observatory. Choosing Benátky nad Jizerou — highest of the three offered crown estates, c. 35 km northeast of Prague above the 'Venice of Bohemia' — Tycho arrived about 20–21 August 1599, had his first instrument mounted by 28 August, and set about remodelling the castle into a new Uraniborg with observatory and chymical laboratory, against the obstruction of the administrator Mühlstein and an empty treasury (imperial resolution of 10 December 1599: 1,000 gulden yearly from the Brandeis-Benátky rents). His first recorded observation there is 11 September 1599; datelines run 'from the imperial castle Benatky' from 7 September 1599 to 15 May 1600. Son Tycho and Claus Mule fetched the great instruments from Denmark; Longomontanus rejoined in January 1600 for the lunar theory; Kepler first met him here on 3 February 1600 and was set to Mars, the contract quarrel mediated by Jessenius on 5 April. David Gans came thrice from Prague, five days each. Observations break off at the end of June 1600, when the emperor recalled him to Prague.

stays.disputes: Departure for Prague: observations end at the end of June 1600 (Studnicka; Christianson 2020 has the household leave after Rudolf's 10 June return) vs early July (Norlind) vs c. August on Barvitius's advice (Dreyer); June followed as the modern consensus, with Friis's dateline gap (15 May 1600 Benátky — 26 September 1600 Prague) bracketing it. Kepler's arrival: 3 February 1600 (Dreyer, McEvoy in Crossroads) vs 4 February summons (Christianson 2020) vs 'January to Prague' (Jönsson, outlier) — 3 February followed. Longomontanus's discharge: 18 July 1600 at Benátky (Christianson 2000) vs 4 August / August 1600 (Christianson 2020, Friis, Norlind, Dreyer). The Hamburg-senate letter's two internal datings (29 September 1599 slug vs '27 jan. n.s. Benatky') disagree; both place Tycho at Benátky in 1599–1600. Jönsson places Benátky 'southwest' of Prague — a geographical error; the castle lies northeast.

stays.narrative: Seen on the castle-selection circuit and passed over — sitting low, the Emperor's favourite hunting-lodge — Brandeis nonetheless anchors the removal to Benátky: on the way there Tycho datelined a letter to Longomontanus at Rostock from Brandeis, 20 August 1599 (new style), reporting a level road about six hours from Prague and that an official of Brandeis would carry him and all his effects to Benátky that day or the next. Brandeis remained the administrative seat, under Kaspar von Mühlstein, from which his Benátky building funds were grudgingly managed. He never resided here.

stays.narrative: Plague refuge. After two thousand deaths in the Benátky district — a travelling companion of the visiting cousin Claus Steensen Bille sickened and died on arrival — Tycho took the frightened household to the castle of Girsitz in the first half of November 1599. He said they stayed six or seven weeks: his first letter from Girsitz is of 16 November, the last officially sent from there of 31 December 1599, with the return to Benátky in the new year; some intervening letters were addressed from Benátky 'just to avoid complicating things', so the exact return is unfixable. Some observations were made in December, and during this visitation the Emperor asked Tycho for the prescription of his elixir against epidemic diseases.

stays.narrative: The Kepler reconciliation. About three weeks after Kepler's angry departure from Benátky on 6 April 1600 and his withdrawal to Baron Hoffmann's house in Prague, Hoffmann's and Jessenius's mediation and Kepler's repentant letter brought the two astronomers together at Prague: Tycho drove into the city — something he had told Kepler he did not like to do — was reconciled with his errant assistant, and fetched him back to Benátky, where Kepler worked a further four weeks before leaving for Graz at the beginning of June.

stays.narrative: At the beginning of May 1600, while resident at Benátky, Tycho attended Caspar von Mühlstein's wedding in Prague — a sign of cordial relations with the estates' captain after the December 1599 settlement of their funding frictions. Tycho's own letter of 15 May 1600 dates it: 'wie ich fur 14 tage zu Prage, auf des Herrn Haubtmans von Brandeis Hochzeit gewesen'. In this period he grew acquainted with Protestant aristocrats including Baron Ehrenfried von Minckwitz, who blazoned the same arms as his Ulfstand grandmother, and Baron Siegfried von Rindscheid, the alchemist who had visited Uraniborg with Erik Lange in 1584.

stays.calendar_note: All Bohemian dates new style (Gregorian, used in Bohemia from 1584). Death 24 October 1601 n.s.; the older literature's '13 October old style' conflates the banquet date, and Kepler's '24 November' in the Rudolphine Tables preface is a slip refuted at length by Gassendi.
stays.narrative: The final residence. Summoned when Rudolf II returned from Pilsen on 10 June 1600, Tycho moved to Prague suddenly and permanently: first weeks in the noisy Golden Griffin inn on Nový Svět below the castle (twice summoned to the palace in one day), then a private house near Baron Hoffmann's by the Loreto square. The twenty-eight instruments — from Benátky, and the great ones from Hven via the Magdeburg transit dispute — arrived by October-November 1600 and were installed at the Belvedere; the press resumed the Progymnasmata; Jacob Monaw brought the Wittich library's annotated De revolutionibus copies in October 1600, and Kepler, expelled from Styria, returned destitute on 19 October 1600 and was set to refuting Ursus. On 25 February 1601 the household moved into the Curtius house, bought by the emperor. Elisabeth married Tengnagel on 17 June 1601; in September 1601 Tycho presented Kepler to the emperor and the Tabulae Rudolphinae were named. His last observation is dated 11 October 1601; the Rožmberk banquet of 13 October began the fatal illness, and he died at home on 24 October 1601, aged 54 years 10 months, charging Kepler to complete the tables in the Tychonic scheme.

stays.disputes: Start of the permanent Prague residence: June 1600 on Rudolf's 10 June return (Thoren, Christianson 2000/2020, Jönsson) vs 'about the beginning of July' (Norlind, from the 3 August postscript 'called a month ago') vs 'about August' (Dreyer) — June followed (modern consensus); Friis's datelines bracket it 15 May – 26 September 1600, his 26 July 'In eil, Prag' letter possibly the move itself. Death date: 24 October 1601 unanimous against Kepler's '24 November' slip (Gassendi's refutation) and the older '13 October old style' (Studnicka's correction: 13 October n.s. is the banquet). Time of death: 'around nine that evening' (Christianson 2020) vs 'between nine and ten in the forenoon' (Jönsson) vs morning (Friis, Dreyer) — morning better attested. Elisabeth's wedding: 17 June 1601 (Thoren, Jönsson, Christianson) vs Friis's 'between Easter and Pentecost 1601'. Cause of death: uraemia from prostatic hypertrophy (Norlind; modern opinion per Thoren; Christianson via Jessenius) vs the contemporary stone attribution (Wittich; no stones found at exhumation); mercury poisoning is excluded by the 2010 exhumation and uraemia is consistent but unproven — Christianson 2000's 'body heavy with quicksilver from Paracelsian elixirs' is not carried as fact. Norlind judges the Capuchin-protocol account of Tycho's court role 'extremely tendentious and certainly historically false in most points'.

stays.calendar_note: Observations resumed at the Belvedere on 2 December 1600 (Studnicka); it served until the Curtius house was fully adapted; Tycho's report of 24 January 1601 describes the establishment.
stays.narrative: Surrogate Uraniborg. In the Royal Summer Palace of Queen Anna — the Belvedere, 'non longe ab Arce in Caesaris quadam magnifice exstructa domo' in Tycho's report of 24 January 1601 — his twenty-eight instruments, arrived in Prague in October–November 1600 (Thoren: sometime in October, a few weeks after the Magdeburg consignment), were stored and mounted on the second-storey porch, and on 2 December 1600 the observations broken off at Benátky at the end of June were resumed; by Christmas night Tycho was observing. Pierre Bergeron (1607) records that the great Danish mathematician made his precise observations in the ground-floor arcaded galleries — reported rather than firmly documented for Tycho's own person. After his death the building housed the astronomical section of Rudolf's collections, a memorial musaeum with two portraits of Tycho.

people.name: Rudolf II
people.role: emperor; owner of the Summer Palace in whose 'magnificently built house' the surrogate Uraniborg was established

instruments: the 28 instruments transported from Denmark and Benátky (stored and mounted at the Belvedere)

evidence.quote: Tycho's provisorisches Observatorium 'Belvedere', wo am 2. December 1600 die Ende Juni in Benátky unterbrochenen Beobachtungen wieder aufgenommen wurden
set up on the second-story porch of a villa (the still-standing Belvedere)... By Christmas night Tycho was making observations
his instruments were placed in Ferdinand I.'s villa
Tycho's own use of the Belvedere is reported, not firmly documented

stays.disputes: Tycho's personal observing in the Belvedere arcades rests on Pierre Bergeron (1607) and the site record grades it 'reported, not firmly documented'; the resumption of the observation series there on 2 December 1600 is documentary (Studnicka), and Thoren has Tycho himself observing by Christmas night 1600.

stays.calendar_note: Move-in 25 February 1601 (Dreyer, Friis, Christianson 2020) against Norlind's 23 February at dawn; death 24 October 1601, all new style.
stays.narrative: Last workplace and deathplace. On 25 February 1601 the familia moved into the refurbished summer palace of the late vice-chancellor Jacob Kurz von Senftenau (Curtius) on Hradčany, bought by the emperor for 10,000 thaler and transformed toward a 'New Imperial Uraniborg'; observing resumed there on 3 March 1601, seven teams having taken the solar culmination simultaneously on 28 February. Elisabeth Brahe married Tengnagel in the house in June 1601; the Pruskowski Mechanica dedication of 12 March 1601, among the latest securely-dated Tycho autographs, was signed in this residence. After the banquet of 13 October Tycho returned here unable to pass water and died on 24 October 1601, Kirsten, Kepler and the household about him, Longomontanus and Tengnagel far from Prague. The Bohemian royal astronomer Alois David fixed the observation tower's coordinates in 1803; the structure was demolished in 1804.

stays.disputes: Move-in date: 25 February 1601 (Dreyer, Friis, Christianson 2020) vs 23 February at dawn (Norlind) — 25 February followed as better attested. The Crossroads/Studnicka sources call the house his 'last workplace' and say he died at his Prague 'home' without one sentence uniting the two; that he died in the Curtius house is standard (so the site record) but partly inferential in those witnesses.

stays.calendar_note: 13 October 1601, new style (Bohemia was Gregorian); the same date read as old style generated the erroneous '13 October' death date in the older literature.
stays.narrative: The fatal banquet. On 13 October 1601 Tycho went with the councillor Ehrenfried von Minckwitz to dine at the palace of Petr Vok z Rožmberka — by Thoren's reckoning (Appendix 5) the Renaissance palace on Hradčany square later known as the Schwarzenberg palace — a magnate of his bookish Prague circle, owner of some 10,000 books and manuscripts. Forbearing, as manners required while his host remained at table, to rise and relieve himself, he held his urine too long; by the time he returned home he could not urinate, and the eleven-day fatal illness began. The retention story is the contemporary tradition transmitted by Kepler's log and the funeral oration, not an established medical fact.

people.name: Petr Vok z Rožmberka
people.role: host of the banquet; owner of the palace from 1600; magnate with a 10,000-volume library

people.name: Baron Ehrenfried von Minckwitz
people.role: councillor who brought Tycho to the dinner

evidence.quote: Fuit ergo Octobris dies xiij. cum ab illustri Rosembergio invitatus nobilis Mincovvitius, Tychonem secum ad coenam deduxit

evidence.note: Appendix 5 identifies the Schwarzenberg palace as the 'last meal' site

evidence.quote: During a banquet on 13 October 1601 at the home of Petr Vok in Hradcany Palace, Tycho was indulging in his usual excessive eating and drinking
Den 13. October 1601 (ny St.) var Tyge Brahe tilligemed en vis Minkawitz indbuden hos Grev Rosenberg
by Thoren's reckoning (Appendix 5) the site of the banquet of 13 October 1601 at which Tycho fell fatally ill

stays.disputes: Venue: the identification of the banquet site with the Schwarzenberg palace on Hradčany square rests on Thoren's Appendix 5 alone (graded C in the site record); McEvoy's 'home of Petr Vok in Hradcany Palace' is loose, and the two accounts are merged here as one event at one (imprecisely fixed) Rožmberk residence. The banquet itself, its date and Tycho's presence are unanimous.

stays.calendar_note: Gregorian (Bohemia).
stays.narrative: The burial. On 4 November 1601 a solemn procession bore the coffin — velvet-covered, hung with his ancestors' gilded arms, preceded by the black damask banner with his title, his led horse and gilt rapier — across the Charles Bridge along the royal way to the Church of Our Lady before Týn in the Old Town, where the utraquist rite still allowed a Protestant service. Twelve noble imperial guardsmen carried him; his younger son Jørgen walked between Count Erik Brahe and Baron von Minckwitz, the widow following; the eldest son and son-in-law Tengnagel were abroad. Jessenius delivered the funeral oration, printed at Prague the same year. The red Slivenec marble monument — armoured effigy, hand on the celestial globe, 'NON FASCES, NEC OPES, SOLA ARTIS SCEPTRA PERENNANT' — still marks the tomb, where Kirsten was laid beside him in 1604. (This final entry records the burial rite of 4 November — Tycho died on 24 October; it closes the itinerary as the body's last journey, not a living presence.)

The grave's afterlife (1901 and 2010 exhumations) is out of scope for the itinerary.

journeys.label: First study journey: Copenhagen to Leipzig, February–March 1562
journeys.purpose: The prescribed foreign educational journey of a young Danish noble: sent by Jørgen Brahe and Inger Oxe to Germany's best law school, nominally for jurisprudence, with the twenty-year-old Anders Sørensen Vedel as preceptor, guardian and treasurer.
journeys.narrative: Departed Copenhagen 14 February 1562, arrived Leipzig 24 March — five and a half weeks by ship across the southern Baltic, then on horseback along the Elbe and Saale, passing through Wittenberg and riding two more days to Leipzig. Wittenberg is the only intermediate station any source names; Dreyer, Friis, Norlind, Jönsson and Christianson 2020 name none. Kinsmen had arranged a good reception in Leipzig in advance.

evidence.quote: Vedel and his pupil left Copenhagen on the 14th February 1562, and arrived at Leipzig on the 24th March following
De forlode Kjøbenhavn ... den 14. Februar 1562, og ankom til Leipzig den 24. Marts.
till vilken han anlände d. 24 mars 1562 efter att ha lämnat Köpenhamn d. 14 febr.
The journey by ship across the Baltic and on horseback along the roads that followed the Elbe and the Saale rivers took five weeks
I februari 1562 korsade de södra Östersjön, för att därefter färdas längs Elbe till Wittenberg, varifrån de landvägen fortsatte till Leipzig
Den 14 februari 1562 lämnade han Danmark i sällskap med den 20-årige Anders Sorensen Vedel.
in February 1562 they set off to Germany's best law school at Leipzig University
destinatus cum Paedagogo Lipsiam, illac sub Martii finem pervenit
He left Copenhagen on February 14, 1562.

journeys.disputes: A source record spanning the whole decade of the 1560s, with an ordering its own source cannot verify after Leipzig, is reduced here to the attested Copenhagen–Leipzig leg.

journeys.label: Return from Leipzig to wartime Denmark, May–June 1565
journeys.narrative: The best-dated of the early journeys: Tycho and Vedel left Leipzig on 17 May 1565 (Hegelund's date), passed through Wittenberg, reached Rostock on 25 May (Stephanius), and crossed the war-time Baltic to Copenhagen without meeting hostile cruisers, the Danish and Swedish fleets massing in the Sound. The onward legs — Copenhagen, Helsingborg, Malmö, Knutstorp, with latitude determinations under way — are Norlind's probable reading of the pole-height list in the oldest observation journal. Gassendi has a direct sail from Rostock to the fatherland.

evidence.quote: They passed through Wittenberg to see Schultz... reached Rostock on 25 May... Tycho proceeded to Helsingborg, Malmö, and finally Knudstrup Manor
Annotationes interiectae occasione puto itineris Lipsia per Witebergam, Rostochium
He left Leipzig on May 17, 1565. He came to Rostock on May 25, 1565.
In late May 1565, after three years in Leipzig, Tycho and Vedel came home to a Denmark locked in war

journeys.disputes: Gassendi's reading of the return as a recall occasioned by Jørgen Brahe's death is rejected (Norlind): the uncle died 21 June, a month after departure. The Scanian waypoints rest on the journal inference; Gassendi has the ship sail 'recta in patriam' from Rostock. Christianson 2020 ends the journey at Aalborghus rather than Knutstorp (see stay-knutstorp-1565 disputes). A parallel stationless record of the same return (Jönsson: probably at Jørgen Brahe's urging; Christianson 2020: home in late May) was merged here.

journeys.label: Second departure: Denmark to Wittenberg, April 1566
journeys.narrative: Early in 1566 Tycho left Denmark for the second time — without a noble hovmester, in the company of the M.A. Hans Aalborg and at least one other Dane — arriving at Wittenberg on 15 April 1566 (Stephanius: 'Returned to Wittenberg on April 15, 1566, from his fatherland'). Gassendi frames the departure as hastened 'not without a show of anger' at his relations' contempt for his studies.

evidence.quote: early in 1566 he left Denmark for the second time, and arrived at Wittenberg on the 15th April

evidence.note: departure from Aalborghus in this account

journeys.disputes: Point of departure within Denmark unspecified by most sources; Christianson 2020 has Aalborghus, Thoren the family seat (Knudstrup).

journeys.label: Plague flight: Wittenberg to Rostock, September 1566
journeys.narrative: An epidemic emptied the congested little university town: Tycho and Aalborg left Wittenberg on 16 September 1566 and reached Rostock on 24 September, 'fleeing on account of the plague' (Stephanius), an eight-day journey; he matriculated at Rostock the following month.

evidence.quote: he was induced to leave it on the 16th September... and to go to Rostock, where he arrived on the 24th September
Den 16. September forlod han Wittenberg; den 24. i samme Maaned ankom han til Rostock
Leaving there September 16, he came to Rostock September 24, fleeing on account of the plague.
Leaving on 14 September 1566, he and Aalborg arrived in Rostock... ten days later

journeys.disputes: Departure 16 September (Stephanius, Dreyer, Friis, the Nationalmuseet essays) against Thoren's 14 September; arrival 24 September is agreed. Stephanius followed.

journeys.label: Summer visit home and return toward Rostock, 1567
journeys.narrative: In the summer of 1567 Tycho travelled home from Rostock to order his affairs and visit kinsmen and friends; dissatisfied with his reception, he set out again at the close of the year. No waypoints are named by any source.

evidence.quote: I Sommeren 1567 gjorde han en Reise til Danmark ... derfor allerede i Slutningen af Aaret reiste tilbage til Rostock

journeys.label: Third trip abroad: Denmark to Rostock, New Year 1568
journeys.narrative: After his twenty-first birthday and the Christmas holidays at home, Tycho embarked on his third trip abroad, arriving at Rostock on 1 January 1568 — this time entirely without a tutor, amid friction with his father over the direction of his studies.

evidence.quote: he returned to Rostock, where he arrived on the 1st January 1568
Two weeks after arriving at Rostock on New Year's Day, 1568

journeys.label: Southward across Germany: Rostock to Basel, 1568
journeys.narrative: During 1568 — under the shadow of the unpaid duel fine, and freed from law by the canonry promise — Tycho travelled south across Germany, purchasing instruments at Nuremberg (Christianson 2020), and was matriculated at Basel by the autumn. The exact route is otherwise unrecorded: Thoren allows a possible meeting with his brother Steen at Arnstadt for the dubbing by Count Günther of Schwarzburg, and a 'perhaps Wittenberg' — both too hedged to log as stays. The traditional intermediate Wittenberg residence (Gassendi, Dreyer, Friis) is rejected by Norlind.

evidence.quote: During the summer of 1568, Tycho traveled southward across Germany. Perhaps he met his brother Steen at Arnstadt

evidence.note: left Rostock spring 1568; Basel autumn 1568; the 1568 Wittenberg stay rejected as a misunderstanding

evidence.quote: he was at Wittenberg some time in 1568, and went to Basle in the course of the same year

evidence.note: hedged early legs; Nuremberg and Ingolstadt placed on this southbound route in this account

evidence.quote: Från Rostock reste han till Wittenberg, varifrån han snart fortsatte till Basel
Anno postea partim illeic partim Wittebergae transacto, lustrare ulterius Germaniam decrevit

evidence.note: Friis has winter 1568–69 at Wittenberg and routes Rostock–Wittenberg–Augsburg with no Basel residence at all

journeys.disputes: The intermediate 1568 Wittenberg stay (Gassendi 'partim illeic partim Wittebergae'; Dreyer with a Mechanica citation; Friis, who even winters him there 1568–69 and omits Basel entirely) is rejected by Norlind — Dreyer's citation is to the wrong edition's foliation, and the documented Basel matriculation supersedes Friis's route; the Zusammenfassung keeps only 'über Wittenberg (?)'. Thoren's Arnstadt/Castle Neideck meeting for Steen Brahe's dubbing is speculative in both Thoren and Christianson 2020 and is not logged as a stay.

journeys.label: Basel to Augsburg by the Danube road, early 1569
journeys.narrative: Leaving Basel at the turn of 1568/69, Tycho turned the road to Augsburg into a tour of south-German astronomical practitioners: Schreckenfuchs's planetary models at Freiburg, the night-long dinner with Leovitius at Lauingen, and (on Norlind's redating) the call on Philip Apian at Ingolstadt, reaching Augsburg in time to observe from 14 April 1569.

evidence.quote: In Freiburg he noted some celestial models... In Lauingen he was invited home... In Ingolstadt he met Phillip Apian... Only in the spring of 1569 when he reached the old imperial city of Augsburg

evidence.note: Lauingen and Ingolstadt on the Basel–Augsburg leg, argued to spring 1569

journeys.disputes: Waypoint order and attachment vary: Thoren has Freiburg–Lauingen–Ingolstadt after Basel; Christianson 2020 places Nuremberg and Ingolstadt before Basel and Freiburg as an excursion from it; Gassendi, Dreyer and Håkansson move the Ingolstadt call to the 1570 homeward journey. Norlind's spring-1569 placement of Ingolstadt is followed.

journeys.label: Homeward from Augsburg to Helsingborg, May–December 1570
journeys.narrative: An unhurried homecoming whose route, previously unknown, is partly fixed by Norlind's find: last Quadrans Maximus observation at Augsburg 16 May 1570; the Textor album leaf proving Wittenberg on 9 September 1570; probably a call on the Rostock professors (Thoren); across the Baltic; and observing at Helsingborg Castle by 30 December 1570, the sextant and unfinished globe left in Paul Hainzel's keeping at Augsburg. The older tradition routed him through Ingolstadt with a Copenhagen landfall; the motive — his father's illness — is itself questioned.

evidence.quote: Witteberge: Anno: 1570: sept: 9.
evidence.note: last Augsburg observation 16 May 1570; Helsingborg observations 30 December 1570

evidence.quote: Tycho did not reach Wittenberg until September and probably visited with his former professors in Rostock before crossing the Baltic to Denmark
Tycho Brahe left Augsburg in 1570, but the exact month is not known, nor the route by which he travelled
forlod idetmindste Augsburg henimod Slutningen af Aaret, og allerede inden Aarets Udgang var han i Helsingborg
Traiecto Danubio, vidit Ingolstadii Philippum Appianum... postquam tamen Hafniam appulsus

journeys.disputes: Friis's late-1570 departure from Augsburg is superseded by the album leaf (Wittenberg 9 September). The Ingolstadt call placed on this journey by Gassendi, Dreyer and Håkansson is redated to spring 1569 by Norlind (followed). Gassendi's Copenhagen landfall, court salute and 1571 homecoming date are rejected on the 30 December 1570 Helsingborg observations (Norlind). The father's-illness motive (Friis, Jönsson, Håkansson 'probably') is doubted by Norlind given the unhurried pace and Otte's death only in May 1571. The Rostock call is Thoren's 'probably'.

journeys.label: The early-1574 Skane-Oresund observing circuit
journeys.purpose: Observation circuit between the family estates, the Bille abbey and the capital, documented from Tycho's manuscript observation books by the 1746 Danske Magazin compiler.
journeys.narrative: The compiler's continuous itinerary sentence has Tycho at the start of 1574 on his Skåne estates, observing at Herrevad Abbey in March and April (Dreyer, from the same books, extends the run into May), and in Copenhagen from late April and May, where he mostly lived for the rest of the year. The compiler also places him on Hven on 22 February 1574 'af hvad Anledning vides ikke'; that leg is excluded here because Dreyer showed the observed Mars-moon conjunction fits 22 February 1576, not 1574 — the first documented Hven visit therefore falls outside this period.

evidence.quote: Udi Begyndelsen af Aaret 1574. haver han opholdet sig paa sit Gods i Skaane, og i Februario ... har han været paa Hveen ... J Martio og April Maaneder har han observeret paa Herisvad Kloster, og sidst in Aprili saa vel som in Majo befindes han at have været i Kiobenhavn
In March, April, and May 1574 Tycho observed at Heridsvad
evidence.note: Dreyer's note refuting the 1574 Hven dating: moon and Mars fit 22 February 1576

journeys.disputes: The compiler (after Langebek, Danske Magazin ii. 194) has Tycho on Hven with observations on 22 February 1574; Dreyer (p. 86 n.) refutes the dating — on that day the moon was a few days old and Mars on the other side of the heavens, whereas the observed close Mars-moon conjunction fits 22 February 1576 exactly. The Hven leg is excluded from the route; the first Hven visit belongs to 1576.

journeys.label: The grand tour of 1575
journeys.purpose: Double agenda: openly, Frederick II's commission to scout artists, artisans and technicians for the Kronborg project (reported at Sorø at Yuletide); privately, reconnaissance for a permanent foreign home — resolved secretly in favour of Basel.
journeys.narrative: Departing about March 1575 as a grand seigneur with servants, portable instruments and probably Flemløs, Tycho went first to Kassel (late March-April, eight to ten days with Wilhelm IV), then to the Frankfurt spring book fair, southwest to Basel (the emigration target chosen), over the Alps to Venice — his farthest south — and back over the Brenner via Innsbruck to Augsburg (late summer to late October: the cracked Schissler globe, Gemperlin recruited), downriver to Regensburg for Rudolf II's coronation on 1 November (Hagecius, the Commentariolus), then home via Nuremberg (Camerarius, Labenwolf), Saalfeld (Reinhold's manuscripts) and Wittenberg (Schuler's triquetrum, the crypto-Calvinist purge), reaching the Yuletide court at Soro by December and Knutstorp for the winter. The outward order Kassel-Frankfurt-Basel-Venice and the return order Augsburg-Regensburg-Nuremberg-Saalfeld-Wittenberg are the consensus of the ordered sources; the two fixed anchors are the spring fair and the 1 November coronation.

evidence.note: Kassel late March; Frankfurt fair, Basel, Alps, Venice; Augsburg late summer; Regensburg 1 Nov; Nuremberg and Saalfeld; Wittenberg and return; Soro report

evidence.quote: he went first to Cassel... From Cassel, Tycho went to Frankfurt-on-the-Main... thence to Basle... through Switzerland to Venice... in the first instance to Augsburg... At Ratisbon... From Ratisbon Tycho returned home via Saalfeld and Wittenberg

Han begav sig først til Cassel ... Fra Cassel begav han sig til Frankfurt am Main ... Herfra drog han til Basel ... opholdt sig nogle Dage i Venedig ... Fra Venedig drog han til Augsburg ... Han begav sig nu til Regensburg

Contendit porro primum in Hassiam... Francofurtum ad Maenum petiit... Basilea placuit... dies aliquot transegit Venetiis... Vindelicorum Augusta transiit... Ratisbonam cum pervenisset... Inter redeundum vidit Saltfeldiae... Vidit etiam Wittebergae
Varen 1575 overgav han i varje fall katedern... I april anlande han till... Kassel... Darefter gick farden vidare mot Regensburg
Första anhalten på denna rekognosceringsresa blev Kassel... Den 1 november 1575 var Tycho närvarande i Regensburg

evidence.note: the journey characterised as reconnaissance for settling abroad; Kassel a week, Frankfurt fair, probably Innsbruck-Brenner-Trento-Treviso to Venice, return probably the same way, Augsburg, Regensburg, short Nuremberg stop, Saalfeld and Wittenberg hedged
the full sequential itinerary; the court at Sorø Abbey for the Christmas season

evidence.quote: Tycho Brahe traveled as a courtier, and his route went mainly to courtly centers of learning.
a visit made in 1575, during the last of his youthful travels around Europe

journeys.disputes: Christianson 2000's station list (Kassel, Venice, Regensburg, Augsburg, Nuremberg, Basel) is an unordered narrative enumeration; the ordered sources (Dreyer, Friis, Gassendi, Christianson 2020, Jönsson, Håkansson, Thoren) agree on Kassel-Frankfurt-Basel-Venice-Augsburg-Regensburg. Gassendi, Dreyer, Friis and Jönsson omit Nuremberg on the return; Christianson 2020, Norlind and Thoren place it after Regensburg — included. Norlind leaves the Saalfeld and Wittenberg placements hedged; the consensus 1575-return placement is followed. Padua (Jönsson 'hogst troligt') and Trento/Treviso (Norlind probable route) are excluded from the canonical route. Departure date: Thoren c. March 1575; Dreyer 'shortly after' the lectures ended early in 1575; Jönsson 'at the beginning of 1575'.

journeys.label: The Ibstrup summons and Hven decision circuit, February 1576
journeys.narrative: A fully dated circuit, documented by Tycho's own account written three days after the audience, that converted the planned Basel emigration into the Hven enterprise: the pre-dawn royal courier at Knutstorp (11 February), the same-day ride to the private audience at Ibstrup, back to Knutstorp to deliberate, consultation rides to Herrevad (Steen Bille) and Copenhagen (Pratensis, Dançay), acceptance at Frederiksborg on 18 February with the 500-daler pension, and the first crossing to Hven with its first observation on 22 February 1576.

evidence.quote: He arrived at Ibstrup that same day... he renewed his service to King Frederick II... on 18 February 1576... Four days after his royal audience at Frederiksborg Castle, Tycho Brahe was on the island of Hven.

En tidig morgon i februari 1576 kom en kunglig budbarare till Knutstorp... redan samma eftermiddag anlande han till det kungliga jaktgodset Ibstrup... red han en vecka senare till Frederiksborgs slott
He started the same day, and arrived in the evening at the king's hunting-lodge at Ibstrup, near Copenhagen
Tycho Brahe gav sig omedelbart i vag mot Sjalland och hann samma dag fram till jaktslottet Ibstrup, dar kungen befann sig.

journeys.disputes: Thoren places the Herrevad and Copenhagen consultation legs in January 1576, before the summons; Christianson's mid-February ordering is followed for the route. Four per-source journey records collapsed into this one canonical circuit.

journeys.label: Final removal from Hven to Copenhagen (February–April 1597)
journeys.narrative: The rolling evacuation of the observatory: Tycho's letter to Rantzau of 22 February 1597 — overlooked by previous biographers (Thoren) — shows the move to Copenhagen already in progress; the last Hven observation was made 15 March; the first crossing over was 18 March, the day the pension stopped; movable instruments, library, laboratory and press were boated to the Farvergade complex through the spring; and on 11 April 1597 the diary records the household's entry into the 'novum Museum Hafniense'. He never returned to the island.

evidence.quote: left Hven for the last time, shortly after Easter, on the twenty-ninth of March

evidence.note: rejects the observing-ledger's 'die 29 Aprilis': Easter 1597 fell 27 March; the household entered the new house 11 April; Tycho's own German account gives over two months at Copenhagen

evidence.quote: tog i April Maaned ind i sit Huus udi Kiøbenhavn, hvorhen han lod sig føre de mindst betydelige af hans Instrumenter, og hele sit Trykkerie
Tycho Brahe and his familia moved into the new 'museum' in Copenhagen. He would never return to the island of Hven.
On 29 April 1597 Tycho left Hveen forever, his press materiel and most of the instruments accompanying him via Copenhagen to Wandsbeck.
Han bröt alltså upp från Hven i mars 1597

journeys.disputes: The final island departure: 29 March 1597 (Thoren; Dreyer's argument from Easter and the diary) vs the observing ledger's 'statim a Paschatis Festo die 29 Aprilis' repeated by Nielsen — 29 March followed (Dreyer's demonstration; Thoren concurs).

journeys.label: Out of Denmark: Copenhagen to Rostock (2 June – mid-June 1597)
journeys.narrative: On Thursday 2 June 1597 (Julian) Tycho, Kirsten, the six children, chaplain Wensøsil, students and servants — more than a score of people, with wagons bearing library, instruments, presses, the great globe and ironbound treasure chests, under armed escort — left Copenhagen and reached Rostock by mid-June. Christianson reconstructs the southern road through Køge and Vordingborg (his foster father's boyhood castles), the Falster crossing, Nykøbing, and embarkation at Gedser; the endpoints and dates are secure, the interior stations are reconstruction. The route deliberately retraced Tycho's boyhood geography, framed by the exempla of returned exiles Peter Oxe, Knud Brahe, Erik Sparre and Erik Lange.

evidence.quote: southward to Køge and on to Vordingborg... to Nykobing... to the port of Gedser... sailed to the free city of Rostock

evidence.pages: Christianson 2000, pp. 211, 213-214; Thoren 1990, p. 389; Björklund 1992, pp. 21, 47, 97
evidence.note: endpoints secure, interior stations Christianson's reconstruction

evidence.quote: Färden gick antagligen över Köge och Lübeck till Rostock.
Conduxit subinde onerariam navim... Vela igitur fecit Tycho aestate paene media, ac iter direxit Rostochium
Den 2 juni 1597 steg Tycho Brahe och hans familj samt en del medlemmar av hans stab ombord på ett fartyg i Köpenhamn.
He must, therefore, have left Copenhagen between the 1st and 10th June
til Rostock, hvortil han ankom midt i Juni Maaned

journeys.disputes: Three incompatible route versions: (1) Christianson's overland caravan through Køge–Vordingborg–Falster–Nykøbing with the sea crossing from Gedser; (2) Norlind's 'probably over Køge and Lübeck to Rostock'; (3) a ship boarded at Copenhagen itself (Gassendi's hired cargo vessel; Jönsson; Friis 'fragtede et Skib'). The 2 June departure from Copenhagen is Tycho's own dated statement and secure; the mode and stations of the crossing are not — all three versions preserved. Gassendi's 'aestate paene media' (almost midsummer) is loose but compatible. Christianson 2000 calls 2 June a Saturday; 2 June 1597 (Julian) fell on a Thursday — the date itself, Tycho's own (Acta 124), is secure; the weekday is Christianson's slip.

journeys.label: Rostock to Wandsburg via Segeberg and Bramstedt (8 September – mid-October 1597)
journeys.narrative: Fleeing the Rostock pestilence with no royal answer in hand, the familia left Rostock on 8 September 1597 and moved westward through Doberan (the Amt just pledged for Tycho's loan) and Wismar into Holstein, reaching the viceregal fortress of Segeberg by 17 September. Rantzau being at Bramstedt, Tycho wrote ahead stating his need of a residence near a printing city; at Bramstedt the viceroy received the party with open arms and lent Wandsburg over its lessee's head. The move formalised the friend-and-guest, not patron-client, relation with Rantzau. Settlement at Wandsbek followed in mid-October (Thoren, Dreyer, Friis) or late September (Christianson).

evidence.quote: took their leave of Rostock on 8 September 1597 and proceeded westward through Doberan and Wismar... By 17 September, they had arrived at Segeberg Fortress

evidence.pages: Christianson 2000, pp. 217–220; Dreyer 1890, p. 266; Björklund 1992, p. 98 (Bilag 4)
evidence.note: arrival late September (Christianson) or mid-October (Dreyer)

evidence.quote: Färden gick sannolikt över Wismar till Segeberg i Holstein
Around the middle of October, therefore, Tycho settled into a nicely renovated old castle on the outskirts of Hamburg
Invitatus ab Henrico Rantzovio omnia Wandesburgum, per Hamburgum transfert
evidence.note: the goods moved via Hamburg; not a bodily Hamburg stay

evidence.pages: Håkansson ed. 2006, scan pp. 70–71; Tycho Brahes Verden, scan p. 214
evidence.note: early-September departure under armed escort (Håkansson) vs the Wandsbeck move 'from mid-October' (Bøggild-Johannsen)

journeys.disputes: Wandsbek settlement: late September 1597 (Christianson) vs mid-October (Dreyer, Thoren, Friis, Björklund, Bøggild-Johannsen) — mid-October adopted, with Thoren's 8 October Bramstedt letter as the hinge. Thoren's unnamed 'first estate, too remote' is identified with Segeberg (same 17 September letter). Dreyer and Friis, lacking the Holstein stations, run Rostock direct to Wandsbek in mid-October — compression, not conflict, once the September stations are admitted.

journeys.label: The interrupted Prague journey: Wandsburg to Wittenberg via Harburg, Magdeburg and Dresden (29 September – 4 December 1598)
journeys.narrative: The first push toward Rudolf II, doubling as a patronage campaign — each halt yielded a recommendation, deposition or princely contact. Out of Wandsburg just after Michaelmas, 29 September 1598, in a caravan of three or more coaches: the Harburg call on Duke Otto II (Mechanica inscribed 5 October); about eight days at Magdeburg (Rollenhagen; Erik Lange's notarised Ursus deposition; instruments stored; Kirsten and the daughters sent back to Wandsburg with Longomontanus); up the Elbe through Wittenberg (album leaf 25 October, the Jessenius acquaintance made in passing); a month at Dresden awaiting imperial instructions (Venice and Magini letters 28 November); then, advised to defer Prague for the plague, the hundred-kilometre retreat to Wittenberg, reached 4 December 1598, for the winter.

evidence.quote: Just after Michaelmas... 29 September 1598... The caravan progressed as far as Magdeburg, where they stayed for a week... to Dresden, where they remained for a month.
Around Michaelmas of 1598, Tycho and his familia departed Wandsburg Castle in a caravan of at least four coaches surrounded by retainers

evidence.pages: Friis 1871 (exact page in the bundled consultation)
evidence.quote: Han gav sig da paa Reisen i Begyndelsen af October Maaned 1598 med sine Sønner og Studenter
evidence.note: Danish quote — Friis's idiom; the pages field bundles the exile-package consultations: Christianson 2000, pp. 233–235; Björklund 1992, p. 98 (Bilag 4); Norlind 1970, p. 298; Thoren 1990, pp. 416–417

evidence.quote: Till Böhmen och Prag bröt man upp först strax efter Michaeli, närmare bestämt i början på oktober.
evidence.note: Tycho's own brief descriptions in letters of December 1598 to Krag, Rosenkrantz, later Vedel

evidence.quote: For the first leg of the journey they traveled some two hundred kilometers to Magdeburg... he had retreated one hundred kilometers back to Wittenberg
evidence.note: the Magdeburg–Dresden passage ran through Wittenberg

evidence.quote: Kort efter reiste Tyge Brahe fra Wandesborg ... Men da han kom til Dresden
evidence.note: compressed route Wandsbek–Dresden–Wittenberg, without Harburg or Magdeburg

evidence.quote: non Pragam usque perrexerit, sed Wittebergae constiterit
evidence.note: maximally compressed: Wandsbek to Wittenberg

evidence.pages: Graphonomicon, specimens rundetaarn-boetius-album-wandsbek-1598, leaf-wittenberg-1598–10-25 and uppsala-waller-dk-00231
evidence.note: the album-leaf itinerary: Wandsbek 13 Sept; Wittenberg 25 Oct; Dresden 10 Nov

evidence.pages: the Epistolarium's letters spine; the specimens as cited
evidence.note: Wandsbek → Wittenberg [1598]; the 'Dresden excursion' framing rejected in favour of the biographies' sequence

journeys.disputes: Departure: 29 September 1598 (Christianson) vs beginning of October (Norlind, Björklund Bilag 4). Route order: an earlier reading framed Wittenberg as reached c. 21 October with Dresden a mid-November excursion; the biographies' Magdeburg → Dresden (month) → Wittenberg 4 December is followed, the 25 October Wittenberg leaf explained by Thoren's note that the Elbe road passed through Wittenberg. Friis and Gassendi compress the route (omitting Harburg and Magdeburg, and Dresden in Gassendi's case). The press materiel and heavy instruments travelled separately and wintered at Magdeburg, reaching Prague only in 1600 (Christianson, p. 337; Nielsen; Wolfschmidt: November 1600).

journeys.label: Wittenberg to Prague via Pretzsch and Dresden, 14 June – early July 1599
journeys.narrative: The definitive move to imperial service on Coraduz's summons. The whole familia left Wittenberg on 14 June 1599 — the departure self-dated in Tycho's farewell album leaf, 'quo Witebergā discessi' — spent the first night at Castle Pretzsch with Johann Löser, and reached Dresden on 16 June, where the female household was left with Johann Tauchmann. Tycho crossed the Ore Mountains with his sons and Claus Mule in his finest carriage, Ursus fleeing Prague at his approach; arrival fell in late June or the first days of July, and the von Wicken album entry of 13 July 1599 attests him at Prague within the month. The family followed from Dresden after the first audience.

evidence.quote: Tycho Brahe and all his familia took leave of Wittenberg on 14 June 1599... He proceeded on to Prague in his finest carriage with his son, Tycho Tygesen, and a few servants.
They left right after summer solstice, traveling en masse to Dresden... On arriving there 'about the beginning of July'
Den 14 juni 1599 g.st. bröt Tycho upp från Wittenberg till Prag
Tyge Brahe begav sig nu paa Reisen dertil strax efter Paaske 1599, og han lagde Veien over Dresden

evidence.pages: Graphonomicon, specimens leaf-wittenberg-1599–06-14 and stralsund-khm-a-1993-160-wicken; the Epistolarium's letters spine
evidence.quote: Wittenberg → Prague [1599]. Entered the service of Rudolf II.

journeys.disputes: Friis dates the departure 'straight after Easter 1599' against the self-dated 14 June album leaf and all modern accounts — June followed. Departure style: Norlind and Thoren mark 14 June as old style; Christianson gives it without style. Arrival: late June (Christianson) vs 'about the beginning of July' (Thoren, from Tycho's own letter) — not resolvable below a fortnight.

journeys.label: The castle-inspection circuit: Lysá, Brandeis, Benátky (summer 1599)
journeys.narrative: Offered the choice of three imperial castles outside Prague 'zur Exercirung seines Studii' — each under a day or half-day from the city — Tycho was conducted around to see them all: Lysá, Brandeis and Benátky. Brandeis, sitting low and the Emperor's favourite hunting-lodge, and Lysá were passed over; Benátky was chosen for its raised site and open horizon. The order of the circuit is not given by any source; the route order here is the sources' listing order, not an itinerary.

evidence.quote: efter at han var bleven foert omkring til dem alle for at besee dem, valgte han det sidstnaevnte
quarum illi Caesar extra urbem optionem dedit, quasque sub Maij finem invisit, tres fuere... Brandisium... Lyssa... Benachia

journeys.disputes: Gassendi dates the circuit 'sub Maij finem' 1599 — irreconcilable with the late-June Prague arrival; the circuit is placed between the July audience and the 20–21 August removal.

journeys.label: Removal from Prague to Benátky via Brandeis, 20-21 August 1599
journeys.narrative: The removal to the chosen castle. On the way from Prague Tycho datelined a letter to Longomontanus at Rostock from Brandeis, 20 August 1599 (new style), reporting a level six-hour road and that a captain of Brandeis would carry him and all his effects to Benátky the same or the following day; by 28 August his first instrument stood at Benátky. Christianson has him formally escorted there in late August.

evidence.quote: skrev han den 20. August (ny Stiil) fra Brandeis
On the way to Benatky, Tycho sent from Brandeis a letter to Longomontanus at Rostock, dated the 20th August
Tycho chose Benatky and was escorted there in late August
By 28 August Tycho had his first instrument set up at Benatky

journeys.label: Plague flight to Girsitz and back, November 1599 – January 1600
journeys.narrative: Escape from the plague that killed two thousand in the Benátky district: in the first half of November 1599 Tycho moved the household to the castle or village of Girsitz (first letter 16 November) and returned to Benátky in the new year after six or seven weeks, the return date blurred by letters diplomatically addressed from Benátky.

evidence.quote: to take the family thirty kilometers down river, to a castle called Girsitz, to escape the plague

journeys.disputes: Direction and distance of Girsitz from Benátky differ across the sources (thirty kilometres downriver vs a few miles south vs 'near Kostelec') — see stay-girsitz-1599.

journeys.label: Final removal from Benátky to Prague, June 1600
journeys.narrative: The end of the Benátky observatory project. Rudolf II returned from Pilsen on 10 June 1600 and summoned his astronomer to the capital for constant consultation — a move Tycho's own 26 September 1600 letter calls made by imperial order ('beschehenes Anordnenn von dannen hieher nach Prage'), and which proved sudden and permanent. The Benátky observation series breaks off at the end of June 1600; the household passed through the Golden Griffin and the Hoffmann-neighbourhood house before the Curtius house; the instruments followed from Benátky, and the great ones from Hven via the Magdeburg transit dispute, to the Belvedere by October-November 1600. Only Tycho's effects, not Tycho, passed through Magdeburg.

evidence.quote: On 10 June, however, the emperor returned home from Pilsen and summoned Tycho to Prague... he was asked to move to Prague, suddenly, and, as it turned out, permanently
beschehenes Anordnenn von dannen hieher nach Prage
Tycho pertaesus incommodorum Benaticae, commorari amplius ea in arce non sustineret

evidence.pages: Studnicka 1901, scan p. 67; Crossroads 2002, scan pp. 129–130

journeys.disputes: Timing of the move: June 1600 (Thoren, Christianson, Studnicka's end-June observation break) vs beginning of July (Norlind) vs c. August (Dreyer); Friis's datelines bracket it 15 May – 26 September 1600. June followed.

non_visits.claim: Schooling at Sorø 1559–62, concurrent with the Copenhagen university years

evidence.quote: Tycho was educated at Sorø (1559–62), Copenhagen (1559–62), Leipzig (1562–65), then Wittenberg, Rostock, Augsburg, and Basel
evidence.note: Same date-range given for Sorø and Copenhagen; internally suspect; graded D on first reading

non_visits.disputes: Single passing mention, internally inconsistent with the same source's Copenhagen claim, uncorroborated in any other source — removed from the stays to the phantom register.
non_visits.label: Sorø (the claimed Latin-school years, 1559–62)
non_visits.narrative: Asserted only by an earlier compilation of the album leaves, which gives Sorø and Copenhagen identical 1559–62 date-ranges in the same sentence — an internal duplication betraying compression or conflation. No other source places Tycho at Sorø in these years; all ten sources for the period put him at the University of Copenhagen. Recorded in the phantom register rather than as a stay; if a Sorø schooling tradition exists it belongs, undated, to the pre-1559 period.

non_visits.label: Alexandria, Egypt (affiliate observatory)
non_visits.claim: Tycho established, or travelled to, the planned affiliate observatory at Alexandria.
non_visits.narrative: The Egyptian station was a recurrent scheme only: proposed to the Doge of Venice in the letter of 28 November 1598, revived around 1600 with Tycho Tygesen and Claus Mule as intended staff, and never executed. The Mechanica's claim that the Venetian Senate approved 300 ducati for the project is unverified — no document has been found in the Venetian archives (Favaro and Norlind both searched). No travel by Tycho, or by anyone, took place.

evidence.note: Scheme proposed 1598, revived c.1600, never executed.
Venetian funding claim unverified in the archives.

non_visits.label: Wartenberg / Brebistorff visits from Benátky (Pentecost 1600)
non_visits.claim: Tycho carried out the visit promised to Carl von Wartenberg for Pentecost 1600, having declined Gotfred von Brebistorff's invitation.
non_visits.narrative: The letter of 15 May 1600 documents intentions only: a promised visit to Wartenberg (with Ehrenfried von Minckwitz) and a declined invitation from Brebistorff. No follow-up in the sources confirms the Wartenberg journey was ever made. Both are logged so that the promise is not silently upgraded to an executed stay — the declined invitation by definition, the promised visit for want of any evidence of execution.

evidence.note: Intentions in a letter; no execution documented.

non_visits.label: Brandýs nad Labem (Brandeis)
non_visits.claim: Tycho resided at Brandýs (Brandeis), the imperial estate Rudolf II offered him in 1599.
non_visits.narrative: Brandeis — the emperor's favourite hunting-lodge — was one of three estates offered in 1599. Tycho inspected it and declined it, taking the smaller hilltop Benátky instead; Thoren suggests he was concerned about depriving the emperor of so grand a property, and it appears in his finances only as a rent source for his salary. His sole attested bodily presence is a datelined letter of 20 August 1599 en route to Benátky — a stop, not a residence.

evidence.note: Imperial castle offered, inspected and declined.
Declined in favour of Benátky; rent source only.
Lehmann's 1598 report of the intended grant; Benátky given in the event.

evidence.quote: Tycho never lived there.

evidence.note: Letter datelined Brandeis 20 August 1599 (n.s.) — transit presence only.

non_visits.label: Breslau/Wrocław (Wittich library)
non_visits.claim: Tycho travelled to Breslau/Wrocław to collect Paul Wittich's library.
non_visits.narrative: Tycho pursued the Wittich books for years by negotiation with the heirs, and the purchase was consummated remotely: Jacob Monaw brought the annotated De revolutionibus copies from Wrocław to Tycho in Prague in October 1600 — only two of Wittich's four annotated copies ever reached him. Tycho did not go to Silesia.

evidence.note: Copies brought TO Tycho in Prague by Monaw, October 1600.

evidence.pages: BRAHE — De revolutionibus (Prague NK 14 B 16) entry
evidence.note: Monaw acquisition channel independently documented.

non_visits.label: Carolinum tower, Prague (eclipse of 22 July 1599)
non_visits.claim: Tycho observed the solar eclipse of 22 July 1599 from the tower of the old Collegium (Carolinum).
non_visits.narrative: Tycho's own letter (TBOO VIII, 183) says the eclipse was observed at the Carolinum tower 'per Iohannem meum Hamburgensem, adstantibus aliis' — by his Hamburg assistant Johannes (Eriksen), with bystanders — while Tycho himself worked with quadrant and sextant at his residence. Christianson agrees: he 'sent Johannes Eriksen up the tower'. The Carolinum therefore never enters Tycho's personal itinerary on this evidence.

evidence.quote: Pragae quoque in turricula veteris Collegii ... per Iohannem meum Hamburgensem, adstantibus aliis

evidence.note: Sent Eriksen up the tower; observed at his residence himself.

non_visits.label: Copenhagen (astronomical observations from the rampart)
non_visits.claim: Tycho observed astronomically at Copenhagen during his visits from Hven, e.g. from the rampart tower by his Farvergade house.
non_visits.narrative: Dreyer states flatly that 'No observations were made at Copenhagen': the lent bastion tower was intended for a planned astronomical building for practising residents, never used so by Tycho before 1597.
