The companion persecution story — that the town bailiff forbade him to observe from it in 1597 — rests solely on Tycho's own German justification and 'sounds very apocryphal' (Norlind). Copenhagen remains a grade-A place for residence and business, not for observation.

evidence.quote: No observations were made at Copenhagen

evidence.note: The 1597 prohibition story judged apocryphal.

non_visits.label: Copenhagen (Christian IV's coronation, August 1596)
non_visits.claim: Tycho attended Christian IV's coronation.
non_visits.narrative: The summons survives — 2 May 1596, commanding the nobility 'at de selv personlig kunne møde hos Kongen' — but only the summons. Friis mentions the coronation's extravagance solely as context for the retrenchments that cost Tycho his fiefs, and Tycho's own letter says merely that he lost Nordfjord 'about Michaelmas straight after the coronation'. Attendance is plausible, but nowhere documented; the chancery rule that invitations do not prove attendance governs.

evidence.pages: Friis 1871 p. 227; Danske Magazin 3R Bd 3 pp. 79–80
evidence.note: Coronation as context only; no presence claim.
Personal summons of 2 May 1596; execution undocumented.

non_visits.label: Hven (visit by Jacob Curtius, c. 1594)
non_visits.claim: Imperial vice-chancellor Jacob Curtius visited Tycho at Hven around 1594 and left a plan of his Prague house.
non_visits.narrative: Gassendi's story of Curtius travelling to Denmark lacks any traceable authority, and Dreyer notes that Curtius is nowhere mentioned in the Meteorological Diary, 'so he can hardly have been at Hveen'. The tale matters because Tycho later died in the Curtius house on Hradčany — a neat narrative arc that the evidence will not carry. Bears on the Hven visitor register, not on Tycho's own itinerary.

evidence.quote: so he can hardly have been at Hveen

non_visits.label: Doberan (loan delivery)
non_visits.claim: Tycho travelled to Doberan in 1597 to deliver the 10,000-daler loan to the Mecklenburg dukes.
non_visits.narrative: Tycho only promised to bring the money to Doberan himself once the bond was corrected (September 1597); Friis records no execution of the promise. At the repayment end in 1601 it was Eske Bille and his servant who went to Doberan and Rostock — Tycho, then in Prague, was never there for the transaction. A probable simple road-stop at Doberan in September 1597 (Norlind) survives as a waypoint stay, distinct from this loan-delivery journey.

evidence.note: Promise only; Eske Bille executed the 1601 repayment errand.

non_visits.label: Family rites off Hven (weddings, funerals, burials)
non_visits.claim: Tycho left Hven for family rites — Axel Brahe's second wedding, his brother-in-law's funeral, the burials of his children at Helsingborg (1576) and Väsby (1577), the Kågeröd mausoleum epitaph.
non_visits.narrative: Ellefsen states the opposite of the natural assumption: at Axel's second wedding both Tycho and Sophie stayed on Hven, and when their sister Margrethe's husband died, Tycho did not leave Uraniborg; Inger Oxe's death and funeral he does not even mention. Verden records the children's burials and Tycho's authorship of the Helsingborg epitaph text without any attendance, and expressly doubts his personal involvement in the Kågeröd mausoleum epitaph. The pattern: Tycho wrote epitaphs from his island; he did not travel to graves.

evidence.note: Stayed on Hven for Axel's wedding; did not leave for the funeral.

evidence.quote: har han naeppe selv vaeret personligt involveret i

non_visits.label: Frankfurt book fairs (1579–98 attendance)
non_visits.claim: Tycho attended the Frankfurt book fairs in person as buyer and distributor.
non_visits.narrative: From Hven, Tycho worked the fairs entirely at arm's length: marked-up fair catalogues sent via Vedel to a Copenhagen intermediary (May 1579), merchant-couriers and Copenhagen dealers; type fonts were obtained at the fair through agents, and Hans Aalborg distributed the Uraniborg broadsides at the 1585 fair. No source places Tycho at a fair. Distinct from the 1575 pass-through visit to Frankfurt, which is attested and kept as a stay.

evidence.note: Purchases THROUGH the fairs only; no bodily attendance.
Agents went: printer Joachim (1584), Hans Aalborg (1585).

non_visits.label: Frauenburg (Frombork) / Danzig / Königsberg
non_visits.claim: Tycho travelled to Frauenburg, Danzig and Königsberg in 1584 to verify Copernicus's latitude.
non_visits.narrative: The 1584 Baltic expedition was made by the assistant Elias Olsen Morsing, sailing with the returning Danish embassy: Copenhagen 1 May, Frauenburg from 13 May, Königsberg 8–28 June, back on Hven 23 July, bringing Copernicus's triquetrum as Hannow's gift. Tycho stayed on Hven and celebrated the relic with a Latin poem. Four independent sources make the correction; readings of Friis's itinerary as Tycho's own travel are explicit errors.

evidence.note: Morsing's expedition, itinerary and triquetrum.
Morsing travelled; Tycho stayed home.

evidence.quote: lod ... en af sine Disciple, nemlig Elias Olai Cimber eller Morsing

evidence.note: Expedition carried out by Morsing, sent by Tycho.

non_visits.label: Roskilde (Frederick II's funeral, June 1588)
non_visits.claim: Tycho attended Frederick II's funeral in Roskilde Cathedral.
non_visits.narrative: Christianson records Rantzau calling at Uraniborg on 27 May 1588 'on his way to the king's funeral in Roskilde', and Tycho's documented lobbying that summer took place on Hven and in Copenhagen (18–23 August). The source is silent on any funeral attendance by Tycho, and no other source supplies it. An attendance that would seem natural for a leading vassal, but which the presence rule cannot pass on silence.

evidence.note: Source silent on Tycho at the funeral; Rantzau went.

non_visits.label: Ven (visit by Frederick II)
non_visits.claim: Frederick II, Tycho's great patron, visited Hven.
non_visits.narrative: A reverse-visit phantom worth registering against the island's glittering guest list: 'remarkably, the star-researcher's great patron, Frederik II' was never among the visitors to Ven, though Queen Sophie, James VI and Prince Christian all came. The king who gave the island never saw Uraniborg. (His planned counterpart at Kassel — Wilhelm IV's 1588 voyage to Hven — was likewise cancelled by Frederick's death.)

evidence.quote: Märkligt nog ingick inte stjärnforskarens store mecenat, Fredrik II

non_visits.label: Gislövgård (Skytts härad, Scania)
non_visits.claim: Tycho was present at Gislövgård when the crown estate changed hands in 1574.
non_visits.narrative: The order of 18 May 1574 commands Tyge Brahe Ottesen to hand over 'Gislom Gaard og Gods' with inventory, letters, registers and land-books to Fru Abbel Breyde. The order documents that he administered the estate, not that he stood on it: the handover's execution and any bodily presence are undocumented. A holding administered on paper; the manor is unpinned, its site unidentified.

evidence.note: Handover order only; presence undocumented.

non_visits.label: Güstrow (Duke Ulrich's court)
non_visits.claim: Tycho travelled to Güstrow to Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg's court in 1597.
non_visits.narrative: The loan negotiation with the Mecklenburg dukes and the duke's intercession with Christian IV were conducted entirely in writing: at the end of July 1597 Tycho wrote from Rostock to Duke Ulrich, whose court was at Güstrow, and received a cordial reply within days. No source consulted records a bodily visit; the phantom arises from compressing the correspondence into a journey.

evidence.note: Letters only; no visit recorded.

non_visits.label: Hamburg (city proper)
non_visits.claim: Tycho was bodily present in the city of Hamburg during the Wandsbek year (1597–98).
non_visits.narrative: Wandsbek was chosen precisely for its proximity to Hamburg, and traffic ran inward: the printer Philipp von Ohr came out from Hamburg to set type on Tycho's press at Wandsburg, and the error-ridden Hamburg printing of the Progymnasmata lunar section was supervised by Longomontanus, who stayed behind. No passage consulted states that Tycho entered Hamburg itself. Recorded as absence of evidence, not a denial.

evidence.note: Proximity documented; entry into the city nowhere stated.
Ohr's Hamburg shop supervised by Longomontanus.

non_visits.label: Helsingør (Øresund toll chamber)
non_visits.claim: Tycho was bodily at Helsingør over the Øresund toll payments that anchored his economy.
non_visits.narrative: The toll chamber paid Tycho repeatedly — fyrpenge for the Kullen light 1581–89, the 400-daler Nordfjord compensation 1586–92, 1050 daler in 1588 — but no chancery entry places him at Helsingør to collect. In the 1594 Pepeler affair the surety at Helsingør was taken by 'Tyge Brahes Tjener paa Tyge Brahes Vegne' — his servant, expressly in his stead. A revenue anchor, not a residence or a documented destination.

evidence.quote: Tyge Brahes Tjener paa Tyge Brahes Vegne

non_visits.label: Copenhagen (Diet/herredag of 1597)
non_visits.claim: Tycho attended (or could have attended) a Diet in 1597 over the Gellius case.
non_visits.narrative: No Diet met in 1597: the Gellius Sascerides matrimonial case was assigned on 5 April 1597 to a special court under Peter Munk precisely 'because the Diet did not meet in 1597'. Any narrative that stages Tycho before a 1597 herredag is structurally impossible on the documented judicial arrangements of that spring.

evidence.quote: because the Diet did not meet in 1597

non_visits.label: Hven (return after 1597)
non_visits.claim: Tycho returned to Hven (or to Danish soil) after leaving in 1597.
non_visits.narrative: After the household moved to the Farvergade house on 11 April 1597 and embarked at Copenhagen on 2 June, Tycho never set foot on Hven or Danish soil again. The island was run by his bailiff David Pedersen; his sons and Claus Mule retrieved the remaining instruments in 1599–1600, and royal commissions were the only official visitors. Christianson and Jönsson both state the denial in categorical terms.

evidence.quote: He would never return to the island of Hven.

evidence.note: Bailiff ran the island; commissions visited.

evidence.quote: Tycho Brahe skulle aldrig mer sätta sin fot på dansk jord

non_visits.label: Kassel (return visits)
non_visits.claim: Tycho returned to Kassel after his Easter 1575 visit, e.g. in 1586 or 1590.
non_visits.narrative: The great Hven-Kassel collaboration ran entirely by correspondence and emissaries: Flemløse carried the letter of 1 March 1586 and reported on the Landgrave's improved instruments; Gellius Sascerides delivered De mundi in 1588. Tycho and Wilhelm IV never met again after April 1575. The Meteorological Diary's 'Kassel' field of 1 August 1590 is Rothmann's provenance — the Landgrave's mathematician arriving with Tycho — not a Tycho destination.

evidence.note: 1586 errand was Flemløse's; the pair never met again after April 1575.
Collaboration by correspondence and emissaries.
Gellius carried De mundi to Kassel, 1588.

evidence.quote: Rediit Tycho vesperi cum Rothmanno, Landtgravii Mathematico

non_visits.label: Kronborg Castle
non_visits.claim: Tycho was bodily at Kronborg Castle (e.g. at the Garter investiture of Frederick II, 13 August 1582).
non_visits.narrative: The visual tradition — the Frederiksborg-series tapestry showing a nobleman taken to be Tycho behind Frederik II before Kronborg — is a depiction, not evidence. Christianson describes the 13 August 1582 Garter investiture without placing Tycho at it; his documented contact with the English delegation is their sail to Hven on 18 August. Morsing notes only that Kronborg was visible from Uraniborg's west windows. Presence in Helsingør town at other dates rests on other sources; presence at the castle is undocumented here.

evidence.pages: Tycho Brahes Verden scan p. 12 (fig. 2); Håkansson ed. 2006 scan p. 51; Morsing 2003 scan pp. 18, 45
evidence.note: Tapestry depiction and king's-speech rhetoric only.
Investiture described without Tycho; delegation visited Hven 18 August 1582.

non_visits.label: Kullagården / Kullen lighthouse
non_visits.claim: Tycho was bodily at Kullagården or the Kullen light he was obliged to maintain.
non_visits.narrative: The holding is richly documented — grant 1577, transfer 1580, re-grant 1581 'so long as he stays living on Hven', maintenance orders and rebukes to 1589 — but no chancery entry documents his presence. The 1581 order that Ugerup proceed to Kullagården 'i Forening med Tyge Brahe' survives only as an order, its execution unrecorded; the 1584 tower-relocation commission names others, convened 'after further notice from Tyge Brahe'. His own argument for keeping the farm was fuel for Hven, not residence. The 27 July 1584 tower-relocation commission (Frederiksborg) named Tycho with Gyldenstjerne and Ugerup and a report was submitted, but no source narrates him on the headland; a former C-grade stay on the commission was withdrawn under the presence rule.

evidence.note: Orders survive; execution and presence undocumented.
Fief-administration only; no bodily presence asserted.

evidence.quote: at de med os elskelige Tyge Brahe til Knudstrup ... skulle begive dem til Kulden ... forfare Lejligheden
evidence.note: the report found the tower ruinous; rebuilding ordered 19 April 1585

evidence.quote: In 1584 the governor of Helsingborg Castle and the chief magistrate of Scania were ordered to proceed to Kullen, together with Tycho, to examine the lighthouse

non_visits.label: Leipzig (second journey, November 1565)
non_visits.claim: Tycho made a second journey to Leipzig in November 1565 (so Dreyer, from a note in the observation journal).
non_visits.narrative: Norlind rejects it outright: the journal note is a copyist's misreading of Tycho's own words in the 1573 nova tract ('Lipsiae tunc temporis studiorum gratia commorati' — recalling the 1562–65 residence), and 'a second journey to Leipzig can naturally not be spoken of'. The related recall-motive story — that the death of his uncle Jørgen called him home — also fails: the uncle died 21 June 1565, a month after Tycho had left Leipzig on 17 May.

evidence.quote: En andra resa till Leipzig kan det naturligtvis ej vara tal om

non_visits.label: Louvain (Arsenius/Mercator workshops)
non_visits.claim: Tycho visited Louvain to acquire his Arsenius cross-staff.
non_visits.narrative: The 1560s cross-staff was a product of the Louvain instrument-making tradition of Gemma Frisius, Mercator and Walter Arsenius, and the workshop pedigree has been read as a visit. Mosley treats Louvain only as the origin of that tradition — whose masters had in any case relocated (Mercator to Duisburg in 1551) — and no source places Tycho in Louvain; the acquisition was a remote purchase.

evidence.note: Louvain named only as tradition of origin; acquisition remote.

non_visits.label: Magdeburg (1599–1600 presence)
non_visits.claim: Tycho was at Magdeburg in the winter of 1599–1600 and/or during the 1600 instrument transport.
non_visits.narrative: Only Tycho's materiel was at Magdeburg in those years: the press equipment sent ahead from Wittenberg, and the great instruments in transit from Ven to Prague, whose Magdeburg transit licence was eased with bribes of Bohemian wine. Likewise the autumn-1598 escort of his wife and daughters to Magdeburg was a companion's journey, Tycho being at Wittenberg. His one attested bodily presence at Magdeburg is October 1598, when the household's travel plan changed there — kept as a stay.

evidence.note: Only press materiel there in winter 1599–1600.
1600 transport: instruments and wine bribes, not Tycho.
The 1598 Magdeburg escort was a companion's; Tycho at Wittenberg.

non_visits.label: Nordfjord (Norwegian fief)
non_visits.claim: Tycho visited his Norwegian fief of Nordfjord.
non_visits.narrative: Nordfjord was a pure revenue holding across its whole tenure (1578–96), administered through a bailiff whom Tycho once dismissed and imprisoned; the latitude work in Norway was Flemløse's. Christianson states the denial outright — 'this Norwegian fief, which Tycho never visited'. The chancery record shows the len only at its end: recalled 16 March 1586 and compensated with 400 daler yearly from the Helsingør toll. No source claims a journey.

evidence.quote: this Norwegian fief, which Tycho never visited but administered through a bailiff

evidence.note: No visit recorded 1578–96; agents (bailiff, Flemløse) did the work.
Len recalled 16 March 1586, compensated from the Helsingør toll; no visit documented.
Fief treated purely as revenue administration; no bodily presence asserted.

non_visits.label: Nuremberg (Walther/Regiomontanus balcony)
non_visits.claim: Tycho visited the Walther/Regiomontanus observing balcony (later Dürer's house) in Nuremberg in 1575.
non_visits.narrative: Purely Christianson's inference from the itinerary: Tycho 'must have seen the high balcony where Walther and Regiomontanus observed the stars'. The Nuremberg pass-through itself is attested and kept as a place-stay; the pilgrimage to the balcony is an editorial embellishment that no source records and that the presence rule cannot admit.

evidence.quote: must have seen the high balcony

non_visits.label: Odense (Latin school)
non_visits.claim: Tycho attended the Latin school in Odense.
non_visits.narrative: Pure conjecture in Norlind: that Tycho attended a formal cathedral or Latin school at all is 'mycket ovisst', and Odense enters only as 'perhaps', because Jørgen Brahe was for a time lensmand there (cf. the Næsbyhoved stay). No source documents schooling in Odense; the claim must not generate a childhood stay in the town itself.

evidence.quote: mycket ovisst

non_visits.label: Pilsen (imperial court in plague exile)
non_visits.claim: Tycho followed Rudolf II to Pilsen during the 1599–1600 plague displacement of the court.
non_visits.narrative: When plague drove the court from Prague in September 1599, the emperor went to Pilsen; Tycho stayed at Benátky (and the Girsitz refuge), sending Rudolf the formula for his Paracelsian plague medicament and communicating exclusively through the courier Daniel Fels, documented 6 January – 7 May 1600. In June 1600 Tycho was still writing that the emperor remained at Pilsen. Norlind's index entry 'Pilsen' concerns the court, not a Tycho stay.

evidence.note: Courier Daniel Fels the only channel; no visit.
Tycho stayed at Benátky, sent the plague remedy.
Index 'Pilsen' = the court's stay, not Tycho's.

non_visits.label: Presentation-copy destinations (Oxford, Paris, Florence, Vienna, Gotha...)
non_visits.claim: The destinations of Tycho's presentation copies (Bodleian/Oxford, Paris, Venice, Florence, Vienna, Gotha etc.) imply his presence there.
non_visits.narrative: The Mechanica / De revolutionibus-era presentation network was serviced entirely by couriers and intermediaries: Wotton took the Grimani copy to England, Tengnagel carried the Magini copy and the 1600 Grimani mission, Sascerides and Monaw served other routes. No dedication despatch in the Mosley appendix attests Tycho at any destination. A standing guard against reading the gift network as an itinerary — the books travelled; the astronomer did not.

evidence.pages: Mosley 2007, Appendix I; Graphonomicon, specimen bodleian-mechanica-grimani
evidence.note: Courier network fully documented; no presence claims.

non_visits.label: Roskilde (Chapel of the Three Holy Kings prebend)
non_visits.claim: Tycho was bodily in Roskilde on the business of his Helligtrekongers Kapel prebend (1579–97).
non_visits.narrative: No chancery entry places Tycho in Roskilde across the prebend's whole tenure. All chapel business — grace-year, singing duties, the ruinous fabric, the vault-removal permission of 8 November 1594 — was conducted by letter and bailiff; on 1 August 1593 it was the king, not Tycho, who had 'now himself been here in the church and inspected the chapel'. Stays recorded from the biographies keep Roskilde in the gazetteer at grade C; the prebend-visit claim itself fails the presence rule.

evidence.note: All prebend business by letter; the king inspected the chapel, not Tycho.
Prebend treated as revenue administration.

non_visits.label: Benátky (visit by Rudolf II)
non_visits.claim: Rudolf II visited Tycho at Benátky.
non_visits.narrative: An entrance was prepared for the emperor, who reserved an adjoining house — but 'whether Rudolph ever came to Benatky while Tycho was there is not known, and it is not likely', the court sitting out the plague at Pilsen through the winter of 1599–1600. The prepared apartments are evidence of hope, not of a visit; the claim stays in the phantom register until positive evidence appears.

evidence.quote: it is not likely

non_visits.label: Sweden proper (within its 16th-century borders)
non_visits.claim: Tycho visited Sweden.
non_visits.narrative: A standing trap of anachronism: Ven and Scania, where Tycho was born, lived and held his fief, only became Swedish in 1658/1660. Within Sweden's borders as they stood in his lifetime, Jönsson states flatly that the Scanian nobleman 'never set his foot on Swedish soil'. Any claimed stay in 16th-century Sweden proper contradicts the source base; the many 'Sweden' locations in this gazetteer are modern-country labels for then-Danish Scania.

evidence.quote: never set his foot on Swedish soil during his lifetime

non_visits.label: Villands Herred / Hammer ('the other Tyge Brahe')
non_visits.claim: Chancery entries on 'Tyge Brahe' of Villands Herred / 'til Hammer' are itinerary data for the astronomer.
non_visits.narrative: They concern Tyge Jensen Brahe, a same-named kinsman: lensmand of Villands Herred (fief letter 1 March 1576) and of Hammer, stabbed to death by Eiler Krause on 6 August 1581. The Krause safe-conduct and reconciliation letters (1582–94), the Villands arrears, the 1580 funeral-procession summons and the 1587 guardianship entry all belong to the kinsman's family. The volume registers separate 'Tyge Jensen' from 'Tyge Ottesen, Lensmand p. Hveen' page by page — an identity guard for every user of this edition.

evidence.note: Registers disambiguate the two men explicitly.

non_visits.label: Hven (Valkendorf in the prince's suite, 3 July 1592)
non_visits.claim: Christopher Valkendorf attended Prince Christian's visit to Hven on 3 July 1592, where the famous dog-kicking quarrel with Tycho occurred.
non_visits.narrative: Dreyer is categorical: 'it is quite certain that Valkendorf did not attend the Prince on his visit to Hveen', and the dog-quarrel traditions in both the 1592 and the Huet versions rest 'on rumour only'. Friis had already judged the Valkendorf identification 'perhaps right, though by no means certain' and the enmity-origin accounts 'highly unreliable'. The visit of the prince stands; the quarrel scene does not.

evidence.quote: it is quite certain that Valkendorf did not attend the Prince
hoist upaalidelige

non_visits.label: Väsby / Tågalycka (birth of the infant Claus, 2 Jan 1577)
non_visits.claim: Tycho was present at the plague refuge (Tågalycka per Christianson, Väsby per Jönsson) for the birth of his son Claus.
non_visits.narrative: Tycho lodged his pregnant wife and daughter away from the plague — at the widow Margrethe Gagge's Tågalycka manor in Christianson's account, at Väsby north of Helsingborg in Jönsson's. The infant Claus was born 2 January 1577 and died six days later; Christianson is explicit that 'Tycho never saw him, but composed a dolorous epitaph for his grave'. Neither source places Tycho at either refuge; the sources' disagreement over the refuge itself is left open. Unpinned: neither manor site is identified.

evidence.quote: Tycho never saw him, but composed a dolorous epitaph for his grave

evidence.note: Family at Väsby; no presence of Tycho recorded; memorial in Väsby church.

non_visits.label: Veneto academies (Vicenza / Padua, 1575)
non_visits.claim: Tycho visited Palladio's Accademia Olimpica in Vicenza and the Accademia dei Rinascenti in Padua in 1575.
non_visits.narrative: Christianson offers the academies only as speculative venues: the Venetian discussions 'may have taken place' in them, and 'Tycho did not record the details'. Only Venice itself is asserted for 1575. Padua enters the gazetteer solely at grade D on Jönsson's garden-model conjecture; Vicenza not at all. The academy visits must not be promoted to stays.

evidence.quote: may have taken place

non_visits.label: Venice (late-career patronage)
non_visits.claim: Tycho travelled to, or relocated to, Venice in connection with the Republic's patronage in his late career.
non_visits.narrative: Pigatto's study calls the entire Venetian engagement 'a Failed Project': Tycho's Italian contacts ran through emissaries only — Gellius Sascerides at Padua 1589–93 and Franz Tengnagel, sent November 1598 with the Grimani presentation copy. No bodily presence of Tycho in Venice belongs to the Bohemian period. Distinct from the attested 1575 visit, which stands as a place-stay.

evidence.note: Emissaries only; 'a Failed Project'.

non_visits.label: Vienna
non_visits.claim: Tycho visited Vienna; the Amalienburg tower clock is a relic of his instruments there.
non_visits.narrative: Thoren states Vienna is 'a city that Tycho seems never to have visited'. The Amalienburg clock legend survives only through Rudolf II's posthumous purchase of the instruments, and professional horologists strongly doubt any such Tycho clock exists. The thesaurus movement of Tycho's manuscripts to Vienna (1621) tracks objects after his death, not his travels.

evidence.quote: a city that Tycho seems never to have visited

evidence.note: Vienna 1621 is an object movement (apographa), not a bodily one.

non_visits.label: Copenhagen (Christian IV's wedding, November 1597)
non_visits.claim: Tycho attended Christian IV's wedding to Anne Catherine of Brandenburg.
non_visits.narrative: Tycho was in exile at Wandsburg. Viceroy Rantzau planned to attend, while Tycho sent him travel-health advice and instructions on what to answer if his return to Denmark were raised at court. He met the bride's parents only afterwards, at Bramstedt on 22 December 1597, as the Brandenburg delegation travelled home. His having never again set foot on Danish soil after 2 June 1597 (see the phantom register) independently excludes attendance.

evidence.note: In exile; met the bride's parents at Bramstedt afterwards.

non_visits.label: Wittenberg (1568 pass-through, with Castle Neideck)
non_visits.claim: Tycho stayed in Wittenberg (and Leipzig, attending Steen Brahe's dubbing at Castle Neideck) on the 1568 way from Rostock to Basel.
non_visits.narrative: Norlind shows Dreyer's supporting citation points to the wrong edition's foliation and that the Mechanica passage says nothing of 1568 — 'the statement must rest on a misunderstanding'; his summary keeps only 'über Wittenberg (?)'. Christianson likewise hedges: 'possibly through Wittenberg and Leipzig', 'may have been at Castle Neideck'. The 1568 route survives only as a question mark and must not be asserted as stays.

evidence.quote: über Wittenberg (?)
possibly through Wittenberg and Leipzig

sites.label: Hven (Ven) — the island fief
sites.description: The island of Hven (Swedish Ven) in the Øresund, granted to Tycho as a fief by Frederik II on 23 May 1576 — rent-free for as long as he lived and continued his mathematical studies, with 400 daler from the treasury toward a house he was to build on the island (Tycho himself supplying the stone and lime; Kancelliets Brevbøger 1576–79 p. 59). Today part of Sweden (Landskrona kommun). In his own words, “The island itself is very high, as if it were a mountain which you might ascend, but on top it is flat all over”; it lies in the Sound “which divides Scania from Sealand,” with Copenhagen three miles to the south-west, and its “latitude from the equator is 55°54½′, as measured several times by us with the greatest care” (Mechanica, trans. Ræder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, pp. 138–139). Tycho's two decades on Hven were also a hard landlordship. He held the island's tenants to heavy labour-service on Uraniborg and its works, and his disputes with them — and with the Crown over their grievances — run through the record: a royal letter of 1587 and another of 1592 document the friction, the latter in the matter of his tenant Rasmus Pedersen of Gundsømagle, whom Tycho had barred from a farm and had imprisoned, the King directing that the suit be heard before the landsdommer Lauge Beck (Becker, Danske Magazin 3. R. IV–V). Even from his Wandsbek exile Tycho went on managing the island at a distance — a Danish letter of 28 May 1598 thanks the Lord High Steward Christoffer Valkendorf for backing his bailiff against the 'disobedient peasants' there (Epistolarium: Tycho to Christoffer Valkendorf, 28 May 1598). The tenants' grievances were among the grounds on which Tycho lost royal favour and, in 1597, the fief itself. The chancery records document the friction in detail: as early as 1578 the Crown forbade Hven's tenants to move off the island without Tycho's leave 'medens han bygger der paa Landet' (KB 1576–79 p. 334); on the tenants' complaint of intolerable labour-service the King sent Arild Ugerup and Axel Gyldenstierne to Hven (20 August 1580), whose report produced the formal 'Ordning og Skik mellem Tyge Brahe og Bønderne paa Hven' of 8 January 1581 — two days' labour-service a week per half-farm, the tenants' claimed freeholder (jordegne) status revoked, and Hven's court cases moved to the Skaane landsting (KB 1580–83 pp. 128–129, 200-201). Tycho's Crown income beyond Hven was itself a knot of fiefs: Kullegaarden on the Kullen peninsula in Skaane (granted 1577), which carried the duty of keeping the Kullen lighthouse 'i Stand og lade den blusse den sædvanlige Tid' and, as Tycho successfully argued in 1579, supplied the firewood for Uraniborg (KB 1576–79 pp. 230, 249, 765; 1580–83 pp. 294–295); the prebend of the Helligtrekongers Kapel in Roskilde Cathedral (held 1579–1597, with jus patronatus over Udbye parish); the Norwegian fief of Nordfjord (1578), exchanged in 1586 for 400 daler yearly from the Øresund toll; and a royal pension terminated in 1581 once the fiefs sufficed. The end came together: a fresh royal commission investigated the tenants' renewed grievances on 9 April 1597, and in June 1597 the Roskilde prebend passed to Chancellor Christen Friis 'saaledes som Tyge Brahe hidtil har haft det' (KB 1596–1602 pp. 113, 168, 170) in the same weeks Tycho gave up Hven. The island passed in 1602 to a new lensmand, Cort Barleben, on ordinary commercial terms (50 daler the first year, 100 thereafter), by which time the buildings were reported 'meget forfalden' (KB 1596–1602 pp. 739, 746).

blaeu.opening_dutch: Tusschen Zeelandt en Schonen legt in de Sond een klijn Eylandt, genomende Hven, ofte Venusia, só genaamt van Tycho Brahe, die daer meer als tweentwintig jaren over de Stelkunde heeft gearbeyt.
blaeu.opening_english: Between Zealand and Scania lies in the Sound a small island, called Hven, or Venusia, so named by Tycho Brahe, who laboured there for more than twenty-two years over astronomy.
blaeu.citation: Joan Blaeu, Grooten Atlas oft Werelt-beschryving (Amsterdam, 1664), p. 174. Universiteitsbibliotheek Utrecht, AC 62 Rariora.

sites.dimensions: highest in the middle and flat on top; latitude 55°54½′ (Tycho's own determination); circumference 8160 passus (Mechanica 1946, pp. 138–139)

sites.label: Uraniborg — the castle of the heavens
sites.fate: decay documented from Tycho's departure — royal commissioners Thomas Fincke and Iver Stub were sent on 2 June 1597 to inspect the damage the Hven tenants had done to the instruments still on Uraniborg (KB 1596–1602 p. 163); by June 1602 the buildings were reported 'meget forfalden' and surveyed for the new lensmand Cort Barleben (KB p. 746). Demolished and quarried in the 17th century; only foundations survive, partly restored
sites.dimensions: central building a square of 49 feet per side; round towers 18 feet in diameter on the north and south sides; narrow entrance towers east and west (Dreyer, p. 96, from Tycho's own Epistolae astronomicae p. 218 + Mechanica fol. H.4)
sites.description: Tycho's great house, built 1576–1580 ön a square rampart-enclosed plot whose four corners pointed to the compass points, with four roads running from those corners to the raised circular space at the centre where the house stood. The central building was a square 49 feet ön a side, with round towers 18 feet in diameter ön its north and south faces (ringed by lower outhouses för fuel) and narrow entrance towers east and west; it was built apparently of red brick with sandstone ornaments in the 'Gothic Renaissance' style then new to the North — epoch-making, Dreyer judged, in the history of Scandinavian architecture. A single building uniting residence, library and upper observatory galleries above än alchemical laboratory in the basement. Its artistic genesis is still debated — advisers proposed from Hans van Paeschen (first builder of Kronborg) to the royal sculptor Johan Gregor van der Schardt — but the 1587 tablet in the great mural-quadrant painting names Tycho himself 'the constructor of the buildings and the astronomical instruments', and the domed-centre-in-a-geometric-garden plan shows a strong affinity with Italian villa architecture, especially Palladio's Villa Rotonda (Johannsen, in Tycho Brahes Verden, 2006). The standard art-historical monograph ön the building — Jern's Uraniborg: herresäte och himlaborg (Lund, 1976) — locates the specific model för the gabled façade not in the villa tradition but in Venetian church fronts, comparing it directly with S. Giovanni in Bragora and S. Maria della Carità, while cautioning that Uraniborg cannot be reduced to any single Renaissance style-circle (Jern 1976). The documented hands are these: the Netherlandish master-builder Hans von Paschen led the work before transferring to Bohus in 1577; Hans van Stenwinkel the Elder completed the interior and built Stjerneborg (royal architect, 1582); the Nuremberg founder Georg Labenwolf laid the lead-pipe water system and fountain; and Tobias Gemperlin painted the great mural quadrant (Jern 1976). Over its two doors Tycho set paired mottoes that made the building's double programme explicit — Suspiciendo despicio ('by looking up I look down') över the eastern, astronomical portal, and Despiciendo suspicio ('by looking down I look up') över the western, alchemical one — so that astronomy and the laboratory's 'terrestrial astronomy' answered each other across the house (Jern 1976). In his own words, Tycho chose “the site highest ön this island … practically in its centre, where I started building from its foundations a castle which was named after the heaven itself in which it was its task to make observations, and hence called Uraniborg.” He gives the rampart-square as three hundred feet ön a side, the central house as “nearly sixty feet” per side under a forty-five-foot wall, and seventy-five feet “from the ground to the Pegasus at the very top” (Mechanica, trans. Ræder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 126). These figures are in Tycho's short foot of 259 mm, so the house is ≈15.5 m square — consistent with the 49-foot figure (in the larger Danish foot) recorded above.

blaeu_illustrations.title_latin: ARCIS VRANIBURGI, A TYCHONE BRAHE, DNO DE KNVDSTRUP, IN INSVLA HELLESPONTI DANICI HVENNA CONSTRUCTAE, QVO AD TOTAM CAPACITATEM, DESIGNATIO
blaeu_illustrations.title_english: Design of the Castle of Uraniborg, built by Tycho Brahe, Lord of Knudstrup, on the island of the Danish Hellespontus Hven, as to its total capacity
blaeu_illustrations.description: Garden plan of Uraniborg: the square rampart with corner pavilions, the four approach roads, the central house, the outhouses, the formal gardens and orchard.

blaeu_illustrations.title_latin: ORTHOGRAPHIA PRAECIPVAE DOMVS ARCIS VRANIBURGI in Insula Danica Venusia, sive Hvenna, Astronomiae restaurandae gratia, circa annum MDLXXVI, a TYCHONE BRAHE aedificatae
blaeu_illustrations.title_english: Elevation of the principal building of Uraniborg on the Danish island of Venusia, or Hven, built ca. 1576 by Tycho Brahe for the restoration of astronomy
blaeu_illustrations.description: South elevation of Uraniborg's main building: the two-storey block with round towers, dome, and observatory galleries. Richly coloured.

blaeu_illustrations.title_english: Floor plan of the house of the Castle of Uraniborg
blaeu_illustrations.description: Floor plan of Uraniborg, with room key letters A–V decoded on p. 183. Observatory rooms O (large southern), N (small southern), R (large northern) and other chambers clearly labelled.

reconstruction.intro: Charles Christensen's measured reconstruction (1921) is the authoritative modern record of how Uraniborg actually looked. It rests on C. V. L. Charlier's 1901 excavation of the foundations, collated against — and correcting — every depiction printed in Tycho's own lifetime.
reconstruction.excavation: C. V. L. Charlier excavated the foundations in 1901. The recovered ground-plan does not agree with the plans Tycho himself printed (which are wrong “end ikke i de store Hovedtræk” — not even in the main outlines); the reconstruction therefore follows the excavated measurements, not the printed figures.

dimensions_compared.note: The printed sources disagree on almost every dimension; the reconstruction uses the excavated measurements. Feet are Tychonic feet.

relics.what: Foundation-stone fragment (porphyry, with Charles Dançay's Latin inscription; the stone reads 1 August, where the Mechanica gives 8 August 1576)
Window-crown fragment (volute-crowned, the motif peculiar to Uraniborg)
Two Arion-on-a-dolphin bronze water-taps from the piped water system

reconstruction.genesis: The design adapts Palladio's Villa Rotonda (known via the engraving in I quattro libri dell'architettura, 1570): Uraniborg keeps the square plan and the four axial corridors but drops the central circular domed hall (impractical in a Nordic house), substitutes octagonal portal-projections for the open loggias, and adds the two round towers N and S. Vitruvian symmetria — invoked by Tycho in the Mechanica's description of the east front, after the architectural learning he had professed since his 1574 oration — governs the whole; the volute window-crowns follow Serlio, the timber cupola Walter Rivius's German Vitruvius (1548). [Jern 1976 later relocates the façade source from the Veneto villa to Venetian church fronts — a competing attribution.]

sites.label: Stjerneborg — the star castle
sites.fate: ruined after 1597; the crypts excavated and reconstructed in the 20th century — now the Tycho Brahe Museum
sites.description: A separate, largely subterranean observatory built in 1584 just south of Uraniborg: five crypts beneath rotating cupolas, each giving one of the largest instruments a permanent, wind-sheltered mounting on solid ground. Stjerneborg ('star castle') answered the chief defect of Uraniborg's high galleries — that wind and an unstable footing spoiled the finest measurements. In his own words, Tycho built it “about the year 1584, on a hill outside the castle … with no small difficulty and expenditure a subterranean observatory with various cellars … of solid masonry,” his purpose “partly to have placed some of the most important instruments securely and firmly in order that they should not be exposed to the disturbing influence of the wind, and should be easier to use,” and partly to separate simultaneous observers so “they should not get in the way of each other” (Mechanica, trans. Ræder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, pp. 135–137).

blaeu_illustrations.title_latin: STELLAEBURGVM sive OBSERVATORIVM SVBTERRANEUM a TYCHONE BRAHE in Insvla Hvena, extra Arcem Vraniam, extrvctvm circa annvm MDLXXXIIII
blaeu_illustrations.title_english: Stjerneborg, or the Underground Observatory, built by Tycho Brahe on the island of Hven, outside the Castle of Urania, constructed around the year 1584
blaeu_illustrations.description: Bird’s-eye coloured view of Stjerneborg: the star-shaped outer enclosure, five underground chambers visible as domed structures, central chamber largest, observer figures in the open spaces. The primary visual source for Stjerneborg’s appearance before destruction.

Floor plan of Stjerneborg showing the five underground chambers (A–E) with letter labels: C = the great equatorial armillary; D = the revolving azimuthal quadrant; F = the great steel quadrant; G = the distance sextant. Corresponds exactly to Tycho’s own plan in the Mechanica.

inscriptions.latin: NON INIMICA ABOLET VIS VLLA NEC VNDA NEC IGNIS
inscriptions.english: No hostile force destroys it, nor flood nor fire

inscriptions.latin: NEC FASCES NEC OPES, SOLA ARTIS SCEPTRA PERENNANT
inscriptions.english: Neither rank nor riches — only the sceptres of art endure
inscriptions.location: Motto on the chambers of Stjerneborg (the principal motto)

inscriptions.latin: TYCHO BRAHE O. F. — HAVE QVI HAEC LEGIS FACISQVE, ET VALE
inscriptions.english: Tycho Brahe, son of Otte. — Hail, you who read and do these things — and farewell.

astronomers_commemorated: Alphonso X of Castile (patron of the Alfonsine Tables)
blaeu.citation: Joan Blaeu, Grooten Atlas oft Werelt-beschryving (Amsterdam, 1664), pp. 206–208. Universiteitsbibliotheek Utrecht, AC 62 Rariora.

sites.dimensions: outer premises 70 feet per side; the central semicircles 24 feet in diameter — Tycho's own figures (Mechanica 1946, p. 137; in his 259 mm foot ≈ 18 m and ≈ 6.2 m)

reconstruction.intro: Christensen's measured reconstruction (1921) of the sunken star-castle: a square warming-room ringed by five round crypts of unequal size (sized to their instruments), the largest to the south. The authoritative modern record behind today's rebuilt crypts.
reconstruction.excavation: Reconstructed from Tycho's own plan and perspective (Epistolae 1596 / Mechanica 1598) checked against the excavated foundations; the crypts were later re-excavated and rebuilt as the Tycho Brahe Museum.

links.label: Tycho Brahe-museet, Ven — the reconstructed crypts are the museum

sites.label: The gardens and ramparts of Uraniborg
sites.fate: lost; the geometry recovered by excavation and partly recreated on site
sites.description: The square earthwork ramparts enclosing Uraniborg, their corners set to the cardinal points, with formal gardens and orchards within and around them — among the finest in Scandinavia by Tycho's own account. Christianson describes the orchard's pippin, Rambour and Gylling apples, Doyenné and blood pears, green and blue Reine Claude plums, morello cherries, apricots, figs, quince and walnuts, and knot gardens laid out as a microcosm; Tycho's sister Sophie Brahe is recorded helping lay out and replant the garden (boxwood cuttings noted in his diary). Tycho rebuilt the ramparts and redesigned and replanted the knot gardens and orchards in the renovations of c.1591. Beyond its beauty the garden carried a symbolic-alchemical programme (Michelsen, in Tycho Brahes Verden, 2006): the medicinal plants were set in precisely planned beds so as to absorb the maximum heavenly influence (a Paracelsian-medicine principle), the enclosed garden read as a microcosm of the cosmic order and a figure of the Opus Magnum — one of the main elements of Tycho's 'earthly chemistry', in harmony with the astronomy pursued in Urania's house at its centre.

sites.label: The alchemical laboratory
sites.fate: lost with Uraniborg; no trace of the furnaces survives
sites.description: The alchemical laboratory in Uraniborg's basement, fitted with sixteen furnaces of nine different kinds — Tycho's 'terrestrial astronomy', where he prepared medicines (the plague elixirs) and pursued the Paracelsian correspondence of macrocosm and microcosm. Visitors were taken down to see it; at the basement's other end lay cellars, pantries and the deep well. Tycho later added a second, smaller laboratory of five furnaces in the converted winter dining room (Thoren, Lord of Uraniborg, pp. 159, 224).
sites.attested_by: Described in Tycho's own published account of Uraniborg (Mechanica, 1598) — the basement laboratory with its sixteen furnaces — and in visitors' reports (Christianson, On Tycho's Island, 2000).

sites.label: The library and the great globe
sites.description: Uraniborg's library, which among its treasures held the great brass globe (globus magnus orichalcicus) onto which Tycho engraved his measured star positions.
sites.attested_by: Described in Tycho's own published account of Uraniborg (Mechanica, 1598), which places the great brass globe in the library (Dreyer 1890).

sites.label: The printing house (Tycho's press)
sites.fate: lost; the press and types dispersed after Tycho left Hven
sites.description: Tycho's own printing house, established on Hven in 1584 so that he controlled his own means of publication and distribution. Its earliest known imprint is the memorial broadsheet Epitaphium Johannis Pratensis (1584); the earliest DATED piece is the occasional pøm Carmen ad Jacobum Ulfeldium, inscribed 'Uraniburgi, 7 Kal. Decemb.' = 25 November 1584 (Nielsen, Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen, p. 176 — correcting the sometimes-cited 27 November 1584, which conflates the date and the piece). The first true book was Elias Olsen Morsing's Diarium astrologicum et meteorologicum / Calendarium (calendar set late 1585, issued 1586). The press went on to produce De mundi (1588), the Danish-language Flemløs Astrologia (1591), the Epistolae (1596) and the advance sheets of the Progymnasmata (1592) — a work only completed at Prague in 1602.
sites.attested_by: Attested by the surviving Uraniborg imprints themselves and by Tycho's correspondence; documented in Nielsen, Tyge Brahes Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen (1921).

sites.label: The paper mill
sites.fate: lost; derelict by 1602 and demolished for salvage on royal order (26 June 1602, to lensmand Cort Barleben; KB 1596–1602 p. 751); site rediscovered and excavated 1933–34
sites.description: The paper mill on Hven that fed Tycho's press — its production a recurring concern in the correspondence (the two papermakers who absconded delayed the Progymnasmata, as Tycho complained to Hájek). Royal chancery records fix the mill's economics and fate: a privilege of 2 March 1592 ordered all inhabitants of Nørrejylland to sell their old linen rags (Lumper) to Tycho before anyone else, since he 'har anlagt en Papirmølle paa Hveen' and needed them to make paper (KB 1588–92 p. 750). A demolition order of 26 June 1602 to the new lensmand Cort Barleben locates the works 'syd for Uraniborg' and calls it a 'Stampemølle eller Papirmølle,' by then wholly derelict, to be torn down and its usable timber and stone re-used (KB 1596–1602 p. 751). The mill dam was built by Valentin von Spangenberg (also written 'Valenthin'), a hydraulic engineer previously employed by Frederick II at Kronborg (1578–88), who arrived on Hven in 1589. The Meteorological Diary records on 26 June 1589 that Valentin promised to complete the mølledæmning (mill dam) within four weeks, and on 22 July 1590: 'Abijt Valentinus opere aggeris apud molendinum confecto' — Valentin departed after completing the dam work (Vellev 2017, from TBOO IX). Tycho named the paper mill's purpose explicitly in a letter to Christoph Rothmann of 24 November 1589 (TBOO VI); Christian IV ordered oak timber felled for the stamp press in a letter to Kirsten Lindenov (Steen Bille's widow, Tycho's aunt) dated 19 March 1590 (Kancelliets Brevbøger 1588–1592, 360). Its ruined site was rediscovered by the amateur astronomer N. A. Møller Nicolaisen (1874–1954), who on a 1929 visit to Hven noticed a man-made mound and identified it as the fallen paper mill; the Scandinavian Tycho Brahe Foundation funded his excavations of 1933–34, an archæological sensation of the period (Vellev 2002).

links.label: Vellev 2017, the excavation and the votive stone (open access)

sites.attested_by: Attested in royal chancery records — the rag-privilege of 2 March 1592 and the demolition order of 26 June 1602 (Kancelliets Brevbøger) — and in Tycho's correspondence with Hájek; the site was excavated 1933–34.

sites.label: Tycho Brahe Museum & the Stjerneborg reconstruction
sites.description: The modern Tycho Brahe Museum on Ven, centred on the excavated and reconstructed crypts of Stjerneborg and the foundations of Uraniborg, with a recreated Renaissance garden — the principal place where Tycho's establishment can be seen today.

links.label: Tycho Brahe-museet, Ven (Landskrona stad) — visitor information

sites.label: The Belvedere (Royal Summer Palace) — Tycho's Prague Musaeum
sites.fate: the building survives; its astronomical contents dispersed after 1612 and removed to the Gallery Building by 1635
sites.description: The Renaissance Royal Summer Palace (Belvedere) in the Royal Garden below Prague Castle. Tycho is reported to have made Prague observations 'in the arcades of the building' (Pierre Bergeron, 1607); after his death in 1601 the Belvedere became a memorial 'Astronomical Museum' housing the astronomy and exact-science part of Rudolf II's collections — the large instruments together with portraits of astronomers (Ptolemy, Albategnius, Copernicus, and two of Tycho himself) and of their royal patrons (Alfonso X, Charles V, Rudolf II, Frederik II of Denmark). The two surviving Tycho-associated sextants by Bürgi and Habermel passed through this collection on their way to the National Technical Museum. Dreyer (1890, p. 365) corroborates the connection from the other side: the Emperor agreed to buy Tycho's own Hven instruments from the family for 20,000 thaler; Tengnagel, as scientific heir from 1602, denied Kepler access to them and had them vaulted under Curtius' house, and Kepler later recorded the 'instrumenta Braheana' as standing 'in viridario Caesaris' (the Emperor's garden, i.e. this Belvedere) in October 1604 — before they were destroyed in the 1619 Bohemian rising against the Habsburgs. Not to be confused with Tycho's principal Prague-period working sites, Benátky nad Jizerou and the Curtius house — the latter the very building under which the instruments were stored. Grade B: the 'Musaeum' reading is Fučíková's, and Tycho's own use of the Belvedere is reported, not firmly documented.

sites.label: Benátky nad Jizerou — Tycho's first Bohemian observatory
sites.fate: the hilltop castle survives (renovated, intended to house a small Tycho museum); the wooden observing cubicles are gone
sites.description: The hilltop castle at Benátky nad Jizerou, about 30 km north of Prague, granted to Tycho by Rudolf II in 1599 as his first Bohemian observatory. He was given leave to build wooden observing cubicles (now vanished); the portion available to him ran to three floors of nearly 500 m² each. Here Johannes Kepler joined Tycho in February 1600, before Tycho moved to Prague proper (Thoren, Appendix 5).

sites.label: The Curtius (Kurtz) house — Tycho's Prague residence and place of death
sites.fate: demolished; only a 7×16 m foundation remnant survives by a later school; statues of Tycho and Kepler stand on the site (since 1984)
sites.description: The summer home built by the imperial vice-chancellor Jacob Kurtz (Curtius), a few minutes' walk west of the Imperial Castle on the Hradčany hill — Tycho's principal Prague residence for most of his Bohemian years (the 20,000-gulden edifice he described) and the house in which he died on 24 October 1601. After his death the imperial-purchased instruments were vaulted under this very house before passing to the Belvedere garden (Dreyer, p. 365; cf. site-belvedere). Only a 7×16 m foundation remnant survives by a later school (Thoren, Appendix 5).
sites.attested_by: Described in Tycho's own letters from Prague; contemporary records place his death there on 24 October 1601 (Dreyer 1890; Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg, 1990).

sites.label: The Schwarzenberg (Rožmberk) palace — Tycho's last banquet
sites.fate: the palace survives on Hradčany square (now a museum)
sites.description: The Renaissance palace on Hradčany square, then owned by Petr Vok z Rožmberka (who had acquired it from Rudolf II by exchange in 1600) — by Thoren's reckoning (Appendix 5) the site of the banquet of 13 October 1601 at which Tycho fell fatally ill. The contemporary story holds that, out of deference to his host Petr Vok, he held his urine too long at table; he sickened with a bladder/uraemic ailment and died eleven days later, on 24 October 1601, at the Curtius house. Grade C: the banquet's location at the Rožmberk palace follows Thoren; the death-by-retention tale is contemporary tradition, not established fact (the 2010 exhumation only excluded mercury poisoning — see the Receptio record of the 2010 exhumation).

sites.label: Church of Our Lady before Týn — Tycho's grave
sites.description: The Church of Our Lady before Týn on Prague's Old Town Square, where Tycho was buried on 4 November 1601. His tomb is marked by a relief effigy in armour with one hand on a celestial globe. The grave's afterlife — the 1901 and 2010 exhumations and the long Danish–Czech contest of memory — is modelled in the Reception pillar.

links.label: Church of Our Lady before Týn — Czech state tourism authority

rooms.name: The great alchemical laboratory
rooms.function: Sixteen furnaces of nine kinds in the south projection; one furnace-base was recovered in the 1901 excavation.

rooms.name: The well cellar
rooms.function: The masonry well (about 40 alen deep) under the north tower that fed the pressurised water system; still extant.

rooms.name: The central crossing and fountain
rooms.function: Where the four axial corridors meet, with a water-spouting Vandkunst at the centre.

rooms.name: Vinterstue (the winter room)
rooms.function: The family living-room (SE); later enlarged, with a hidden five-furnace spagyric laboratory built behind its chimney.

rooms.name: The mural-quadrant room
rooms.function: The SW ground-floor room: the great brass mural quadrant on the meridian wall (its west window blinded, a slit cut in the south wall), and above the arc the 1587 trompe-l'oeil wall-painting of Tycho in effigy.

rooms.name: The guest rooms
rooms.function: Two further ground-floor chambers, each with a fireplace and beds; the NE one opened to the kitchen.

rooms.name: The kitchen
rooms.function: In the north tower, around the masonry well.

rooms.name: The library and museum
rooms.function: The study in the south tower, housing the great brass globe and painted portraits of ancient and modern astronomers.

rooms.name: The Blue Chamber
rooms.function: In the earliest (Marburg/Braunius) captions, the Queen's Chamber.

rooms.name: The Red Chamber
rooms.function: In the earliest captions, the King's Chamber — the names later dropped.

rooms.name: The Yellow Chamber
rooms.function: The octagonal room in the portal projection.

rooms.name: Sommerstue (the Green Room)
rooms.function: The west room, with a painted plant ceiling and a view over the Sound.

rooms.name: The great southern observatory
rooms.function: Atop the south tower.

rooms.name: The great northern observatory
rooms.function: Atop the north tower; later the display place of Copernicus's own parallactic rules.

rooms.name: The smaller southern observatory
rooms.function: On the gallery.

rooms.name: The smaller northern observatory
rooms.function: On the gallery.

rooms.name: The attic and cupola
rooms.function: Eight cramped student cells; above them the cupola with the clock and the gilt Pegasus weather-vane.

rooms.name: Hypocaustum (the warming room, B)
rooms.function: The square central room; its flat cupola painted with Tycho's world-system and eight astronomers; alcoves O and Q for rest, table V for recording, clocks and an iron stove; its turf-covered vault above ground formed the Parnassus mound, bearing a one-alen brass Mercury turned by a mechanism (given in 1590 to Duke Heinrich Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel).

rooms.name: South crypt C (the largest)
rooms.function: The great equatorial armillary, its declination axis borne on a globe carried by the Atlas pillar.

rooms.name: North-east crypt D
rooms.function: The revolving quadrant.

rooms.name: North-west crypt E
rooms.function: The zodiacal armillary, reached by a single internal step.

rooms.name: South-west crypt F
rooms.function: The revolving steel quadrant within a geometric steel square; three wall-niches held lamps.

rooms.name: East crypt G
rooms.function: The astronomical sextant on a ball-and-socket globe mount.

rooms.name: The entrance portal A and stair
rooms.function: The Gotland-stone portal bearing the inscription 'Nec Fasces Nec Opes / Sola Artis / Sceptra Perennant. (15)85', and the descending stair; niche S marks the start of the never-finished tunnel to Uraniborg.

rooms.name: The railed premises
rooms.function: Corner posts K, L, N, T bearing globes for sextants; stone table M; columns HH and II for the Ptolemaic rules (triquetrum) and smaller armillae.

sources.contributes: The prosopographical backbone: who was with Tycho where, and the household's movements. Supplies the assistants' and family members' presence at nearly every stay after 1570.

sources.contributes: The reference-work summary of the observatories; used for the site records' baseline description.

sources.full: Gudrun Wolfschmidt, 'The Observatories and Instruments of Tycho Brahe', in Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science (2002), pp. 207ff.
sources.contributes: The observatories and instruments as built structures; the architectural description of the two observatories.

sources.label: Dreyer, Tycho Brahe (1890)
sources.full: J. L. E. Dreyer, Tycho Brahe: a picture of scientific life and work in the sixteenth century (Edinburgh, 1890).
sources.contributes: The foundational nineteenth-century life, built directly on the observation journals. The default source for dated observations that fix a presence, and the origin of several datings later corrected.
sources.url_label: full scan at the Internet Archive

sources.label: Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg (1990)
sources.full: Victor E. Thoren, The Lord of Uraniborg: A Biography of Tycho Brahe (Cambridge, 1990). Where a citation gives the scan's page ('scan p.'), it runs 13 ahead of the printed page.
sources.contributes: The standard scholarly biography. The authority on the Wanderjahre route, the instrument-making stops and the exile's negotiations; its chronology is the one most often tested against the others here.

sources.label: Nielsen, Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen (1921)
sources.full: Lauritz Nielsen, 'Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen', Nordisk tidskrift för bok- och biblioteksväsen VIII (1921), pp. 175–214.
sources.contributes: The canonical narrative of the Hven press: its founding, its output and its dispersal, and the dating of the printing house and paper mill.

sources.label: Fučíková, 'The Belvedere in Prague as Tycho Brahe's Musaeum' (2002)
sources.full: Eliška Fučíková, 'The Belvedere in Prague as Tycho Brahe's Musaeum', in Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science (Frankfurt: H. Deutsch, 2002), pp. 276–281.
sources.contributes: Identifies the Prague Belvedere as Tycho's Musaeum — the evidence for the imperial summer palace as his first Prague observing station.

sources.label: Vellev, 'Tycho Brahe's Paper Mill on Hven and Møller Nicolaisen's Excavations, 1933–1934' (2002)
sources.full: Jens Vellev, 'Tycho Brahe's Paper Mill on Hven and N. A. Møller Nicolaisen's Excavations, 1933–1934', in Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science (Frankfurt: H. Deutsch, 2002), pp. 333–355.
sources.contributes: The paper mill and Møller Nicolaisen's excavations of 1933–34 — the archaeological record of the mill.

sources.label: Vellev, 'Et industrianlæg og en votivsten på Hven fra renæssancen' (2017)
sources.full: Jens Vellev, 'Et industrianlæg og en votivsten på Hven fra renæssancen: Om Tycho Brahes papirmølle', Renæssanceforum — Nordic Journal of Renaissance Studies 12 (2017), pp. 107–130.
sources.contributes: Identifies Valentin von Spangenberg as the dam-builder and dates the mill's construction from the meteorological diary and the Christian IV / Kirsten Lindenov letter of 19 March 1590; reconstructs the votive stone's worn inscription.

sources.label: Tycho Brahes Verden (Nationalmuseet, 2006)
sources.full: Poul Grinder-Hansen (ed.), Tycho Brahes Verden: Danmark i Europa 1550–1600 (Copenhagen: Nationalmuseet, 2006).
sources.contributes: The National Museum's exhibition catalogue; the material and architectural context of the establishment, and the education essays.

sources.label: Jern, Uraniborg: herresäte och himlaborg (Lund, 1976)
sources.full: Carl Henrik Jern, Uraniborg: herresäte och himlaborg (Lund: Studentlitteratur, 1976).
sources.contributes: The standard art-historical monograph on Uraniborg as a building: the Venetian-church façade thesis and five appendices translating Tycho's own architectural texts.

sources.label: Ræder, Strömgren & Strömgren, Tycho Brahe's Description of his Instruments (1946)
sources.full: Hans Ræder, Elis Strömgren & Bengt Strömgren (trans.), Tycho Brahe's Description of his Instruments and Scientific Work as given in Astronomiae instauratae mechanica (Wandsbek 1598) (Copenhagen: Royal Danish Academy, 1946). The Appendix gives Tycho's own descriptions of Uraniborg, Stjerneborg and Hven.
sources.contributes: The English Mechanica: Tycho's own description of Uraniborg and Stjerneborg, with the editors' metrology key that converts his cubits and feet.

sources.label: Beckett & Christensen, Uraniborg og Stjærneborg (1921)
sources.full: Francis Beckett (text) & Charles Christensen (measured drawings), Tyge Brahes Uraniborg og Stjærneborg paa Hven (København: Selskabet til Udgivelse af Danske Mindesmærker / London: Oxford University Press, 1921).
sources.contributes: The foundational measured reconstruction of Uraniborg and Stjerneborg — Christensen's drawings are the primary architectural record and supersede the inherited Blaeu print tradition.

sources.label: Becker (ed.), 'Bidrag til Astronomen Tyge Brahes Historie' (Danske Magazin 3. R. IV–V)
sources.full: T. A. Becker (ed.), 'Bidrag til Astronomen Tyge Brahes Historie' — royal letters of 1587 (kongebrev) and 1592 (the Rasmus Pedersen tenant case) bearing on Tycho's administration of Hven; Danske Magazin, 3. Række, IV. Bind pp. 263–264 and V. Bind p. 22.
sources.contributes: The royal letters of 1587 and 1592 on the Hven tenant conflicts — the documented friction behind the loss of the fief.

sources.label: Kancelliets Brevbøger vedr. Danmarks indre Forhold (Rigsarkivet, ed. Laursen)
sources.full: The royal chancery register (Kancelliets Brevbøger vedrørende Danmarks indre Forhold, Rigsarkivet, ed. Laursen), 1551–1660; the Tyge-Brahe/Hven entries 1571–1602 consulted via a page-by-page index; free full volumes at ronlev.dk.
sources.contributes: The royal chancery register — the documentary spine of the fiefs and of the Hven administration. It is also the negative evidence that keeps holdings out of the itinerary: a grant is not a visit.

sources.label: Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (2020)
sources.full: John Robert Christianson, Tycho Brahe and the Measure of the Heavens (London: Reaktion, 2020). Where a citation gives the scan's page ('scan p.'), it runs 5 behind the printed page.
sources.contributes: The modern narrative biography; carries the itinerary at month precision and the Bohemian years in most detail.

sources.label: Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871)
sources.full: F. R. Friis, Tyge Brahe. En historisk Fremstilling efter trykte og utrykte Kilder (Kjøbenhavn, 1871). Citations are printed pages.
sources.contributes: The first documentary Danish life. Supplies the Danish court and chancery context and several route details found nowhere else.

sources.label: Friis, Breve og Aktstykker (1875)
sources.full: F. R. Friis (ed.), Breve og Aktstykker angaænde Tyge Brahe og hans Slægtninge (Kjøbenhavn, 1875).
sources.contributes: Friis's companion edition of the letters and documents; the printed text of several instruments of the fief and family business.
sources.url_label: full scan at the Internet Archive

sources.label: Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning (1970)
sources.full: Wilhelm Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning med nya bidrag belysande hans liv och verk (Lund, 1970).
sources.contributes: The archival corrective. Norlind worked from the journals and the chancery record and refutes a series of Gassendi's and Dreyer's datings; where he and Dreyer disagree on a date, he is followed.

sources.label: Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei Vita (1654/55)
sources.full: Pierre Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei, equitis Dani, astronomorum coryphaei, vita (2nd ed., The Hague: Vlacq, 1655). The headwater of the biographical tradition; cited as the origin of anecdotes, not as a stand-alone factual authority.
sources.contributes: The seventeenth-century vita, headwater of the whole biographical tradition — cited as the origin of an anecdote or a claim, never as stand-alone factual authority; his datings are twice rejected here.
sources.url_label: full scan at the Internet Archive

sources.label: Jönsson, Tycho Brahe: Världsmedborgaren från Ven (2025)
sources.full: Åke Jönsson, Tycho Brahe: Världsmedborgaren från Ven (2025 edition; first published 2004). Citations are printed pages; where one gives the scan's page ('scan p.'), it runs 2 ahead of the printed page.
sources.contributes: The Swedish popular-scholarly life from Ven; useful for the Scanian and island topography and for dates absent elsewhere.

sources.label: Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science (2002)
sources.full: John Robert Christianson et al. (eds.), Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science (Acta Historica Astronomiae 16; Frankfurt: H. Deutsch, 2002).
sources.contributes: The Prague conference volume; the Bohemian sites and the imperial court context.

sources.label: Studnička, Prager Tychoniana (1901)
sources.full: F. J. Studnička, Prager Tychoniana (Prague, 1901).
sources.contributes: The Prague Tychoniana of 1901; the Bohemian manuscripts and the topography of Tycho's Prague.

sources.label: Björklund, Tycho Brahe og Kamarillaen (1992)
sources.full: O. Björklund, Tycho Brahe og Kamarillæn (København, 1992).
sources.contributes: The political analysis of the 1596–97 fall from favour; the sequence of the last Danish winter.

sources.label: Zeeberg, Den praktiske muse (1993)
sources.full: Peter Zeeberg, Den praktiske muse: Tycho Brahes brug af latindigtningen (København: Museum Tusculanum, 1993).
sources.contributes: Tycho's Latin verse as evidence of place: the departure-period poems and the geography they encode.

sources.label: Mosley, Bearing the Heavens (2007)
sources.full: Adam Mosley, Bearing the Heavens: Tycho Brahe and the Astronomical Community of the Late Sixteenth Century (Cambridge, 2007).
sources.contributes: The astronomical community and its correspondence; the reason a correspondent's presence at a place is not inferred from a letter.

sources.label: Gingerich & Westman, The Wittich Connection (1988) / Gingerich, Annotated Census (2002)
sources.full: Owen Gingerich & Robert S. Westman, The Wittich Connection: Conflict and Priority in Late Sixteenth-Century Cosmology (Philadelphia, 1988); Owen Gingerich, An Annotated Census of Copernicus' De revolutionibus (Leiden: Brill, 2002).
sources.contributes: The Wittich connection and the census of De revolutionibus copies — why a book's movement is not its owner's journey.

sources.label: The album-amicorum leaves, in the Graphonomicon
sources.full: The album-amicorum leaves in Tycho's hand, as recorded in the Graphonomicon of Tycho Brahe (Tychoniana, Manus); an earlier hand profile of this edition is superseded by it.
sources.contributes: The album-amicorum series and the education itinerary derived from it; superseded for hand attribution by the Graphonomicon.

sources.label: Graphonomicon of Tycho Brahe (Tychoniana)
sources.full: The Graphonomicon of Tycho Brahe (Tychoniana, Manus): the dated and placed autograph specimens.
sources.contributes: Dated and placed autograph specimens — an album-amicorum leaf signed at a named place on a named day is direct evidence of presence.

sources.label: The Epistolarium's letters spine (Tychoniana)
sources.full: The letters spine of the Tychoniana Epistolarium: every letter with its date and place of writing.
sources.contributes: The letters spine: a letter written at a named place on a named date is presence evidence, and the spine is what makes that datable.

sources.label: The Meteorological Diary 1582–1597 (via the Tychoniana Diarium)
sources.full: Tycho's meteorological diary kept on Hven 1582–1597 (TBOO IX), as modelled in the Tychoniana Diarium.
sources.contributes: Tycho's own meteorological diary, kept on Hven 1582–1597. Its daily entries record his departures and returns and are the only day-level evidence for several short Scanian and Copenhagen absences.

sources.label: The site register of this edition's first version
sources.full: The Hven and Prague site register of this edition's first version (2026), carried forward unchanged beneath the life-geography.
sources.contributes: The predecessor store — the Hven and Prague site layer, carried forward unchanged beneath the life-geography.

sources.label: Christianson, 'Tycho Brahe's Facts of Life' (1970)
sources.full: John Robert Christianson, 'Tycho Brahe's Facts of Life', Fund og Forskning 17 (1970), pp. 21–28.
sources.contributes: The authority on the birth and family data, from Tycho's own lost self-horoscope as transmitted by Stephanius; the source of the birth hour and of the Stephanius itinerary notes.

sources.label: Håkansson (ed.), Att låta själen flyga (2006)
sources.full: Håkan Håkansson (ed.), Att låta själen flyga mellan himlens tinnar: Tycho Brahe och renässansen (Stockholm: Atlantis, 2006).
sources.contributes: The Swedish essay collection; the intellectual-history reading of the Rostock and Basel years and of the Paracelsian connections.

sources.label: Morsing, Den ukendte Tycho Brahe (2003)
sources.full: Ole Morsing, Den ukendte Tycho Brahe (2003).
sources.contributes: A revisionist Danish reading of Tycho's career; used for context, never for a date.

sources.label: Ellefsen, Søsteren og astronomen (2023)
sources.full: Trine A. Ellefsen, Søsteren og astronomen: På sporet av Sophie Brahe (Oslo: Humanist forlag, 2023).
sources.contributes: Sophie Brahe's life; the family stations in Scania and the sibling circle around Knutstorp and Herrevad.

sources.label: The edition's register of refuted claims (unpublished)
sources.full: The register of claims about Tycho that research has overturned, kept by this edition; consulted before every verdict in the phantom register so that a refutation is stated once. Not yet published.
sources.contributes: The standing register of overturned claims, consulted before every phantom-register verdict so a refutation is stated once and not re-derived.

sources.label: The editor's research files (unpublished)
sources.full: The editor's unpublished research files; each evidence note that draws on one says so.
sources.contributes: Unpublished working papers of this project; each evidence note names the dossier it draws on.
